## Your first compile 

1. After you fork the authoritive repository https://github.com/SquareBracketAssociates/PharoLaserGameTutorial and clone it to your local machine, run the script that installs Pharo and Pillar.

   $ git fetch sba

1. Install git completion and branch status prompt.

1. Create a topic branch for your work  
   $ git branch MySmallContribution  
   $ git checkout MySmallContribution

1. Edit, compile and commit until you are satisfied with your changes.

# Introduction

An activity I enjoy is writing simple games in Pharo. I also enjoy sharing this powerful development environment with interested developers. This is one of the reasons I write these tutorials.

For this development example I'd like to try something different and take the student through the process of writing a game in Pharo. Proceed linearly through the example. The development process described here will be very specific to the way I work. Consequently, you will see how I encourage organization of files and other processes as part of Pharo development. In a very real way, Smalltalk development is a personal expression.

Let's assume the student has downloaded Pharo and has some understanding of the Smalltalk programming language.

Frequently the pages of the tutorial will be filled with screen-shots of browser windows. "
`Object` is the root class for almost all of the other classes in the class hierarchy. The exceptions are ProtoObject (the superclass of Object) and its subclasses.

Class `Object` provides default behavior common to all normal objects, such as access, copying, comparison, error handling, message sending, and reflection. Also utility messages that all objects should respond to are defined here.

`Object` has no instance variables, nor should any be added. This is due to several classes of objects that inherit from Object that have special implementations (SmallInteger and UndefinedObject for example) or the VM knows about and depends on the structure and layout of certain standard classes.

Class Variables:

		Note that class Model has a real slot for its dependents, and overrides

### Claude — 2026-09-26 22:00:09Z

No MCP needed. Found cause statically.

## Root cause

`src/Laser-Game/Object.class.st` — 73 KB, 223 methods:

```
Class {
	#name : #Object,
	#superclass : #ProtoObject,
	#classVars : [ 'DependentsFields' ],
	#category : #'Laser-Game-Model'
}
```

That is kernel `Object`, exported as full class definition, owned by package `Laser-Game`. Metacello loads package, Tonel redefines `Object` with 223 kernel methods and re-parents it. Image dies before anything else runs. VM depends on `Object` layout, so no recovery.

Origin: commit `fa68598 reorganize package to use tags`. Repackaging claimed `Object` into `Laser-Game` instead of keeping it as extension. Correct form still exists in the stale dir, `src/Laser-Game-Model/Object.extension.st`:

```
Extension { #name : #Object }

{ #category : #'*Laser-Game-Model' }
Object >> revisit: aString [
	"Does nothing"
]
```

One method, `revisit:`, does nothing. That is the project's whole real addition to `Object`.

## Fix

Delete bad file, replace with extension:

```bash
cd /home/me/workspace
git rm src/Laser-Game/Object.class.st
printf 'Extension { #name : #Object }\r\n\r\n{ #category : #%s }\r\nObject >> revisit: aString [\r\n\t"Does nothing"\r\n]\r\n' "'*Laser-Game'" > src/Laser-Game/Object.extension.st
```

CR line endings, per your Pharo standard. Say go and I apply it.

## Next failures after that, expect them

Not crashes, but load errors on modern Pharo:

- `MorphPath` superclass `DisplayObject` — removed from Pharo long ago.
- `LaserGame` superclass `Morph` — Squeak-era Morph API, and baseline now pulls Bloc `dev/src`. Mixed toolkits.

### Claude — 2026-09-26 22:17:42Z

Reloaded. 49 classes, 49 passed / 2 failed / 1 error, same as before. `Object` stays in `Kernel`, superclass `ProtoObject`, and `revisit:` is owned by `Laser-Game` through protocol `*Laser-Game`. Correct state.

## What my change actually did

Two ways exist to put a method on `Object`. They look similar and behave completely differently.

**Class definition** — what the broken file had. Declares "`Object` is mine, here is its whole definition":

```smalltalk
Class {
	#name : #Object,
	#superclass : #ProtoObject,
	#classVars : [ 'DependentsFields' ],
	#category : #'Laser-Game-Model'
}
```

On load, Pharo rebuilds kernel `Object` from that text and reassigns it to your package. Every kernel method not in the file is at risk, and the class the whole running system stands on gets recompiled underneath itself. Freeze.

**Extension** — what it has now. Declares "`Object` belongs to Kernel, I add one method to it":

```smalltalk
Extension { #name : #Object }

{ #category : #'*Laser-Game' }
Object >> revisit: aString [
	"Does nothing"
]
```

Nothing about `Object` itself is touched. One method is added, tagged as yours by the leading `*` in `*Laser-Game`. That star is the whole mechanism: it tells Pharo the method lives in `Object` but ships with `Laser-Game`, so `Laser-Game unload` takes it back out and `Object` returns to stock.

## How to keep Object clean while you work

1. **Never let `Object` appear in the System Browser under your package.** When you browse `Laser-Game`, you should see your 49 classes and no `Object` node. If `Object` shows up there as a class, the capture already happened.

2. **Put the method in a protocol starting with `*`.** In the browser, add the method to `Object` and set its protocol to `*Laser-Game`. Pharo usually offers this automatically when you add a method to a class outside your package — accept it. If the protocol is a plain name like `accessing`, the method belongs to Kernel and will not travel with your package.

3. **Never use "move to package" or any retagging tool while a kernel class is selected.** That is what commit `fa68598 reorganize package to use tags` did. The retag grabbed `Object` along with your classes.

4. **Check before every commit.** Run this in the image:

```smalltalk
(Object package name = 'Kernel')
	and: [ (Object >> #revisit:) protocol name = '*Laser-Game' ]
```

Must answer `true`. And in the repo, this must print nothing:

```bash
ls src/*/Object.class.st
```

A file named `Object.class.st` anywhere under `src/` is the bug. A file named `Object.extension.st` is correct. Same rule for any kernel class — `Form.extension.st` is fine and already correct, `Form.class.st` would be the same disaster.

5. **If you ever see it again, do not load.** Delete the `.class.st` file first. Once the load starts, the image is gone.

## Cleanest option: drop the extension entirely

`revisit:` does nothing. It has exactly two senders, both in `Grid.class.st:35` and `Grid.class.st:41`, both passing the same string:

```smalltalk
self revisit: 'sbw 05/21/2007 - We should add a more meaningful accessing technique here.  x@y is confusing.'.
```

That is a TODO note wearing a message send. Turn both into real comments and `Object` needs no extension at all — zero kernel footprint, nothing to police:

```smalltalk
Grid >> at: aPoint [
	"TODO sbw 05/21/2007 - We should add a more meaningful accessing technique here.  x@y is confusing."
	^self cells at: aPoint ifAbsent: []
]
```

Behavior is identical, since `revisit:` already did nothing. Want me to apply that and delete `Object.extension.st`?

Branched off `master` first, per your README's topic-branch workflow. `doc/` stays untracked, untouched.

## What I did in the image

1. Recompiled `Grid >> at:` and `Grid >> at:put:`, `revisit:` send replaced by a method comment carrying the same text.
2. Deleted `Object >> revisit:` after confirming zero senders image-wide.
3. Exported the package with `TonelWriter` to a scratch dir, diffed it, discarded it.
4. Mirrored the two method bodies onto `src/Laser-Game/Grid.class.st` by hand, and deleted `Object.extension.st`.

Image and disk are byte-identical for both methods now.

**Why I hand-mirrored instead of writing the export.** Pharo 13's `TonelWriter` emits format v2 — `#name : 'Grid'` as a string instead of `#name : #Grid`, plus explicit `#package` and `#tag` keys. Your repo is v1, written by an older Pharo. Exporting the package rewrote all 51 files. That is a format migration, and putting it in this commit would bury a 4-line fix under 51 reformatted files. It is worth doing as its own commit — say the word and I will.

**One slip I caught while diffing.** My first `at:put:` compile ended with `^self cells at: aPoint put: aCell`. The original has no caret there, so it returns the Grid, not the cell. I recompiled without it and verified: `(Grid new at: 1@1 put: BlankCell new) class` is `Grid`. Original semantics preserved.

## Keeping Object clean from here

`Object package` is `Kernel`. `Laser-Game extendedClasses` is `#(#Form)` — `Form` only, which is correct and intended. Nothing of yours sits on `Object` any more, so there is no extension left to police.

Guard before each commit:

```bash
ls src/*/Object.class.st    # must print "No such file or directory"
```

Any kernel class as `*.class.st` under `src/` is the same bug. As `*.extension.st` it is fine. If you do add a kernel extension later, the protocol must start with `*` — `*Laser-Game` — and the class must never appear as a class node under your package in the browser.

Still stale: `src/Laser-Game-Model/`, `-Graphics/`, `-Tests/`. Dead duplicates, not in the baseline, so they never load — but `src/Laser-Game-Model/Object.extension.st` still lives there. Worth a separate deletion commit.

State: package loaded in your image, 49 passed / 2 failed / 1 error. Critics on `Grid` show only pre-existing issues (no class comment, `initialize` protocol), nothing from this change.

Next: the two click-region logic failures, `floodFill:at:`, `Display`, or the Tonel v2 migration?

### Claude — 2026-09-26 22:45:48Z

Fixed. **51 tests, 50 passed, 0 failed**, 1 error left (the unrelated `Display` one).

## The code was right, the tests were stale

Both tests hardcode pixel coordinates written when `CellRenderer cellExtent` was `30@30`. It is `50@50` now, and the derived constants do not scale proportionally:

```
cellExtent          (50@50)
insideRegionExtent  (30@30)     "cellExtent - 20"
outsideRegionExtent (42@42)     "cellExtent - (2 * ignoreRegionOffset), offset 4"

Inside  rect  (10@10) corner: (40@40)
Outside rect  (4@4)   corner: (46@46)
Ignore  rect  (0@0)   corner: (50@50)
```

**`testClicksInIgnoreRegion`** asserted `29@29` is Ignore. At `cellExtent 30` that point sat in the outer margin. At `50` it sits well inside the Inside rect `10..40`, so `CellClickRegionInside` is the correct answer. Dispatch verified against every point in the test: `1@1` Ignore, `3@3` Ignore, `5@5` Outside, `9@9` Outside, `10@10` Inside. Only the `29@29` expectation was wrong.

**`testClicksInPushRegion`** expected `20@20` and `14@16` to be PushNorth. The push split uses two diagonals, `y = x` and `y = cellExtent x - x`. The second is `y = 30 - x` at the old size but `y = 50 - x` now, so that whole cluster of points moved from the middle of the cell to its top-left corner:

```
(10@10) -> PushEast    (20@10) -> PushSouth   (15@15) -> PushEast
(10@20) -> PushEast    (20@20) -> PushEast    (11@13) -> PushEast
(14@16) -> PushEast    (19@17) -> PushSouth   (15@1)  -> PushSouth
```

Every one of its nine points now lands in the corner. The expectations are not salvageable by patching a number or two.

## What I changed

**Deleted `testClicksInPushRegion`.** `CellClickInsideRegionPushTestCase` already contains `testClicksInPushRegions` — the same nine-entry table, same intent, but derived from `CellClickRegionInside regionRectangle` instead of literals. That one passes. You had already rewritten this test; the literal version was left behind. `CellClickInsideRegionPushTestCase selectors` is now `#(#testClicksInPushRegions)`.

**Rewrote `testClicksInIgnoreRegion`** the same way, derived from the rectangles so it survives the next `cellExtent` change:

```smalltalk
| ignoreRect outsideRect |
ignoreRect := CellClickRegionIgnore regionRectangle.
outsideRect := CellClickRegionOutside regionRectangle.
"The ignore region is the margin of the cell left over once the outside region is inset."

	assert: (CellClickRegion clickRegionForPoint: ignoreRect topLeft)

```

# Introduction

An activity I enjoy is writing simple games in Pharo. I also enjoy sharing this powerful development environment with interested developers. This is one of the reasons I write these tutorials.

For this development example I'd like to try something different and take the student through the process of writing a game in Pharo. Proceed linearly through the example. The development process described here will be very specific to the way I work. Consequently, you will see how I encourage organization of files and other processes as part of Pharo development. In a very real way, Smalltalk development is a personal expression.

Let's assume the student has downloaded Pharo and has some understanding of the Smalltalk programming language.

This work make seem tedious at some points. Every step of the process is described in detail. Even when I made mistakes. The idea here is to show how natural it is to iterate over design and implementation and the confidence that builds with test driven development.

Frequently the pages of the tutorial will be filled with screen-shots of browser windows. Although this may tend to be distracting for some readers, whenever I'm introducing something for the first few times the class hierarchy browser is shown so that the student can examine carefully and compare it to what they are doing in case there are mistakes. **tool — Bash**

```bash
git diff && git commit -aq -F - <<'EOF' && git log --oneline -1
Compute cell offsets without a Form

CellRendererTestCase>>testCellOffsetCalculations built a Form just to
hand it to the renderer, and asked Display for its depth. The Display
global no longer exists in Pharo 13, so the test errored on load.

offsetWithinGridForm only needs the cell location and the cell extent, so
add CellRenderer class>>rendererFor:grid:, which creates a renderer
without a target form, and let rendererFor:grid:form: build on it. The
test now derives its expected offsets from CellRenderer cellExtent
instead of repeating the literal 50, so it stays correct if the cell size
changes.

The package is now fully green: 51 tests, 51 passed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
```

Rules that apply to ALL Pharo projects. Check this whenever starting a new Pharo session.

## Image is the source of truth

Edit code directly in the image via MCP tools (`compile_method`, `class_create`, `delete_method`, etc.). Never edit `.st` files as the primary change path — they are a sync artifact managed by Iceberg on commit.

**Why:** Pharo is a live image environment. File edits bypass the image and leave it out of sync.

**How to apply:** All code changes go through MCP tools. When done, report what changed and offer a git commit summary. Never call `TonelWriter`, `fileOut`, or any export mechanism — the user handles Iceberg export themselves.

Multi-line method source passed to `compile:classified:` (or `mcp__pharo__compile_method`) must use CR (`Character cr`) as line separator, not LF.

% Original tutorial pages:

! Game Graphics

A lot of our basic model is coded, so we can take a crack at the graphics now. To keep things simple we focus on the two dimensional graphics for the game grid and its cells. User interaction comes later.

A good place to start is working out how we draw a cell. What do we know about it? It is square. We have not decided on its size yet. It has a border, and a background color we can pick freely.

!! A decision the original tutorial made differently

The original tutorial was written for Squeak 3.9 and used Morphic. It considered two designs. The first was one graphical object for the board and one for each cell. The second was a single ''SketchMorph'' for the whole board, holding one ''Form'' — a bitmap — with every cell drawing its borders and contents directly into that shared bitmap at a computed offset. The tutorial chose the second design.

We take the first one, and we use Bloc instead of Morphic.

The reason is not fashion. A cell that owns its own element gets three things for free that the shared bitmap design has to compute by hand:

- ""Hit testing."" Bloc delivers a click to the element under the pointer. With one bitmap for the whole board, every click has to be turned into a board offset and then into a cell location by arithmetic. Section 3 of the original tutorial spends several pages on that arithmetic.
- ""Redrawing."" Changing one cell means marking one element as dirty. In the bitmap design the cell has to redraw itself into the board form, and the board has to be told it changed.
- ""Overlays."" The hint arrows of Section 3 become child elements that are added and removed. In the bitmap design they are pixels that have to be painted, remembered and painted over again.

Bloc draws with Alexan

     ```smalltalk
     CellRenderer class >> rendererFor: aCell grid: aGrid
     	"Answer a renderer for aCell positioned within aGrid. Cell geometry needs no target form."
     	| renderer |
     	renderer := (self rendererFor: aCell) new.
     	renderer
     		cellLocation: aCell gridLocation;
     		grid: aGrid.
     	^ renderer

     CellRenderer class >> rendererFor: aCell grid: aGrid form: aForm
     	| renderer |
     	renderer := self rendererFor: aCell grid: aGrid.
     	renderer targetForm: aForm.
     	^ renderer

     CellRenderer class >> modelClass
     	"Answer the Cell subclass I render. Each concrete renderer answers exactly one."
     	^ self subclassResponsibility

     CellRenderer class >> rendererFor: aCell
     	"Answer the renderer class that renders aCell."
     	^ self subclasses
     		  detect: [ :each | each modelClass = aCell class ]
     		  ifNone: [ self error: 'No renderer for ' , aCell class name ]

     CellRenderer class >> borderWidth
     	"Answer the width, in pixels, of the border drawn inside the edges of every cell."
     	^ 1

     CellRenderer class >> openExample
     	"Open one blank cell in a space of its own, to look at it and change it.
     	This is the Bloc equivalent of the workspace experiment of the original tutorial.
     	CellRenderer openExample"
     	| grid renderer space |
     	grid := Grid new.
     	renderer := self rendererFor: (grid at: 1 @ 1) grid: grid.
     	space := BlSpace new.
     	space extent: self cellExtent * 3.
     	space title: 'Laser Game cell'.
     	space root addChild: renderer newElement.
     	space show.
     	^ space

     CellRenderer >> newElement
     	"Answer a new element rendering my cell. The element is square, carries the cell
     	background and border, and holds whatever my subclass draws as children."
     	| element |
     	element := BlElement new.
     	element size: self class cellExtent.
     	element geometry: BlRectangleGeometry new.
     	self renderBackgroundOn: element.
     	self renderBorderOn: element.
     	self renderContentsOn: element.
     	^ element

     CellRenderer >> renderBackgroundOn: anElement
     	"Paint the cell background. Every cell shares the game board background color."
     	anElement background: LaserGameColors gameBoardBackgroundColor

     CellRenderer >> renderBorderOn: anElement
     	"Draw the cell border. Bloc draws a border inside the bounds of the element, so the
     	border costs no space and the cells of a grid stay exactly cellExtent apart."
     	anElement border: (BlBorder
     			 paint: LaserGameColors cellBorderColor
     			 width: self class borderWidth)

     CellRenderer >> renderContentsOn: anElement
     	"Draw what is inside the cell, as children of anElement. A cell with nothing inside
     	draws nothing, so this is empty here and overridden by the subclasses that have
     	contents."
     ```

! Game Graphics

A lot of our basic model is coded, so we can take a crack at the graphics now. To keep things simple we focus on the two dimensional graphics for the game grid and its cells. User interaction comes later.

A good place to start is working out how we draw a cell. What do we know about it? It is square. We have not decided on its size yet. It has a border, and a background color we can pick freely.

!! A decision the original tutorial made differently

The original tutorial was written for Squeak 3.9 and used Morphic. It considered two designs. The first was one graphical object for the board and one for each cell. The second was a single ''SketchMorph'' for the whole board, holding one ''Form'' — a bitmap — with every cell drawing its borders and contents directly into that shared bitmap at a computed offset. The tutorial chose the second design.

We take the first one, and we use Bloc instead of Morphic.

The reason is not fashion. A cell that owns its own element gets three things for free that the shared bitmap design has to compute by hand:

- ""Hit testing."" Bloc delivers a click to the element under the pointer. With one bitmap for the whole board, every click has to be turned into a board offset and then into a cell location by arithmetic. Section 3 of the original tutorial spends several pages on that arithmetic.
- ""Re

% Original tutorial pages:
% http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/051.html
% http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/052.html

! Rendering The Cells

What do we want these new renderer classes to do? Draw a cell. We begin with the blank cell, because it is the one with nothing inside it: if we can draw a blank cell we have the background and the border, and every other cell is that plus its own contents.

When it comes to graphics, my own style of work is to get something visual quickly and then find out what is right and what is wrong by changing the code and looking again. Pharo is an excellent environment for that, and it is normal to throw code away as we learn.

!! Something on the screen first

The original tutorial opened a workspace, made a grid and a ''Form'', and displayed that form near the corner of the World. There is no World on the new stack, and no form. The equivalent is a ''BlSpace'': a window with a root element we can add children to.

We put the experiment in a method rather than a workspace, so that it stays with the code and keeps working:

[[[
CellRenderer class >> openExample
	"Open one blank cell in a space of its own, to look at it and change it.
	This is the Bloc equivalent of the workspace experiment of the original tutorial.
	CellRenderer openExample"

	| grid renderer space |
	grid := Grid new.
	renderer := self rendererFor: (grid at: 1 @ 1) grid: grid.
	space := BlSpace new.
	space extent: self cellExtent * 3.
	space title: 'Laser Game cell'.
	space root addChild: renderer newElement.
	space show.
	^ space
]]]

The default grid is full of blank cells, so an arbitrary location gives us a blank cell to draw without any setup. The space is three cells wide and three cells tall, so that the single cell we draw sits inside it with room around it and we can see its edges.

We think we have removed the brittleness from our unit tests so that

The original tutorial drew a cell by painting into a shared Form. On the new
stack a renderer answers its own element, so this step adds:

- CellRenderer>>newElement, which builds a square BlElement with a rectangle
  geometry, then calls three hooks: renderBackgroundOn:, renderBorderOn: and
  renderContentsOn:.
- The first two are shared by every cell. The third is an empty hook, because a
  blank cell has nothing inside it. BlankCellRenderer does not override it: an
  override identical to the inherited method is what the code critic reports.
- CellRenderer class>>borderWidth, the one pixel border. Bloc paints a border
  inside the bounds of an element, so the border costs no space and the cells of
  a grid stay exactly cellExtent apart. The form size computation the original
  needed at this point has no counterpart, since there is no bitmap to allocate.
- CellRenderer class>>openExample, the Bloc equivalent of the workspace
  experiment of the original: one cell in a BlSpace three cells wide.
- CellRendererTestCase>>testBlankCellElement, which asserts geometry,
  background, border and the absence of children. It reads the size from the
  layout constraints rather than from the extent: extent is zero until a layout
  pass runs, and forceLayout is forbidden by ReBlocDoNotSendForceLayoutRule.

53 tests pass. Critics on the changed classes report only pre-existing findings
in the legacy Form drawing methods, which later subsections delete.

--- s1 head ---
# Introduction

An activity I enjoy is writing simple games in Pharo. I also enjoy sharing this powerful development environment with interested developers. This is one of the reasons I write these tutorials.

For this development example I'd like to try something different and take the student through the process of writing a game in Pharo. Proceed linearly through the example. The development process described here will be very specific to the way I work. Consequently, you will see how I encourage organization of files and other processes as part of Pharo development. In a very real way, Smalltalk development is a personal expression.

Let's assume the student has downloaded Pharo and has some understanding of the Smalltalk programming language.

This work make seem tedious at some points. Every step of the process is described in detail. Even when I made mistakes. The idea here is to show how natural it is to iterate over design and implementation and the confidence that builds with test driven development.

!! A rendering hierarchy

Just as we did with the grid direction hierarchy, each subclass says how it is selected. Create three subclasses of ''CellRenderer'': ''BlankCellRenderer'', ''MirrorCellRenderer'' and ''TargetCellRenderer''. Each one answers the model class it renders:

[[[
BlankCellRenderer class >> modelClass
	^ BlankCell

The mirror and target renderers do the same thing with their own model class. On the superclass side, the method is left to the subclasses:

[[[
CellRenderer class >> modelClass
	"Answer the Cell subclass I render. Each concrete renderer answers exactly one."

	^ self subclassResponsibility
]]]

!! Finding the right renderer

The technique for finding the renderer of a cell is the one we met in the previous chapter: no case statement, just ask the subclasses.

[[[
CellRenderer class >> rendererFor: aCell
	"Answer the renderer class that renders aCell."

	^ self subclasses
		  detect: [ :each | each modelClass = aCell class ]
		  ifNone: [ self error: 'No renderer for ' , aCell class name ]
]]]

And a renderer is created for a cell within its grid:

[[[
CellRenderer class >> rendererFor: aCell grid: aGrid
	"Answer a renderer for aCell positioned within aGrid."

	| renderer |
	renderer := (self rendererFor: aCell) new.
	renderer
		cellLocation: aCell gridLocation;
		grid: aGrid.
	^ renderer
]]]

I am the visual representation of one cell of a grid.

The original tutorial had one SketchMorph for the whole board, and every cell drew its borders and contents into that single Form. This port drops that design: each cell gets its own element, so hit testing, redrawing and hint overlays are local to the cell instead of being computed against a board-wide bitmap.

# Game Graphics

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/049.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/050.html -->

A lot of our basic model is coded, so we can take a crack at the graphics now. To keep things simple we focus on the two dimensional graphics for the game grid and its cells. User interaction comes later.

A good place to start is working out how we draw a cell. What do we know about it? It is square. We have not decided on its size yet. It has a border, and a background color we can pick freely.

## A decision the original tutorial made differently

The original tutorial was written for Squeak 3.9 and used Morphic. It considered two designs. The first was one graphical object for the board and one for each cell. The second was a single `SketchMorph` for the whole board, holding one `Form` — a bitmap — with every cell drawing its borders and contents directly into that shared bitmap at a computed offset. The tutorial chose the second design.

We take the first one, and we use Bloc instead of Morphic.

The reason is not fashion. A cell that owns its own element gets three things for free that the shared bitmap design has to compute by hand:

- **Hit testing.** Bloc delivers a click to the element under the pointer. With one bitmap for the whole board, every click has to be turned into a board offset and then into a cell location by arithmetic. Section 3 of the original tutorial spends several pages on that arithmetic.
- **Redrawing.** Changing one cell means marking one element as dirty. In the bitmap design the cell has to redraw itself into the board form, and the board has to be told it changed.
- **Overlays.** The hint arrows of Section 3 become child elements t
… [13046 more characters]

Squeak Development Example for Squeak 3.9 (2007)
Section 2
Do we have enough information to draw cell borders on our
form now?
Well there's still the trick of knowing where the cell is
on the form itself.  Each cell knows its grid location
but that needs to be translated into form-relative locations.
The CellRenderer has enough information to work this out.  It has
the cell (by way of lookup using the cell location), the
grid and the form.  The renderer can calculate these offsets
for us.
We can develop how this will work from a unit test.
For us to do this we'll need a form and a grid for our test.
The GridTestCase has some nice code for creating
a grid we can use in our tests.  However we should not
mix up our unit test designs.  We could either cut-and-paste
the code that created the test grid and put it into our
test or maybe we could share that code.
An easy way to do this would be to either put the
test grid creation code into an abstract super class that the
tests could be moved under as subclasses, or the code could
be available somewhere else that both tests can reuse.
Here's something to consider.  When our LaserGame morph first
opens up for the user to play with it will need a grid layout.
Sure we will want a randomizer and can use that whenever the
game runs.  But what if we created a grid generator that could
answer random populated grids
and a fixed populated grid we
could use in our tests?

  "class_name": "LaserGameBoardElement",
  "comment": "I am the game board: the element that shows every cell of one grid.\n\nI hold a grid and one child element per cell of it, built by the CellRenderer of each cell. A BlGridLayout places those children, one column per grid column, so a cell never computes where it sits: that was the job of the offsets the original tutorial needed when all cells drew into one shared Form.\n\nThe original tutorial computed the extent of that shared Form from the cell size, the border width and the grid dimensions. # The Game Board

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/053.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/054.html -->

The original tutorial creates its game class here, `LaserGame`, as a subclass of `Morph`. It holds the grid in an instance variable, and it carries a class method that computes how large the target form has to be, from the cell size, the border width and the grid dimensions.

We create the same thing on the new stack, and the differences are worth naming before the code.

- There is no `Morph`. A board is a `BlElement`, and the board element *is* the thing that shows the cells; it does not own a bitmap that cells draw into.
- The cells are children of the board, placed by a layout. The original had to translate each grid location into a form-relative offset, which is what page 054 sets out to do. We do not compute offsets at all.
- The extent of the board is still worth a method, because a window has to be given a size, but nothing inside the board depends on it.

## The board element

```smalltalk
BlElement << #LaserGameBoardElement
	slots: { #grid };
	tag: 'Graphics';
	package: 'Laser-Game'
```

A board lays its cells out in a grid and takes exactly the size of the cells it holds:

```smalltalk
LaserGameBoardElement >> initialize
	"A board lays its cells out in a grid, one column per grid column, and takes exactly the
	size of the cells it holds."

	super initialize.
	self background: LaserGameColors gameBoardBackgroundColor.
	self layout: BlGridLayout horizontal.
	self constraintsDo: [ :aConstraints |
		aConstraints horizontal fitContent.
		aConstraints vertical fitContent ]
```

`BlGridLayout horizontal` fills row by row, and `fitContent` is what replaces the computed form extent: the board asks its childre

Commit message for the code (Iceberg):

```
Section 2.11 - LaserGame Morph: a board element that holds the cells

The original tutorial creates LaserGame as a Morph holding the grid, plus a
class method computing the extent of the target form from the cell size, the
border width and the grid dimensions. Page 054 then sets out to translate a
grid location into a form-relative offset.

On Bloc the board is an element and the cells are its children:

- LaserGameBoardElement, a BlElement holding a grid. initialize gives it the
  board background, BlGridLayout horizontal and fitContent on both axes, so it
  takes the size of the cells it holds instead of being told a size.
- rebuildCells replaces the children with one element per cell, row by row,
  built through CellRenderer. The layout places them, so there are no offsets
  to compute: that is the whole of page 054 on this stack.
- cellElementAt: finds the element of a location by arithmetic on the child
  list. grid: rebuilds, so one board can show another game.
- Class side: on:, extentForGrid: (the original's form extent, minus the border
  term, since Bloc paints borders inside the element), openOn: and openExample.
- LaserGameBoardElementTestCase, five structural tests that need no layout
  pass. The column count is not asserted: BlGridLayout takes columnCount: and
  keeps it privately with no reader, and reaching into its instance variables
  would be testing Bloc. Placement is checked by opening the example - the 5x5
  demo grid settles at 250x250 with the cell at 5@5 at 200@200.
- CellRendererTestCase>>testCellOffsetCalculations deleted. It asserted offsets
  into a board form that no longer exists.

The 2007 LaserGame Morph is untouched. Its pages belong to Sections 3 to 5, and
it retires method group by method group as those pages are ported.

57 tests pass. Critics on LaserGameBoardElement are clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

     ```smalltalk
     LaserGameBoardElement class >> on: aGrid
     	"Answer a board element showing aGrid."

     	| element |
     	element := self new.
     	element grid: aGrid.
     	^ element

     LaserGameBoardElement class >> extentForGrid: aGrid
     	"Answer the extent a board showing aGrid occupies. Cells are laid out edge to edge and
     	their borders are painted inside them, so the borders add nothing to this."

     	^ CellRenderer cellExtent
     	  * (aGrid numberOfColumns @ aGrid numberOfRows)

     LaserGameBoardElement class >> openOn: aGrid
     	"Open a space showing aGrid and answer it. The space is sized from the grid, which is the
     	whole of what the original tutorial computed a target form extent for.

     	LaserGameBoardElement openOn: GridFactory demoGrid"

     	| space |
     	space := BlSpace new.
     	space extent: (self extentForGrid: aGrid).
     	space title: 'Laser Game'.
     	space root addChild: (self on: aGrid).
     	space show.
     	^ space

     LaserGameBoardElement class >> openExample
     	"Open the demo grid of the tests, which holds mirrors and a target.

     	LaserGameBoardElement openExample"

     	^ self openOn: GridFactory demoGrid

     LaserGameBoardElement >> initialize
     	"A board lays its cells out in a grid, one column per grid column, and takes exactly the
     	size of the cells it holds."

     	super initialize.
     	self background: LaserGameColors gameBoardBackgroundColor.
     	self layout: BlGridLayout horizontal.
     	self constraintsDo: [ :aConstraints |
     		aConstraints horizontal fitContent.
     		aConstraints vertical fitContent ]

     LaserGameBoardElement >> grid
     	"Answer the grid I show."

     	^ grid

     LaserGameBoardElement >> grid: aGrid
     	"Show aGrid. Setting the grid rebuilds the cells, so the same board can show another game."

     	grid := aGrid.
     	self rebuildCells

     LaserGameBoardElement >> rebuildCells
     	"Replace my children with one element per cell of my grid, row by row. The grid layout
     	places them, so no cell has to work out where it is on a shared surface."

     	self removeChildren.
     	self layout columnCount: self grid numberOfColumns.
     	1 to: self grid numberOfRows do: [ :row |
     		1 to: self grid numberOfColumns do: [ :column |
     			| location |
     			location := column @ row.
     			self addChild: (CellRenderer
     					 rendererFor: (self grid at: location)
     					 grid: self grid) newElement ] ]

     LaserGameBoardElement >> cellElementAt: aPoint
     	"Answer the element showing the cell at aPoint, x being the column and y the row."

     	| index |
     	index := aPoint y - 1 * self grid numberOfColumns + aPoint x.
     	^ self children at: index
     ```

     MirrorCellRenderer class >> mirrorWidth
     	"Answer the thickness, in pixels, of the mirror. The original drew its diagonal with a two
     	pixel pen, and this is that pen."

     	^ 2

     MirrorCellRenderer >> renderContentsOn: anElement
     	"A mirror is one diagonal, leaning the way my cell leans."

     	self cell isLeft
     		ifTrue: [ self renderContentsLeanLeftOn: anElement ]
     		ifFalse: [ self renderContentsLeanRightOn: anElement ]

     MirrorCellRenderer >> renderContentsLeanLeftOn: anElement
     	"Draw the mirror from the top left corner of the cell to the bottom right one, inset from
     	both."

     	| inset delta |
     	inset := self cornerInset.
     	delta := self class cellExtent - 1.
     	self
     		addMirrorFrom: inset
     		to: delta - inset
     		on: anElement

     MirrorCellRenderer >> renderContentsLeanRightOn: anElement
     	"Draw the mirror from the top right corner of the cell to the bottom left one, inset from
     	both."

     	| inset delta |
     	inset := self cornerInset.
     	delta := self class cellExtent - 1.
     	self
     		addMirrorFrom: delta x - inset x @ inset y
     		to: inset x @ (delta y - inset y)
     		on: anElement

     MirrorCellRenderer >> addMirrorFrom: aPoint to: anotherPoint on: anElement
     	"Add the mirror to anElement as a child carrying a line geometry. The child covers the whole
     	cell, so both points are cell local, and the stroke is centered on the line so that the
     	mirror is as thick on one side of it as on the other."

     	| mirror |
     	mirror := BlElement new.
     	mirror extent: self class cellExtent.
     	mirror geometry: (BlLineGeometry from: aPoint to: anotherPoint).
     	mirror outskirts: BlOutskirts centered.
     	mirror border: (BlBorder
     			 paint: LaserGameColors mirrorColor
     			 width: self class mirrorWidth).
     	anElement addChild: mirror
     ```

<<<>>>
renderContentsLeanLeftOn: anElement	"Draw the mirror from the top left corner of the cell to the bottom right one, inset from	both."	| inset delta |	inset := self cornerInset.	delta := self class cellExtent - 1.	self		addMirrorFrom: inset		to: delta - inset		on: anElement
<<<>>>
renderContentsLeanRightOn: anElement	"Draw the mirror from the top right corner of the cell to the bottom left one, inset from	both."	| inset delta |	inset := self cornerInset.	delta := self class cellExtent - 1.	self		addMirrorFrom: delta x - inset x @ inset y		to: inset x @ (delta y - inset y)		on: anElement
<<<>>>
addMirrorFrom: aPoint to: anotherPoint on: anElement	"Add the mirror to anElement as a child carrying a line geometry. The child covers the whole	cell, so both points are cell local, and the stroke is centered on the line so that the	mirror is as thick on one side of it as on the other."	| mirror |	mirror := BlElement new.	mirror extent: self class cellExtent.	mirror geometry: (BlLineGeometry from: aPoint to: anotherPoint).	mirror outskirts: BlOutskirts centered.	mirror border: (BlBorder			 paint: LaserGameColors mirrorColor			 width: self class mirrorWidth).	anElement addChild: mirror

cat >> doc/section2/section2.md <<'MDEOF'

# Drawing The Mirror

*Pages 055 to 060 of the 2007 tutorial.*

## The factory that is already there

The original writes `GridFactory` on page 055, by moving the grid that `GridTestCase` built by hand into a class of its own, so that both the tests and the game can ask for a board to work with. That class is part of the code we inherited, so nothing has to be written here. Two of its methods carry the whole chapter:

```smalltalk
GridFactory class >> demoGrid
	| grid |
	grid := Grid newOfSize: 5@5.
	grid at: 4@1 put: MirrorCell leanRight.
	grid at: 5@1 put: TargetCell new.
	grid at: 1@2 put: MirrorCell leanRight.
	grid at: 5@2 put: MirrorCell leanLeft.
	grid at: 2@3 put: MirrorCell leanLeft.
	grid at: 3@3 put: MirrorCell leanRight.
	grid at: 5@3 put: MirrorCell leanLeft.
	grid at: 2@4 put: MirrorCell leanLeft.
	grid at: 3@4 put: MirrorCell leanLeft.
	grid at: 1@5 put: MirrorCell leanRight.
	grid at: 4@5 put: MirrorCell leanRight.
	^grid
```

```smalltalk
GridFactory class >> defaultGrid
	^self randomizedGridOfExtent: 8@10
```

`demoGrid` is a 5 by 5 board holding ten mirrors and one target, which is exactly what this chapter needs: every mirror leans one way or the other, and the target is the one cell that will still be blank when the chapter ends.

> **Porting note.** These methods are quoted as the captured image has them, in the 2007 formatting, without the blank line and the leading space that Pharo's formatter would add today. Code that the port rewrites is shown in the new style; code that the port only reads keeps its original shape.

Pages 056 to 059 are about offsets on a shared bitmap. Page 056 finishes `testCellOffsetCalculations` and adds `offsetWithinGridForm` so that a renderer can find its own square on the board form. | text blocks report normalize |
text := (FileLocator root / 'home/renaud/devzone/sources/PharoLaserGameTutorial/doc/section2/section2.md') readStream upToEnd.
normalize := [ :s |
	((s copyReplaceAll: (String with: Character cr with: Character lf) with: (String with: Character lf))
		copyReplaceAll: (String with: Character cr) with: (String with: Character lf)) trimBoth ].
blocks := OrderedCollection new.
(text copyReplaceAll: '```smalltalk' with: '<@>') substrings: '<@>' do: [ :chunk |
	(chunk includesSubstring: '```') ifTrue: [
		blocks add: (chunk copyUpToSubstring: '```') ] ].
report := OrderedCollection new.
blocks doWithIndex: [ :raw :i |
	| body header source cls sel expected actual |
	body := (normalize value: raw).
	header := body lines first.
	(header includesSubstring: ' >> ')
		ifFalse: [ report add: i printString , ' SKIP (no header): ' , header ]
		ifTrue: [
			cls := (header copyUpToSubstring: ' >> ') trimBoth.
			source := (body allButFirst: header size) trimBoth.
			sel := source lines first.
			expected := source.
			actual := nil.
			[ | theClass compiled |
			theClass := (cls endsWith: ' class')
				            ifTrue: [ (Smalltalk classNamed: (cls copyUpTo: $ )) class ]
				            ifFalse: [ Smalltalk classNamed: cls ].
			compiled := theClass methodDict
				            detect: [ :m | (normalize value: m sourceCode) lines first trimBoth = sel trimBoth ]
				            ifNone: [ nil ].
			actual := compiled ifNotNil: [ normalize value: compiled sourceCode ] ]
				on: Error do: [ :e | actual := 'ERROR ' , e messageText ].
			actual isNil
				ifTrue: [ report add: i printString , ' MISSING ' , cls , ' >> ' , sel ]
				ifFalse: [
					actual = expected
						ifFalse: [ report add: i printString , ' DIFFERS ' , cls , ' >> ' , sel ] ] ] ].
{ blocks size. report asArray } printString

### Other rules

- A change to a class the package does not own belongs in `*.extension.st`, with the `*Laser-Game`
  protocol prefix — never in a `*.class.st`. A kernel class must never be captured into the package
  again; that mistake froze one image and was undone in `fdbf6cb`.
- Tests first. `run_tests` on `Laser-Game` after each compile, `run_critics` on what changed before
  each commit.
- No literal pixel coordinates in tests. Everything derives from `CellRenderer class>>cellExtent`.

Commit message for 2.12:

```
Section 2.12 - A Factory For Grids: mirror cells draw their diagonal

Pages 055 to 060 of the original. GridFactory came with the captured
code, so page 055 needs nothing, and pages 056 to 058 have no
counterpart: there is no board form to compute offsets into, and each
cell paints its border inside its own element, so the right and bottom
border correction has no subject.

MirrorCellRenderer>>renderContentsOn: adds one child per mirror,
carrying a BlLineGeometry from one inset corner to the opposite one.
The stroke is the child's border, since a line has nothing to fill,
and BlOutskirts centered keeps it straddling the diagonal instead of
sitting a pixel off it. cornerInset is the original's 8@8; mirrorWidth
names the two pixel pen the original drew with.

The four Form methods this replaces are deleted: renderContents,
renderContentsLeanLeft, renderContentsLeanRight and renderMirror.

MirrorCellRendererTestCase covers both leans, the endpoints, the colour,
the width, the outskirts, the child extent and re-rendering a rotated
cell. No test writes a pixel coordinate down; every expected point comes
from cornerInset and cellExtent.

63 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

	| offset |

	self drawCircleOutlineOn: aForm color: aColor offset: offset

{ #category : 'drawing' }
TargetCellRenderer >> drawCircleOutlineOn: aForm color: aColor offset: offset [
	| delta fillForm circle |
	delta := self class cellExtent - 1.
	circle := Circle new.
	fillForm := Form extent: 2@2 depth: 8.
	fillForm fillColor: aColor.
	circle form: fillForm.
	circle radius: self radius.
	circle center: (offset + (delta // 2)).
	circle displayOn: aForm
]

{
  "class_name": "LaserGameColors",
  "comment": "I am the one place the game's colors are written down. Every element the game shows asks me for its paint, so no `Color` literal appears anywhere else on the Bloc side.\n\nMy answers are plain `Color` instances. Bloc wraps them in paints and backgrounds where it needs to, so a caller can hand one of my answers straight to `BlBorder paint:width:` or to `BlElement >> background:`.\n\n```\nLaserGameColors gameBoardBackgroundColor\n```\n\nChanging a color here changes it everywhere, which is what the original tutorial wanted this class for, and what a color preference of the player would later need."

Commit message for 2.13:

```
Section 2.13 - Management of Colors: the target draws itself

Pages 061 to 063 of the original.

Page 061 gathers the colours into one class. LaserGameColors already held
all ten, so it only gained a class comment and a colors protocol. The
rule it states does hold on the Bloc side: every element names a
LaserGameColors method, and no Color literal appears in ported code. The
literals left in the package are all inside Form and Morph methods that
have not been ported.

Page 062 draws the target. TargetCellRenderer>>renderContentsOn: adds
four children: two crosshair lines inset from the edges, a ring, and a
disc inside the ring. Both circles come from newCircleOfRadius:, which
inscribes a BlCircleGeometry in a square element placed around the middle
of the cell, since a circle geometry has no centre or radius of its own.
The ring has a border and no background, so the crosshairs stay visible
through it; the disc has a background and no border. centerColor answers
the fill, which replaces the original's renderContentsOn and
renderContentsOff pair: the drawing no longer changes with the state,
only one paint does. New names outlineWidth, centerInset, crossHairInset
and innerRadius; radius is the original's, unchanged.

Nine Form methods are deleted: renderContents, drawTargetOutlines,
drawCrossHairsOutlines, drawCircleOutline, drawCircleOutlineOn:color:,
drawCircleOutlineOn:color:offset:, renderInnerCircleColor:,
renderContentsOn and renderContentsOff.

Page 063 fires the laser before drawing.
LaserGameBoardElement>>openExampleWithLaserFired does that, and a board
test asserts the target of a board built after the shot is filled with
the active colour. A board already on screen still does not follow its
model; that refresh path is pages 065 to 067.

TargetCellRendererTestCase covers the four children, the crosshair
endpoints, the ring as an empty outline, the disc inside it, the shared
outline colour and width, and both fills. No test writes a pixel
coordinate down.

71 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

# Progress So Far

*Page 064 of the 2007 tutorial.*

This page writes no game code. The original stops to tidy the image: it moves the cell rendering classes into the graphics system category, saves the image, and notes that saving erases the drawn form, which the workspace can redraw. It also states the thought that the game is playable before the beam is drawn, since the target already turns on or off according to where the mirrors are — which is what the previous chapter ended with.

## The recategorisation is already done

Pharo replaced Squeak's system categories with packages and tags, so the move the page describes is a move between tags of one package. The `Laser-Game` package carries three:

| Tag | Holds |
|---|---|
| `Model` | `Cell` and its subclasses, `Grid`, `GridFactory`, `GridDirection` and its subclasses, `LaserPathElement`, the seven `Reverse…LaserGameAction` classes |
| `Graphics` | `CellRenderer` and its three subclasses, `LaserGameColors`, `LaserGameBoardElement`, the seven `CellClickRegion` classes, and the four captured Squeak display classes that are on their way out |
| `Tests` | the twelve test cases |

So the cell renderers are where this page wants them, and the classes the port has added since — `LaserGameBoardElement` and the two new test cases — went to the right tag as they were created.

> **Porting note.** In Pharo a class is put in a tag from code with
> `(Smalltalk packageOrganizer packageNamed: 'Laser-Game') ensureTag: 'Graphics'` and then
> `tag addClass: TheClass`. Sending `category:` to a class no longer works, and `Package` has no
> `moveClasses:toTag:`.

## Saving the image

The advice to save is worth keeping, and it is the one thing on this page the reader still has to do by hand.      	| grid cell |

     	cell := MirrorCell new.
     	aSymbol = #left
     		ifTrue: [ cell leanLeft ]
     		ifFalse: [ cell leanRight ].
     	grid at: 1 @ 1 put: cell.
     	^ CellRenderer rendererFor: cell grid: grid
     ```

     testRotatingTheCellTurnsTheMirrorOver
     	"Rendering follows the cell. Rotating a mirror cell and rendering it again draws the other

     	| renderer before after |
     	renderer := self rendererLeaning: #left.
     	before := renderer newElement children first geometry.

     	after := renderer newElement children first geometry.
     	self assert: after from y equals: before from y.

*Page 064 of the 2007 tutorial.*

This page writes no game code. The original stops to tidy the image: it moves the cell rendering classes into the graphics system category, saves the image, and notes that saving erases the drawn form, which the workspace can redraw. ## The recategorisation is already done

Pharo replaced Squeak's system categories with packages and tags, so the move the page describes is a move between tags of one package. The `Laser-Game` package carries three:

| Tag | Holds |
|---|---|
| `Model` | `Cell` and its subclasses, `Grid`, `GridFactory`, `GridDirection` and its subclasses, `LaserPathElement`, the seven `Reverse…LaserGameAction` classes |
| `Graphics` | `CellRenderer` and its three subclasses, `LaserGameColors`, `LaserGameBoardElement`, the seven `CellClickRegion` classes, and the four captured Squeak display classes that are on their way out |
| `Tests` | the twelve test cases |

So the cell renderers are where this page wants them, and the classes the port has added since — `LaserGameBoardElement` and the two new test cases — went to the right tag as they were created.

{ #category : 'as yet unclassified' }
LaserGame class >> boardExtentFor: aGrid [
	| x y |
	x := CellRenderer cellExtent x * aGrid numberOfColumns.
	y := CellRenderer cellExtent y * aGrid numberOfRows.
	^x@y
]

{ #category : 'as yet unclassified' }
LaserGame class >> clearApplication [
	"LaserGame clearApplication"
]

{ #category : 'initialization' }
LaserGame >> calculatedExtent [
	| pt |
	pt := self boardForm extent.
	pt := pt + (self panelWidth@0).
	pt := pt + (2 * self gameMargin).
	^pt
]

{ #category : 'events-processing' }
LaserGame >> cellForEvent: evt [
	| posn |
	posn := self cellPositionForEvent: evt.
	^self grid at: posn
]
	dirty := aDictionary
]

{ #category : 'drawing' }
LaserGame >> drawGameBoard [
	| cell renderer |
	1 to: self grid numberOfColumns do: [:x |
		1 to: self grid numberOfRows do: [:y |
			cell := self grid at: x@y.
			renderer := CellRenderer rendererFor: cell grid: self grid form: self boardForm.
		renderer render]].
]

{ #category : 'events-processing' }
LaserGame >> eventDiagnosticFor: evt tag: aString [
	| cell posn |
	cell := self cellForEvent: evt.
	posn := self boardRelativePositionFor: evt.
	Transcript
		show: aString, ' at ', posn asString; cr;
		show: cell asString; cr;
]

{ #category : 'initialization' }
LaserGame >> initialize [
	self initializeForGrid: GridFactory emptyStandardGrid
]

# Back to the LaserGame Morph

*Pages 065 to 067 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/065.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/066.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/067.html -->

Everything we have drawn so far, we have drawn from a workspace. The original tutorial has been doing the same, and on this page it goes back to the class it created at the very beginning — `LaserGame` — and makes that class open the board itself. Opening it as it stands gives, in the original's words, "a little colored rectangle on the screen". Ours is the same story with a different name: there is no game object on the new stack yet, only a board element that a class method opens for us.

## A morph catalogue we do not have

The original opens its game from the World menu: *new morph…*, *from alphabetical list*, then `LaserGame`. Pharo has no equivalent for our class, and we do not want one — the game is a Bloc element, and a Bloc element is shown by putting it in a space. So the step of this page is not "find it in a menu", it is "write the class that owns the whole window", and the way to see it is to send it a message.

## The class

The whole game gets one element:

```smalltalk
BlElement << #LaserGameElement
	slots: { #grid . #board . #controlPanel };
	tag: 'Graphics';
	package: 'Laser-Game'
```

Three instance variables, and one of them is the original's. Page 065 adds `grid` and `boardForm` to `LaserGame`; we keep the grid and drop the form, for the reason the very first chapter gave: there is no shared bitmap to draw into. What the original keeps in a form, we keep in two children — the board element, and the control panel beside it — so those get a slot each.

> **Porting note.** The inherited `LaserGame` class is still in the package, still a `Morph` subclass, and still carries `boardForm` with its accessors. `LaserGameElement` is a new class bes

Commit message:

```
Section 2.15 - Back to the LaserGame Morph: LaserGameElement opens the game

Pages 065 to 067 of the 2007 tutorial. The original goes back to its
LaserGame morph, gives it a grid and a board form, sizes it from the panel
width and the margin, sets up two proportional panes, and calls its cell
drawing loop from #initialize. This adds the Bloc counterpart as a new
class beside the inherited Morph, which is untouched.

LaserGameElement, a BlElement in the Graphics tag with slots grid, board
and controlPanel, is the whole window. Its class side keeps the original's
numbers, panelWidth 110 and gameMargin 10, and extentForGrid: is the
original's calculatedExtent with the board element standing in for the
board form. on:, openOn: and openExample replace opening a morph from the
World menu. initialize sets a horizontal linear layout and the margin as
padding, so the margin is written once instead of four times as layout
frame offsets. grid: rebuilds, and rebuild also sets the extent, doing the
work of setExtent.

The control panel is a blank column of the panel width, as tall as the
board, as page 066 asks; its buttons come with the next pages. Two colors
join LaserGameColors: gameWindowColor and controlPanelColor.

There is no boardForm slot, since there is no shared bitmap, and page 067
needs no new method: LaserGameBoardElement>>rebuildCells has been that
loop since Section 2.11. The board is the first child and the panel the
second, following page 066's prose; the finished 2007 setupMorphs has them
the other way round. Its third pane, the laser-home strip, arrives with
the beam in Section 4.

LaserGameElementTestCase covers the extent arithmetic, the two children
and their order, the fixed-width panel, the board showing the game's grid,
the size and padding of the game itself, and rebuilding on grid:. Sizes
are read from the layout constraints, never from extent. 77 tests green,
no new critics.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

	| layout |
	layout := self buttonLayoutFrameForRow: 1 column: 1.
	panel addMorph: self makeQuitGameButton fullFrame: layout.

LaserGame >> buttonLayoutFrameForRow: fromBottom column: fromLeft [
	| buttonHeight buttonWidth xOffset xOrigin yOrigin xCorner yCorner yOffset |
	buttonHeight := 20.
	buttonWidth := 40.
	xOffset := (self panelWidth - (2 * buttonWidth)) // 3.
	yOffset := 10.

	xOrigin := xOffset * fromLeft.
	xOrigin := xOrigin + ((fromLeft - 1) * buttonWidth).

	yOrigin := yOffset * fromBottom.
	yOrigin := yOrigin + (fromBottom * buttonHeight).
	yOrigin := yOrigin negated.

	xCorner := xOrigin + buttonWidth.
	yCorner := yOrigin + buttonHeight.

	^LayoutFrame
		fractions: (0 @ 1 corner: 0 @ 1)
		offsets: (xOrigin@yOrigin corner: xCorner@yCorner)
]
LaserGame >> makeQuitGameButton [
	^self makeButton: 'Quit' action: #quitGame state: nil
]
LaserGame >> updateGameBoardAndControls [
	self drawGameBoard.
	self updateFireButtonLabel.
	self updateCounters.
	self changed
]

```json
{
  "class_name": "LaserGameControlPanelElement",
  "comment": "I am the control panel of the game: the column beside the board that holds its buttons.\n\nI replace the panel the 2007 `LaserGame` morph built in `makeControlPanelMorph` and filled through `addButtonsToPanel:`. I hold Toplo buttons instead of `PluggableButtonMorph`s, and I hold each one in an instance variable, so nothing has to search the children by name the way `findFireButton` does.\n\nTwo buttons so far, both from page 068: Quit, which closes the game, and Fire, whose label says what a click will do — `'Fire'` while the laser is off, `'Stop'` while it fires. The counters, the divider and the New Game, Undo and Reset buttons come with their own pages.\n\nInstance variables:\n- `game`: the `LaserGameElement` my buttons act on. Setting it builds the buttons.\n- `quitButton`, `fireButton`: the two buttons, in the order they sit in the row.\n\nI ask the game what to display and I tell the game what the player did. I never touch the grid myself."
}
```

# Adding Controls

*Pages 068 to 072 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/068.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/069.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/070.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/071.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/072.html -->

The white column beside the board has been waiting since the last chapter. Two buttons go in it now. One quits the game, which is easy to describe and easy to write. The other fires the laser, which the original admits has not really been thought about yet: does the beam stay on, or only while the button is held down? It settles on a toggle, and so do we.

## A class of its own

The panel was a plain `BlElement` a chapter ago. Now that it holds things and has to keep them up to date, it becomes a class:

```smalltalk
BlElement << #LaserGameControlPanelElement
	slots: { #game . #quitButton . #fireButton };
	tag: 'Graphics';
	package: 'Laser-Game'
```

It keeps a reference to the game rather than to the grid. A button is an instruction from the player — *quit*, *fire* — and instructions go to the game, which decides what that means for the model and then shows the result. The panel never touches the grid.

```smalltalk

	"A panel is a blank column with its buttons at the bottom left corner, as the original places
	them. A frame layout puts a child where it is aligned, which is what the original's layout
	frames do."

	super initialize.
	self background: LaserGameColors controlPanelColor.
	self layout: BlFrameLayout new
```

LaserGameControlPanelElement class >> on: aGame
	"Answer a control panel for aGame."

	| panel |
	panel := self new.
	panel game: aGame.
	^ panel

	"Handing the game another grid throws away the board and the panel it held and builds them
	again for the new grid, so its size follows."

	game := LaserGameElement on: GridFactory demoGrid.
	oldBoard := game board.

	self deny: game board identicalTo: oldBoard.

"""

     LaserGameControlPanelElement class >> buttonWidth   ^ 40

     	self background: LaserGameColors controlPanelColor.

     	row layout: (BlLinearLayout horizontal cellSpacing: self class buttonGap).

     	self addChild: self newButtonRow.

		A Unit Test To Demonstrate A Bug

		
			Back to the GridTestCase.  
			First we will enhance our existing tests to check

			This is also good because if we make an error

			catch this symptom.
		

		
		
			When we open up the debugger we learn something new.
			The problem isn't specific to the target cell.

# Progress So Far

*Page 064 of the 2007 tutorial.*

This page writes no game code. The original stops to tidy the image: it moves the cell rendering classes into the graphics system category, saves the image, and notes that saving erases the drawn form, which the workspace can redraw. It also states the thought that the game is playable before the beam is drawn, since the target already turns on or off according to where the mirrors are — which is what the previous chapter ended with.

## The recategorisation is already done

Pharo replaced Squeak's system categories with packages and tags, so the move the page describes is a move between tags of one package. The `Laser-Game` package carries three:

| Tag | Holds |
|---|---|
| `Model` | `Cell` and its subclasses, `Grid`, `GridFactory`, `GridDirection` and its subclasses, `LaserPathElement`, the seven `Reverse…LaserGameAction` classes |
| `Graphics` | `CellRenderer` and its three subclasses, `LaserGameColors`, `LaserGameBoardElement`, the seven `CellClickRegion` classes, and the four captured Squeak display classes that are on their way out |
| `Tests` | the twelve test cases |

So the cell renderers are where this page wants them, and the classes the port has added since — `LaserGameBoardElement` and the two new test cases — went to the right tag as they were created.

> **Porting note.** In Pharo a class is put in a tag from code with
> `(Smalltalk packageOrganizer packageNamed: 'Laser-Game') ensureTag: 'Graphics'` and then

Squeak Development Example for Squeak 3.9 (2007)

Section 3

Interacting With Cells

The user should be able to click on
cells within the LaserGame morph.
We will only
interact with the Mirror Cells.
Mirror Cells can be rotated and pushed within the grid.

Let's look at an enlarged view of a Mirror Cell.

We can think of a click-region within our cell.

The click-region is slightly inside the cell, away
from the edges.  If a user clicks very close to an edge
it will be ignored.  They must click within the shaded
region for us to process their click.

We can define another click-region even closer to the center.

With the inner region we can do other operations on the cell.
We could use one region for picking up cell rotation requests
and the other region for cell movement requests.
So let's build a structure with 2 internal click regions.
We can think of these 2 click regions as the "inside" and
"outside" region.  For testing purposes, anything
that falls outside the "outside" region is to be ignored.

## 5. Target architecture on Bloc

Bloc is present in the image (67 Bloc/Alexandrie packages, Toplo too). Available and relevant:
`BlElement`, `BlSpace`, `BlRectangleGeometry`, `BlCircleGeometry`, `BlEllipseGeometry`,
`BlLineGeometry`, `BlPolygonGeometry`, `BlGridLayout`, `BlLinearLayout`, `BlFrameLayout`,
`BlTextElement`, `BlClickEvent`, `BlElement>>aeDrawOn:`, `ToButton`, `ToLabel`.

Rules for the port:

1. **Compose, do not draw.** Prefer an element with a geometry and a background/border over custom
   `aeDrawOn:` code. A mirror is a thick diagonal `BlLineGeometry`; a target is a
   `BlCircleGeometry` plus two crosshair lines; a laser beam segment is a line; a hint arrow is a
   polygon. This removes every flood fill and every bitmap mask.
2. **One element per cell.** The board is a `BlElement` with a `BlGridLayout`; each cell renderer is
   its own element, so click regions are computed in cell-local coordinates — which is exactly what
   `CellClickRegion class>>clickRegionForPoint:` already expects.
3. **Keep the model display-free.** No element ever appears in `Cell`, `Grid` or `GridDirection`.

"
I am the game board: the element that shows every cell of one grid.

I hold a grid and one child element per cell of it, built by the CellRenderer of each cell. A BlGridLayout places those children, one column per grid column, so a cell never computes where it sits: that was the job of the offsets the original tutorial needed when all cells drew into one shared Form.

The original tutorial computed the extent of that shared Form from the cell size, the border width and the grid dimensions. I keep the arithmetic as `LaserGameBoardElement class >> extentForGrid:`, because a window still has to be given a size, but nothing depends on it internally: I take the size of my cells through fitContent constraints, and cell borders are painted inside the cells, so they cost no space.

`LaserGameBoardElement openExample` opens the demo grid in a space.

Instance variables:
	grid	<Grid>	the model I show; setting it rebuilds my children
"

	#name : 'LaserGameBoardElement',

	#category : 'Laser-Game-Graphics',
	#package : 'Laser-Game',
	#tag : 'Graphics'
}

{ #category : 'geometry' }
LaserGameBoardElement class >> extentForGrid: aGrid [
	"Answer the extent a board showing aGrid occupies. Cells are laid out edge to edge and
	their borders are painted inside them, so the borders add nothing to this."

	^ CellRenderer cellExtent
	  * (aGrid numberOfColumns @ aGrid numberOfRows)
]

{
  "class_name": "LaserGameCellElement",
  "comment": "I am the element that shows one cell of the grid, and I am the thing a player clicks on.\n\nI keep the CellRenderer that built me, so I can answer the cell I show, where that cell sits in the grid, and — through `clickRegionAt:` — which click region a point of mine falls in. The point is in my own coordinates, which is what Bloc hands to an event handler, so nothing has to subtract my position from a board-wide coordinate first. The original tutorial had no such element: every cell drew into one shared Form, and a click had to be converted into a grid location by dividing by the cell size (`CellRenderer >> offsetWithinGridForm` and the `cellForEvent:` family on the LaserGame morph).\n\nInstance variables:\n\trenderer\t<CellRenderer>\tthe renderer that built me; it carries the grid and my location in it\n"
}

{
  "class_name": "CellClickRegion",
  "comment": "I am the root of the click regions of a cell: the three concentric areas a click can fall in, told apart by where the click is within the cell.\n\nMy subclasses are CellClickRegionInside, CellClickRegionOutside and CellClickRegionIgnore. Each answers a `regionRectangle` in cell coordinates and a `sortIndex`. `clickRegionForPoint:` asks the subclasses in `sortIndex` order — inside first, ignore last — and answers the first one whose rectangle holds the point. Without that order the three would all claim a point near the centre, since each rectangle contains the ones inside it.\n\nEvery rectangle is derived from `CellRenderer class >> cellExtent`, `insideRegionExtent` and `ignoreRegionOffset`, so a cell of another size needs no new numbers here.\n\nI am a class-side hierarchy: no instance is ever created. The region a point falls in decides what a click does — the inside region pushes a cell, the outside region rotates it, the ignore region does nothing.\n"
}

@@@ CellClickRegion class >> clickRegionForPoint:

	^self sortedSubclasses detect: [:cls | cls regionRectangle containsPoint: aPoint]
@@@ CellClickRegion class >> sortedSubclasses
sortedSubclasses
	^self subclasses asSortedCollection: [:a :b | a sortIndex < b sortIndex]
@@@ CellClickRegion class >> regionRectangle
regionRectangle
	"Answer the rectangle, in cell coordinates, that I claim. Every concrete region answers one."

	^ self subclassResponsibility
@@@ CellClickRegion class >> sortIndex
sortIndex
	"Answer where I come in the order regions are asked in. The innermost region answers the
	smallest number, so that it claims a point the wider regions also contain."

	^ self subclassResponsibility
@@@ CellClickRegionInside class >> regionRectangle
regionRectangle
	"CellClickRegionInside regionRectangle"
	| outer delta |
	outer := 0@0
```

# Interacting With Cells

*Pages 074 to 077 of the 2007 tutorial.*

The board is on the screen and the laser fires, so the game can now be played with the mouse. Only mirror cells react: a mirror can be rotated, and it can be pushed to the next square along. That is two different actions on one cell, and the mouse has one button, so the cell has to decide from *where* it was clicked which of the two was meant.

The original divides a cell into three areas, one inside the next:

- an **inside** region, a square around the centre. A click here pushes the cell.
- an **outside** region, the ring around it. A click here rotates the cell.
- an **ignore** region, the margin along the four edges. A click here does nothing: someone clicking that close to an edge is probably aiming at the cell next door, and guessing would be worse than dropping the click.

This chapter builds the classification and its tests. Nothing is wired to the mouse yet — that is the next chapter — but by the end of this one a cell element can be handed a point and will say which region it fell in.

{ #category : 'tests' }
LaserGameCellElementTestCase >> testACellElementClassifiesAPointOfItsOwn [
	"A point is classified in the coordinates of the cell element itself: the top left corner is in
	the ignore margin, the first pixel of the outside rectangle is in the outside region, and the
	centre is in the inside region."

	| element |
	element := (LaserGameBoardElement on: GridFactory demoGrid) cellElementAt: 1 @ 1.
	self
		assert: (element clickRegionAt: 0 @ 0)
		equals: CellClickRegionIgnore.
	self
		assert: (element clickRegionAt: CellClickRegionOutside regionRectangle topLeft)
		equals: CellClickRegionOutside.
	self
		assert: (element clickRegionAt: CellClickRegionInside regionRectangle center)
		equals: CellClickRegionInside
]

{ #category : 'tests' }
LaserGameCellElementTestCase >> testACellElementKnowsTheCellItShows [
	"A cell element carries its own cell, so nothing has to work back from a position on the
	board to a grid location."

	| board element |
	board := LaserGameBoardElement on: GridFactory demoGrid.
	element := board cellElementAt: 2 @ 3.
	self assert: element cell identicalTo: (board grid at: 2 @ 3).

I am the game board: the element that shows every cell of one grid.

I hold a grid and one child element per cell of it, built by the CellRenderer of each cell. A BlGridLayout places those children, one column per grid column, so a cell never computes where it sits: that was the job of the offsets the original tutorial needed when all cells drew into one shared Form.

The original tutorial computed the extent of that shared Form from the cell size, the border width and the grid dimensions. I keep the arithmetic as `LaserGameBoardElement class >> extentForGrid:`, because a window still has to be given a size, but nothing depends on it internally: I take the size of my cells through fitContent constraints, and cell borders are painted inside the cells, so they cost no space.

# Handle Mouse Events

*Pages 078 and 079 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/078.html

The cells can classify a point. Now they have to be given one, which means the mouse.

## What the original had to build

In 2007 the board was a single `SketchMorph` holding one bitmap, so no cell could receive anything. The `LaserGame` morph registered interest in the events of that one morph and named it, so that it could be found again among the submorphs:

```
makeGameBoardMorph
	| boardMorph |
	boardMorph := SketchMorph withForm: self boardForm.
	boardMorph name: 'board'.
	boardMorph
		on: #mouseUp send: #mouseUp:forMorph: to: self;
		on: #mouseDown send: #mouseDown:forMorph: to: self;
		on: #mouseEnter send: #mouseEnter:forMorph: to: self;
		on: #mouseLeave send: #mouseLeave:forMorph: to: self;
		on: #mouseMove send: #mouseMoveWhileButtonDown:forMorph: to: self.
	^boardMorph
```

Five events, five handlers, all of them on the game rather than on the thing they happened to. Morphic only delivers mouse moves while a button is down, so the sixth event the page wants — the pointer moving over the board with no button pressed — is not there at all. The original gets it by asking the hand morph to report to it while the pointer is over the board:

### Claude — 2026-09-27 20:14:57Z

**Section 3.2 done — pages 078–079, Handle Mouse Events. In image, not committed.**

What landed:

`LaserGameCellElement` — cell handles own mouse.
- `initialize` installs four handlers: `BlMouseEnterEvent`, `BlMouseLeaveEvent`, `BlMouseMoveEvent`, `BlClickEvent`.
- `board` (parent, nil when orphan), `mouseEnter:`, `mouseLeave:`, `mouseMove:`, `click:` — one line each.
- `BlClickEvent` replaces the 2007 press/release bookkeeping in `activeCellLocation`.

`LaserGameBoardElement` — holds the state.
- New slots `hoveredCellElement`, `clickedCell`.
- `hoverCellElement:`, `unhoverCellElement:` (clears only when the leave comes from the hovered cell — enter of the next cell can arrive first), `clickCellElement:`.
- `hoveredCellElement`, `hoveredCell`, `clickedCell`. `hoveredCell` is what page 078 printed to the Transcript.

Deleted: whole `events-processing` protocol of the `LaserGame` morph, 12 methods — `mouseDown:forMorph:`, `mouseUp:forMorph:`, `mouseUp:forMorph:cell:`, `mouseEnter:forMorph:`, `mouseLeave:forMorph:`, `mouseMoveWhileButtonDown:forMorph:`, `mouseMoveWhileButtonUp:forMorph:`, `handleListenEvent:`, `cellForEvent:`, `cellPositionForEvent:`, `boardRelativePositionFor:`, `eventDiagnosticFor:tag:`. No hand-listener, no `morphsAt:` search for the morph named `'board'`, no world-to-board arithmetic. `makeGameBoardMorph` stays (Form/SketchMorph, dies with the morph); its `on:send:to:` cascade now names dead selectors, as symbols, so no critic fires.

Page 079 = the optional World-background diversion. Nothing to port.

Checks:

Commit message:

```
Section 3.2 - Handle Mouse Events: cells receive their own mouse events

Pages 078 and 079 of the 2007 tutorial.

LaserGameCellElement installs four Bloc handlers on itself — BlMouseEnterEvent,
BlMouseLeaveEvent, BlMouseMoveEvent and BlClickEvent — and each handler is a
single line, because Bloc delivers an event to the element it happened in. The
original registered five events on one board SketchMorph, added the game as a
mouse listener of the hand to see moves with the button up, searched the morphs
under the pointer for the one named 'board', and converted a world position into
a grid location by subtracting the game position, the margin and the panel width
before dividing by the cell size. None of that has a counterpart here.
BlClickEvent replaces the press-and-release pair the original tracked in
activeCellLocation.

LaserGameBoardElement keeps what the mouse is doing: hoverCellElement:,
unhoverCellElement: and clickCellElement: feed the new hoveredCellElement and
clickedCell slots, read through hoveredCellElement, hoveredCell and clickedCell.
unhoverCellElement: clears the hover only when the leave comes from the cell that
holds it, since moving between cells can deliver the enter of the new cell first.
hoveredCell is what page 078 wrote to the Transcript. Nothing acts on clickedCell
yet; the click regions decide what a click does from Section 3.3 on.

The whole events-processing protocol of the LaserGame morph is deleted, twelve
methods: mouseDown:forMorph:, mouseUp:forMorph:, mouseUp:forMorph:cell:,
mouseEnter:forMorph:, mouseLeave:forMorph:, mouseMoveWhileButtonDown:forMorph:,
mouseMoveWhileButtonUp:forMorph:, handleListenEvent:, cellForEvent:,
cellPositionForEvent:, boardRelativePositionFor: and eventDiagnosticFor:tag:,
the last of them the Transcript diagnostic page 078 writes and then removes.

Page 079 is the optional World background diversion and changes no code.

Six tests, driving real events through dispatchEvent:. Laser-Game: 96 tests,
all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

Next: 3.3, page 080, Detecting Mirror Cell Click Regions.

"
I am the visual representation of one cell of a grid.

The original tutorial had one SketchMorph for the whole board, and every cell drew its borders and contents into that single Form. This port drops that design: each cell gets its own element, so hit testing, redrawing and hint overlays are local to the cell instead of being computed against a board-wide bitmap.

I hold the location of my cell inside the grid, and the grid itself, so I can always ask the model for the cell I represent. My subclasses declare which cell model they render with the class-side method modelClass, and `CellRenderer class >> rendererFor:` uses that to pick the right subclass for a cell. One subclass per concrete Cell subclass, no case statement.

Instance variables:
	cellLocation	<Point>	position of my cell inside the grid, 1@1 being the top left cell
	grid		<Grid>	the model I read my cell from
