MirrorCellRendererTestCase >> mirrorElementLeaning: aSymbol [
	"Answer the mirror child of the element rendered for a mirror cell leaning aSymbol."

	^ (self rendererLeaning: aSymbol) newElement children first
]

{ #category : 'running' }
MirrorCellRendererTestCase >> rendererLeaning: aSymbol [
	"Answer a mirror renderer for a mirror cell leaning aSymbol, #left or #right, sitting at 1@1
	of a fresh grid."

	| grid cell |
	grid := Grid new.
	cell := MirrorCell new.
	aSymbol = #left
		ifTrue: [ cell leanLeft ]
		ifFalse: [ cell leanRight ].
	grid at: 1 @ 1 put: cell.
	^ CellRenderer rendererFor: cell grid: grid
]

{ #category : 'tests' }
MirrorCellRendererTestCase >> testLeanLeftMirrorRunsFromTopLeftToBottomRight [
	"A left leaning mirror goes down and to the right, inset from both corners it points at."

	| renderer mirror inset delta |
	renderer := self rendererLeaning: #left.
	mirror := renderer newElement children first.
	inset := renderer cornerInset.
	delta := MirrorCellRenderer cellExtent - 1.
	self assert: mirror geometry class equals: BlLineGeometry.

{
  "class_name": "LaserGameCellElement",
  "comment": "I am the element that shows one cell of the grid, and I am the thing a player clicks on.\n\nI keep the CellRenderer that built me, so I can answer the cell I show, where that cell sits in the grid, and — through `clickRegionAt:` — which click region a point of mine falls in. The point is in my own coordinates, which is what Bloc hands to an event handler, so nothing has to subtract my position from a board-wide coordinate first. The original tutorial had no such element: every cell drew into one shared Form, and a click had to be converted into a grid location by dividing by the cell size (`CellRenderer >> offsetWithinGridForm` and the `cellForEvent:` family on the LaserGame morph).\n\nI listen to the mouse myself: entering, leaving, moving and clicking all reach me because Bloc delivers an event to the element it happened in. I tell my board what happened (`hoverCellElement:`, `unhoverCellElement:`, `clickCellElement:`), and my board holds the state the game reads. The original registered five events on one board morph, added itself as a listener of the hand morph to see moves with the button up, and searched the submorphs under the pointer for the morph named 'board'; none of that has a counterpart here.\n\nWhile the pointer is in me I also keep a hint: `showPositionHintAt:` asks my renderer what applies at that point and `clearPositionHint` forgets it when the pointer leaves. Only a mirror answers a region, since a click acts on mirrors only.\n\nInstance variables:\n\trenderer\t<CellRenderer>\tthe renderer that built me; it carries the grid and my location in it\n\thintRegion\t<CellClickRegion class>\tthe region the pointer is in, nil when it is elsewhere or my cell offers no hint\n"
}

```
Section 3.3 - Detecting Mirror Cell Click Regions: cells answer their hint region

Page 080 of the 2007 tutorial.

CellRenderer>>hintRegionAt: answers nil and MirrorCellRenderer>>hintRegionAt:
answers CellClickRegion clickRegionForPoint:. That keeps the polymorphism the
page teaches — the message goes to whatever renderer the cell has, and only the
mirror has anything to say, because a click acts on mirrors only — while turning
the original command into a question: the renderer says what applies at a point,
it does not go drawing.

LaserGameCellElement holds the answer in a new hintRegion slot, set by
showPositionHintAt: and cleared by clearPositionHint, so mouseMove: and
mouseLeave: each gain one line. The original's three lines of arithmetic, which
subtracted offsetWithinGridForm from a board-wide position to get a point within
the cell, have no counterpart: localPosition is already cell local. Its Transcript
logging has none either; the slot holds what the page printed, and an inspector
on the element shows it change as the pointer moves.

CellRenderer>>showPositionHintFromWithinBoardOffset: deleted: it was the empty
superclass method of the page, and hintRegionAt: is now the method every renderer
answers. The MirrorCellRenderer override stays, since the captured source holds
the finished version that draws a hint arrow and swaps the cursor, which is the
text Section 3.6 ports.

Five tests: the mirror classifies a point, every other renderer answers nothing,
and both facts again through real BlMouseMoveEvent and BlMouseLeaveEvent
dispatches. Laser-Game: 101 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

     	self addEventHandlerOn: BlClickEvent do: [ :anEvent | self click: anEvent ]

     board

===== CellClickRegion.class.st
"
I am the root of the click regions of a cell: the three concentric areas a click can fall in, told apart by where the click is within the cell.

My subclasses are CellClickRegionInside, CellClickRegionOutside and CellClickRegionIgnore. Each answers a `regionRectangle` in cell coordinates and a `sortIndex`. `clickRegionForPoint:` asks the subclasses in `sortIndex` order — inside first, ignore last — and answers the first one whose rectangle holds the point. Without that order the three would all claim a point near the centre, since each rectangle contains the ones inside it.

Every rectangle is derived from `CellRenderer class >> cellExtent`, `insideRegionExtent` and `ignoreRegionOffset`, so a cell of another size needs no new numbers here.

I am a class-side hierarchy: no instance is ever created. The region a point falls in decides what a click does — the inside region pushes a cell, the outside region rotates it, the ignore region does nothing.

"

	#package : 'Laser-Game',
	#tag : 'Graphics'

CellClickRegion class >> clickRegionForPoint: aPoint [
	^self sortedSubclasses detect: [:cls | cls regionRectangle containsPoint: aPoint]
]

{
  "class_name": "LaserGameShapes",
  "comment": "I am the repository of the shapes the game draws on top of its cells: the four push arrows and the cross hair.\n\nI hold each shape as a vertex array in the coordinates the original drew it in, around 260 pixels wide, and I answer elements: `pointsOf:scaledToExtent:` stretches an array onto the rectangle a caller asks for, and `arrowElementFromPoints:ofExtent:` wraps the result in a `BlElement` with a `BlPolygonGeometry`. A shape therefore has no size of its own, and the same array serves a hint of twelve pixels and a drawing of two hundred.\n\nI replace `LaserGameForms` of pages 081 to 083, which cached one `Form` per shape. It drew an outline line by line into a form of 330 pixels, flood filled the inside, reversed black and white so that only the filled pixels would be painted, and scaled the bitmap down at the point of use. A polygon geometry is filled by the renderer and drawn at any size, so the workspace experiments of pages 081 and 082, the flood fill, the reversal and the cache all have no counterpart here. What survives from them is the numbers: my four vertex arrays are the ones those pages typed in.\n\nI am a class-side repository: no instance of me is ever created. The colours I paint with, `arrowColor` and `crossHairColor`, are the defaults of the original drawings; a caller that knows whether a move is allowed sets its own on the element it gets.\n"
}
```

The answer follows the pointer — `a MirrorCell`, `a BlankCell`, `a TargetCell` — exactly the names page 078 watches scroll past in its Transcript, and it is nil as soon as the pointer leaves the board. Click a cell and `element board clickedCell` is that cell. Nothing on the screen moves yet: this chapter delivers the events, and the next one lets a cell answer back.

## Page 079, the World background

Page 079 is a diversion the tutorial itself calls optional: the author sets a gradient background on the Squeak World so that the edges of the game morph stand out against it, and shows the desktop with the Test Runner minimised in a corner. Nothing of the game changes. Pharo 13 has its own desktop and themes, the game opens in a window of its own rather than as a morph dropped on the World, and its background is `LaserGameColors gameWindowColor`, so there is nothing to port here.

# Detecting Mirror Cell Click Regions

*Page 080 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/080.html -->

The events arrive and the regions can classify a point. This page joins the two: while the pointer moves over the board, the cell under it works out which of its regions the pointer is in. That answer becomes a visual hint a few chapters later; here it is only computed and looked at.

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/081.html -->

The previous chapter left a cell able to say which of its regions the pointer is in. To turn that answer into something the player can see, the game needs pictures to show: an arrow per push direction, and a cross hair to mark the point the pointer is at. The original draws them as bitmaps and stores them in a cache. This port keeps the drawings and drops the bitmaps, which is why the chapter is called Creating Custom Shapes here.

Commit message:

```
Section 3.4 - Creating Custom Shapes: arrows and cross hair as polygon elements

Ports pages 081 to 085 of the 2007 tutorial, where the chapter is called
"Creating Custom Forms".

LaserGameShapes replaces the drawing half of LaserGameForms. It keeps the four
arrow vertex arrays of page 082 verbatim, scales them onto any extent with
pointsOf:scaledToExtent:, and answers BlElements whose geometry is a
BlPolygonGeometry. The cross hair of page 083 becomes an element holding two
centred bars. Colours are the defaults of the original drawings and a caller
may override them on the element it is given.

A polygon is filled by the renderer at whatever size the element has, so the
330 pixel drawing form, the flood fill, the reverse, the Form oldPaint rule and
the CachedForms dictionary have no counterpart here.

LaserGameForms itself stays for now: the rotate arrows and the laser beam masks
still ask it for their pictures.

Pages 084 and 085 only divide the inside click region into four push regions.
Those four classes are already in the package with their finished
containsPoint:, which the next subsection explains and tests.

Seven tests, all green; 108 tests in Laser-Game.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

     ```smalltalk
     LaserGameShapes class >> northArrowPoints
     	"Answer the outline of an arrow that points north, as the original typed it into a workspace
     	on page 082. The numbers are the ones LaserGameForms holds."

     	^ { 100 @ 0. 200 @ 110. 120 @ 110. 120 @ 260. 80 @ 260. 80 @ 110. 0 @ 110 }

     LaserGameShapes class >> eastArrowPoints
     	^ { 0 @ 80. 150 @ 80. 150 @ 0. 260 @ 100. 150 @ 200. 150 @ 120. 0 @ 120 }

     LaserGameShapes class >> southArrowPoints
     	^ { 100 @ 260. 0 @ 150. 80 @ 150. 80 @ 0. 120 @ 0. 120 @ 150. 200 @ 150 }

     LaserGameShapes class >> westArrowPoints
     	^ { 260 @ 80. 110 @ 80. 110 @ 0. 0 @ 100. 110 @ 200. 110 @ 120. 260 @ 120 }

     LaserGameShapes class >> pointsOf: anArrayOfPoints scaledToExtent: anExtent
     	| bounds scale |
     	bounds := Rectangle encompassing: anArrayOfPoints.
     	scale := anExtent x / bounds width @ (anExtent y / bounds height).
     	^ anArrayOfPoints collect: [ :each |
     		  ((each - bounds origin) * scale) asFloatPoint ]

     LaserGameShapes class >> arrowElementFromPoints: anArrayOfPoints ofExtent: anExtent
     	^ BlElement new
     		  geometry: (BlPolygonGeometry vertices:
     					   (self pointsOf: anArrayOfPoints scaledToExtent: anExtent));
     		  extent: anExtent;
     		  background: self arrowColor;
     		  yourself

     LaserGameShapes class >> northArrowElementOfExtent: anExtent
     	^ self arrowElementFromPoints: self northArrowPoints ofExtent: anExtent
     	"east/south/west are the same line with their own array"

     LaserGameShapes class >> arrowColor    ^ Color gray
     LaserGameShapes class >> crossHairColor    ^ Color black

     LaserGameShapes class >> crossHairElementOfExtent: anExtent
     	| span thickness |
     	span := (anExtent x min: anExtent y) // 3.
     	thickness := (span // 5) max: 1.
     	^ BlElement new
     		  extent: anExtent;
     		  background: Color transparent;
     		  addChild: (self crossHairBarOfExtent: span @ thickness within: anExtent);
     		  addChild: (self crossHairBarOfExtent: thickness @ span within: anExtent);
     		  yourself

     LaserGameShapes class >> crossHairBarOfExtent: aBarExtent within: anExtent
     	^ BlElement new
     		  extent: aBarExtent;
     		  position: (anExtent - aBarExtent) / 2;
     		  background: self crossHairColor;
     		  yourself
     ```

## What the port keeps and what it drops

The three lines of coordinate arithmetic go: a mouse move reaches the cell element, and `localPosition` is already the point within the cell. The polymorphism stays, since it is the design the page is teaching. It moves to a question rather than a command: the renderer is asked what hint applies, and does not itself go drawing.

	nothing: a click acts on mirrors only."

Commit message:

```
Section 3.5 - Determine Push Regions: a region answers the hint that applies at a point

Pages 086 to 092. The push-region arithmetic came with the captured source and
needs no change: the two diagonals are equations of the cell extent, both line
tests ask <, and the four push classes answer one row each of the truth table of
page 088.

What is new is the use. Page 092's showPositionHintFromWithinCell: becomes a
query: every click region answers hintRegionForPoint: with itself, the inside
region answers the push region of the point, and MirrorCellRenderer>>hintRegionAt:
chains the two, so a point in the middle of a mirror cell now answers a push
direction rather than the inside region. showPositionHintFromWithinCell: is
deleted, having no sender left, and CellClickRegionInside gains a
subclassResponsibility containsPoint:.

The original tests nine hand-picked points of a 30 pixel cell, and pages 090 and
091 correct several of them once the code proves right and the test wrong. Four
tests in CellClickInsideRegionPushTestCase say the same things without those
numbers, deriving every point from regionRectangle: the four triangles cover the
inside region without overlapping, a point near an edge pushes away from it, a
point on a line is not under it, and the lines still meet the corners of the
inside region. Three tests of Section 3.3 move their expectation from
CellClickRegionInside to a push region, and the superseded
testAMirrorAnswersTheClickRegionOfAPoint is deleted.

Class comments on the four push regions, and protocols for their class-side
methods. 113 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

# Drawing Push Hints On The Game Board

*Pages 093 and 094 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/093.html -->
<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/094.html -->

The pointer moves inside a mirror cell and the game knows which way that cell would be pushed. This chapter shows the player: the arrow of the push region appears in the cell under the pointer, and goes when the pointer does.

Page 093 lists four things to settle first:

- the arrow forms are not to scale for the board;
- the exact place to draw the arrow has to be known;
- the arrow has to be drawn over the correct cell;
- old arrows must not be left cluttering the board.

Two of them are gone before the chapter starts. The arrows have been polygons since Section 3.4, so scale is not a problem to solve but a number to pass; and "the correct cell" is the element the pointer is in, since the event was delivered to it. What is left is where in the cell the arrow sits, and what removes the previous one.

## The original's scaling experiment

Page 093 tries the scaling in a workspace, painting an arrow straight onto the display:

```
Section 3.6 - Drawing Push Hints On The Game Board: the hint becomes an arrow in the cell

Pages 093 and 094. A push region is asked for a picture rather than a form:
hintElementOfExtent: answers nil on CellClickRegion and the arrow of its own
direction on the four push regions, built by LaserGameShapes at the size asked
for. CellRenderer class>>hintArrowExtent and hintArrowOffset hold the two numbers
page 094 computes, a couple of pixels less than a cell and centred in it.

LaserGameCellElement gains a hintElement slot and updateHintElement. The arrow is
a child of the cell it belongs to, so showing another one removes the previous
one; that is the fourth design consideration of page 093, which the original has
to meet by redrawing the cell under its arrow. showPositionHintAt: and
clearPositionHint compare the new region with the one held before rebuilding, so
a pointer moving within one region builds nothing.

The original's scaling experiment has no counterpart, since a polygon is drawn at
whatever size its element has. MirrorCellRenderer>>showPositionHintFromWithinBoardOffset:
is deleted, every line of it now living somewhere else, and with it
CellClickRegionInside class>>scaledHintArrowAndOffsetFromWithinCell: and the four
push arrowForm methods. LaserGameForms keeps its arrow accessors, which nothing
sends any more; the class goes when the rotate arrows and the beam masks have
moved too.

Four tests added and one of Section 3.3 extended: a push region answers the arrow
of its direction, a pointer inside a mirror cell puts it in the cell centred,
moving to another push region replaces it rather than adding to it, the arrow
goes when the pointer leaves or reaches a region without a picture, and cells
that are not mirrors draw nothing. 117 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

 Section 3
 Using "Halt Once"
 My concern here, as we saw when logging to the Transcript earlier, is that
 we will receive many "hint" messages in a row. Until we are sure this works, we
 really only want to draw the tiny arrow once. So we need to write a little

 When I began to write Graphical User Interface code with Digitalk's much loved
 Smalltalk/V back in the late 1980's, I wrote a troubleshooting enhancement
 called "Halt Once". In 2004 I published it for
 the Squeak community. The original enhancement code for Squeak can still be found
 here. However you do not need to install it.
 It's now built-in to Squeak 3.9. We're going to use it.
 Instead of adding "self halt" to the code, we add "self haltOnce". Like this.
 [IMG images/448.jpg]
 To turn it on we "enable" it from the debug menu.
 [IMG images/449.jpg]
 [IMG images/450.jpg]
 When the code executes it will halt the first time it hits this statement. It then
 immediately disables the Halt Once switch and allows later passes through the code
 to resume without stopping. Hence, we'll get to see the state of things the first time
 an arrow is called-up.
 By the way,
 you can always see the state of the Halt Once flag by examining the debug menu.

Pages 095 to 098 debug the hint drawing of the previous section: the arrow
does not appear until the next repaint, and arrows accumulate because the
cell is not blanked first. Section 3.6 answered both by making the hint a
child element of its cell, so there is no `self changed` and nothing to
re-render here. `Object >> haltOnce` still exists in Pharo 13, but the port
has nothing to trap: `hintRegionAt:` and `hintElementOfExtent:` answer
values the tests read directly.

Pages 099 and 100 draw the curved arrow the rotate regions need, and that
is the code of this section.

LaserGameShapes keeps the numbers of page 099 — the centre both arcs turn
about, the two radii, the arrow head array with its offset — and derives
the angle at which the original's closing line crossed the ring.
`arcPointsFromAngle:toAngle:radius:` turns an arc into 24 segments, and
`counterClockwiseArrowPoints` walks the outline once: head, outer arc, cut,
inner arc back, head again. The two arcs, the line, the flood fill and the
wide white pen that erased the line become the order the points are listed
in. The ring is as wide as the stem of the head, which is what closed the
shape in the original and what closes it here.

`clockwiseArrowPoints` mirrors the outline, as page 099 flips the form, and
the two element factories go through the `arrowElementFromPoints:ofExtent:`
of Section 3.4. Nothing is cached: a polygon is filled at whatever size its
element has, so the 450 pixel form, the CachedForms entries and page 100's
warning to re-initialize the cache by hand have no counterpart.

LaserGameForms keeps its two curved forms for one more section: the rotate
`arrowForm` methods are their last senders, and those go at Section 3.8.

Four tests: every outline point belongs to the head or to one of the two
circles, the ring width equals the stem width, the clockwise arrow is the
mirror of the other, and both scale to the extent asked for. 121 tests green.

Commit message:

```
Section 3.8 - Determine Rotate Regions: rotate hints on the outside region

Page 101 cuts the outside region of a mirror cell in half with one
horizontal line at half the height of the cell: the upper half turns the
mirror clockwise, the lower half counter clockwise, and which way the mirror
leans makes no difference. The two classes were already in the package with
that line written as an expression of the cell, so it holds at any cell
size, and page 103's boundary decision — a point on the line belongs to the
upper half — is the `<=` on one side against the `>` on the other.

`CellClickRegionOutside class >> hintRegionForPoint:` answers the rotate
region of the point, exactly as the inside region has answered the push
region since Section 3.5, and each rotate class answers
`hintElementOfExtent:` with the curved arrow Section 3.7 built. Nothing else
changes: `LaserGameCellElement >> updateHintElement` asks the hint region
for an element and does not care which region answers, so the curved arrows
appear in the cells with no new drawing code. `containsPoint:` is added to
`CellClickRegionOutside class` as `subclassResponsibility`, both rotate
classes gain class comments, and the comment on
`CellClickRegion class >> hintElementOfExtent:` is rewritten now that six
regions answer a picture.

Page 106 refactors the bitmap hints: ask the region for a scaled arrow and
its offset together in an Association, on three implementors, and delete the
old method. Section 3.5 made that move for its own reason — a region is
asked what applies, it is not told to draw — and the element carries its own
position, so there is nothing to pair. What the page deletes does apply:
both rotate `arrowForm`, `CellClickRegionOutside class >>
scaledHintArrowAndOffsetFromWithinCell:` and the `^nil` of the same name on
`CellClickRegion class`. After them nothing in the game asks LaserGameForms
for an arrow or a cross hair; the four laser beam methods of CellRenderer
are its last references, and the class goes with them in Section 4.

Tests: the fifteen-point table of pages 103 and 104 was already in
CellClickOutsideRegionRotateTestCase, which now has a class comment; beside
it go the properties it samples — every point of the region turns the mirror
one way and not both, the dividing line belongs to the upper half, and the
region refines the hint it answers. The cell element shows the clockwise
arrow in the upper half and the counter clockwise one in the lower.
`testOnlyAPushRegionAnswersAHintElement` and
`testOnlyTheInsideRegionRefinesTheHintItAnswers` were named for a world in
which the outside region had nothing to say, and are rewritten as
`testEachRegionWithAPictureAnswersTheArrowOfItsDirection` and
`testTheInsideAndOutsideRegionsRefineTheHintTheyAnswer`; the mirror renderer
test now expects a direction where it expected the outside region itself.
125 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

{ #category : 'drawing' }
MirrorCellRenderer >> renderContentsLeanLeftOn: anElement [
	"Draw the mirror from the top left corner of the cell to the bottom right one, inset from
	both."

	| inset delta |
	inset := self cornerInset.
	delta := self class cellExtent - 1.
	self
		addMirrorFrom: inset
		to: delta - inset
		on: anElement
]

{ #category : 'drawing' }
MirrorCellRenderer >> renderContentsLeanRightOn: anElement [
	"Draw the mirror from the top right corner of the cell to the bottom left one, inset from
	both."

	| inset delta |
	inset := self cornerInset.
	delta := self class cellExtent - 1.
	self
		addMirrorFrom: delta x - inset x @ inset y
		to: inset x @ (delta y - inset y)
		on: anElement
]

{ #category : 'rendering' }
MirrorCellRenderer >> renderContentsOn: anElement [
	"A mirror is one diagonal, leaning the way my cell leans."

	self cell isLeft
		ifTrue: [ self renderContentsLeanLeftOn: anElement ]
		ifFalse: [ self renderContentsLeanRightOn: anElement ]
]

When I lean right it runs from my top right corner to my bottom left one, and the same beam leaves by the west.\n\n`leanLeft` and `leanRight` set the lean and all four exit sides together, which is why `rotate` uses them instead of flipping `leansLeft` on its own: pages 107 to 110 of the original spend three pages on exactly that bug.\n\n`rotateClockwise` and `rotateCounterClockwise` are both `rotate`. A diagonal has only two positions, so either direction lands on the other one."
}

A click in the inside region pushes a cell. A click in the outside region turns a mirror, clockwise or counter clockwise, and this chapter decides which. It is the same walk as Sections 3.5 and 3.6, one ring further out: divide the region, name the halves, give each a hint, and delete the bitmap code the hint replaces.

## One line, two halves

Page 101 takes the easy decision, and says so: imagine the outside region cut in half by a horizontal line, the upper half turns the mirror one way and the lower half the other. Which way the mirror leans makes no difference, exactly as it made none for the push regions.

The two classes are already in the package, with their question written as an expression of the cell rather than of the region:

``​`smalltalk
CellClickRegionRotateClockwise class >> containsPoint: aPoint
	^aPoint y <= (CellRenderer cellExtent y // 2)
``​`
``​`smalltalk
CellClickRegionRotateCounterClockwise class >> containsPoint: aPoint
	^aPoint y > (CellRenderer cellExtent y // 2)
``​`

Commit message:

```
Section 3.9 - Rotate A Mirror Cell: printing and inspecting the model that turns

The model side of pages 107 to 110 was already captured with Section 2: the
empty rotate hooks on Cell, MirrorCell's rotate through leanLeft and leanRight
(page 110's fix), Grid's two rotateCell...At: methods and the grid tests that
fire the laser at a turned mirror. What pages 108 and 109 spend in a debugger
is what this section adds.

Cell prints where it is and whether it is on, on one line, with a
printDetailsOn: hook that MirrorCell fills with the way it leans;
LaserPathElement names its cell and the side the beam enters from. The rest of
what the original wanted from a debugger pane becomes inspector tabs: Cell
shows one row per side with the side a beam leaves by and whether it is lit,
which is exactly the disagreement pages 109 and 110 hunt; Grid shows the board
drawn by LaserGameBoardElement and the laser path a step at a time.

The six rotation methods gain comments recording the pages they come from,
their bodies unchanged.

Critics on what this section reads: class comments for Cell, MirrorCell, Grid
and LaserPathElement, MirrorCell class >> leanLeft and leanRight sending self
new instead of super new, Cell >> initializeExitSides as subclassResponsibility,
and protocols for LaserPathElement's four unclassified methods and two Grid
methods.

Seven new tests, among them LaserPathElementTestCase, whose
testTheNextElementFollowsTheMirrorAfterItIsRotated asks the question of page 109
directly: the demo mirror at 4@1 sends a beam entering from the south out east,
and west once it is turned. 132 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

   - **3.9 code (image, uncommitted)** — printing/inspecting plus critics work:
     ```smalltalk
     MirrorCell class >> leanLeft
     	"Answer a mirror on the diagonal from my top left corner to my bottom right one."
     	^ self new leanLeft

     MirrorCell class >> leanRight
     	"Answer a mirror on the diagonal from my top right corner to my bottom left one."
     	^ self new leanRight

     Cell >> initializeExitSides
     	"Fill exitSides with the side a beam leaves by for each side it can enter from. Every
     	subclass answers this differently, which is what makes a cell blank, a mirror or a target,
     	so I am abstract here."
     	^ self subclassResponsibility
     ```
     plus class comments on `Cell`, `MirrorCell`, `Grid`, `LaserPathElement`; protocols: `Grid>>initialize` → 'initialization', `Grid>>calculatePath` → 'action', `LaserPathElement>>activateCell`/`clearCell` → 'action', `nextElementIn:` → 'accessing', `LaserPathElement class>>cell:entrySide:` → 'instance creation'.

   - **3.10 code (image, uncommitted)** — the click wiring:
     ```smalltalk
     CellClickRegion class >> canActOnCellAtPoint: aPoint cell: aCell withinGrid: aGrid
     	"… the ignore margin is a region where a click is a click on nothing … Page 114 …: this guy will do nothing."
     	^ false

     CellRenderer >> mouseUpAt: aPoint
     	"… only a mirror answers a click … page 114 … the renderer superclass does nothing …"
     	^ nil

     MirrorCellRenderer >> mouseUpAt: aPoint
     	"… the outside region turns my mirror one way or the other, the inside region pushes it when there
     	is room, and the ignore margin does nothing. Page 114 … passes the cell and the grid down to the region …"
     	| region |
     	region := CellClickRegion clickRegionForPoint: aPoint.
     	^ (region canActOnCellAtPoint: aPoint cell: self cell withinGrid: self grid)
     		  ifTrue: [ region mouseUpWithinCellAtPoint: aPoint cell: self cell withinGrid: self grid ]
     		  ifFalse: [ nil ]

     LaserGameCellElement >> click: anEvent
     	"… which the original checked by keeping the location of the press in activeCellLocation …"
     	self clickAt: anEvent localPosition

     LaserGameCellElement >> clickAt: aPoint
     	"… my board records that I was clicked, my renderer decides whether my cell acts … and the board
     	draws itself again when something changed …"
     	self board ifNotNil: [ :board | board clickCellElement: self ].
     	(self renderer mouseUpAt: aPoint) ifNil: [ ^ self ].
     	self board ifNotNil: [ :board | board redrawCells ]

     LaserGameCellElement >> redraw
     	"… The cell standing at my location may be another one than before, since a push swaps two cells,
     	so the renderer is chosen again; my hint is kept … The original repainted a rectangle of the board form …"
     	| grid location region |
     	grid := self renderer grid.
     	location := self gridLocation.
     	region := hintRegion.
     	self removeChildren.
     	hintElement := nil.
     	hintRegion := nil.
     	self renderer: (CellRenderer rendererFor: (grid at: location) grid: grid).
     	self renderer renderBackgroundOn: self.
     	self renderer renderBorderOn: self.
     	self renderer renderContentsOn: self.
     	hintRegion := region.
     	self updateHintElement

     LaserGameBoardElement >> redrawCells
     	"… a turned mirror sends the beam somewhere else, and a pushed mirror leaves its old place empty …"
     	self children do: [ :each | each redraw ]
     ```
     Deletions: `MirrorCellRenderer >> mouseUpWithinBoardOffset:` (no senders after 2.16), `LaserGame >> activeCellLocation`, `LaserGame >> activeCellLocation:`, the `activeCellLocation` instance variable (`LaserGame removeInstVarNamed: 'activeCellLocation'`), and the `self activeCellLocation: nil.` line from `LaserGame >> reset` and `LaserGame >> newGame` (both recompiled verbatim otherwise, protocol 'actions').

Commit message:

```
Section 3.10 - Click And Rotate A Cell: click a mirror to rotate it

Pages 111 to 115. The mouse up walks the chain the hints already walk:
cell element, renderer, click region, cell.

LaserGameCellElement>>click: forwards to a new clickAt:, which records the
click on the board, asks its renderer to act, and redraws when something
changed. CellRenderer>>mouseUpAt: answers nil, since only a mirror reacts to
a click, and MirrorCellRenderer>>mouseUpAt: asks CellClickRegion for the
region of the point and passes the cell and the grid down to it. It replaces
the Form-era mouseUpWithinBoardOffset:, deleted here; the captured region
handlers and the two rotate mouseUpForCell:withinGrid: needed no change.

CellClickRegion class>>canActOnCellAtPoint:cell:withinGrid: is new and
answers false, which is page 114's "this guy will do nothing" for the ignore
margin. The outside and inside regions already refined it, so mouseUpAt:
guards itself with no special case for the margin.

Pages 111 and 112 keep the location of the press in activeCellLocation so
that a release outside the cell pressed is not a click. BlClickEvent is that
rule, so LaserGame>>activeCellLocation, its setter, the instance variable and
the sends left in reset and newGame are deleted rather than ported.

Page 115 repaints one cell with redrawCell and self changed. A turned mirror
moves the beam, so cells it has left stay lit - the bug the original meets on
page 127. LaserGameCellElement>>redraw draws the cell again, choosing the
renderer anew for the cell now standing at that location, keeping the element
and its hover hint, and LaserGameBoardElement>>redrawCells does it for the
whole board after an action.

One deviation, stated in the tests: page 114 leaves the inside region's
mouseUpForCell: unsent until page 122, but the captured regions implement it
on all six leaves, so a click near the middle of a mirror already pushes it,
guarded by canPushCell:withinGrid:. Pages 122 to 126 keep the push hints, the
counters and page 127's visual bug.

Six new tests in LaserGameCellElementTestCase, all dispatching real
BlClickEvents: the two outside halves turn the mirror clockwise and counter
clockwise, the ignore margin and a cell that is not a mirror do nothing,
turning a mirror on the beam redraws the whole board, and a click inside a
mirror pushes it. 138 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

{
  "class_name": "LaserGameHintEventTestCase",
  "comment": "I check the part of the hint behaviour that belongs to Bloc rather than to the game: which events a cell element is given when the pointer moves quickly, and what is left on the board afterwards.\n\nPages 116 and 117 of the original chase ghost rotation arrows. Their cause is that mouse moves are samples: the cursor can cross a cell without the game ever being told, and the cell then keeps the arrow that was drawn onto the shared board form. My tests run in a real, headless space, so the enter and leave events come from the Bloc mouse processor instead of from a test, and they show that a cell the pointer has left keeps no arrow — neither when the pointer jumped over the cells in between, nor when it left the board entirely.\n\nI take my space from `BlParameterizedHostTest`, which opens it on a headless host and closes it again after each test."

## Click, not mouse down and mouse up

The original tracks a press and a release itself. `mouseDown:forMorph:` stores the grid location of the cell pressed in `activeCellLocation`, and `mouseUp:forMorph:` acts only if the release falls in the same cell — otherwise the player pressed on one cell, dragged off it and let go somewhere else, which is not a click and must do nothing.

`BlClickEvent` is exactly that rule, already written: Bloc sends it when a press and a release land on the same element. So the port keeps the behaviour and drops the bookkeeping, and `activeCellLocation` has no counterpart on the Bloc side.

## The board holds what the mouse is doing

The handlers report to the board, which is where the game will read them:

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameBoardElement >> hoverCellElement: aCellElement
	"Remember that the pointer is over aCellElement. A cell tells me this when the pointer
	enters it and while it moves inside it."

	hoveredCellElement := aCellElement
``​`

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameBoardElement >> unhoverCellElement: aCellElement
	"Forget the pointer position, but only when aCellElement is the cell I hover. Moving from
	one cell to the next can deliver the enter of the new cell before the leave of the old one."

	hoveredCellElement == aCellElement ifTrue: [ hoveredCellElement := nil ]
``​`

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameBoardElement >> clickCellElement: aCellElement
```

Commit message:

```
Section 3.11 - Clean Up Left-Over Hints: no ghost arrows

Pages 116 and 117. Page 116 finds the cause of the left-over rotation
arrows in the event log: mouse moves are samples, so a fast cursor crosses
cells that are never told they were entered or left, and whatever was
painted on them stays. Page 117 answers with a dirty-cell Dictionary on the
LaserGame morph, a sweep of the flagged cells before every hint, redrawCell
moved up to CellRenderer, and one more sweep for the cursor that leaves the
grid.

The port needs none of that machinery. A hint is a child element of the cell
that shows it, so nothing has to be cleaned off a shared form, and Bloc
derives the enter and the leave events from a hit test on every move, so the
cell the pointer jumped away from is told even when the cells in between
were skipped.

What it takes from page 117 is the strategy, in the smallest form it has
here. At most one cell holds a hint, so the dictionary of dirty cells is the
board's hoveredCellElement, and the sweep is one line in hoverCellElement:,
which clears the hint of the cell hovered before. It runs where
sweepDirtyCells ran, on every enter and every move, and it keeps the port
from resting on a promise of the event system.

Deleted with their instance variable and their sends in reset and newGame:
LaserGame>>dirty, dirty:, initializeDirty, setDirty:, setClean:, isDirty:,
sweepDirtyCells and redrawCell:. redrawCell goes with them, from CellRenderer
and from MirrorCellRenderer both; LaserGameCellElement>>redraw of the
previous section replaced it, and nothing sends it any more.

Three new tests. The skipped event of page 116 is dispatched by hand: one
cell is given a move, then another one is, and no leave arrives in between.
The other two live in the new LaserGameHintEventTestCase, which opens a
headless space and moves the pointer with BlEventSimulator, so the enter and
leave events come from the Bloc mouse processor and not from a test - one
jump from one mirror to a distant one, and one move off the board entirely.
141 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

```
Section 3.12 - Bug With Target Cell: inspector tab over the cells, and a test that every cell element still shows its cell

Page 118 finds the target lit while nothing feeds it, and finds it by hand:
halos on the game morph, "explore morph", then an object explorer walked
down to `cells` and opened twice. The fix the pages go on to make is already
in the port — `Grid >> rotateCellClockwiseAt:` and its counter-clockwise twin
clear the beam, turn the cell and light the new path, and the click chain has
carried the grid since Section 3.10 — so what this section adds is the way to
see the state, and a standing check that the picture keeps agreeing with it.

`Grid >> inspectionCells:` is a third inspector tab beside Board and Beam. It
lists every cell in the order the board lays them out, with what the cell is
and whether it is lit.

`LaserGameCellElementTestCase >> testEveryCellElementAgreesWithItsCellAfterATurn`
fires the laser, turns a mirror through a real click, and then asks every cell
element whether it still shows its own cell: the renderer matches the cell's
class, and the target's centre is lit exactly when the target is on.
`GridTestCase >> testTheCellsTabListsEveryCellWithItsState` covers the new tab.

143 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

===== 122 =====
Squeak Development Example for Squeak 3.9 (2007)

Section 3

Push A Cell

Our game should provide a way for the user to move a cell orthogonally.
The only cells that can be moved are mirror cells.  The target cell may
not be pushed.  Only individual mirror cells may be pushed.
For example, if there are mirror cells adjacent, the user cannot
move them together.

[IMG images/604.jpg]

Moving an individual mirror cell with a push is legal.

[IMG images/605.jpg]

Since neighboring cells impact what we do when a push operation is
performed, we obviously will be working at the Grid level.  Also,
the mirror cells are not really pushed.  They merely appear to be pushed.
In reality we will be swapping their location with the adjacent blank cell.

There is the key detail for our push logic.  If the adjacent cell where we want to
push is a blank cell, we trade places.  Otherwise nothing happens.

We can now write the four push instance methods on the Grid class.  They don't have
to do anything yet.  We just want a method we will call from the unit test we intend to write.
Here's the first push-north method.

[IMG images/606.jpg]

The other 3 directions are easy to write.

pushCellEastFromLocation: aPoint

pushCellSouthFromLocation: aPoint

pushCellWestFromLocation: aPoint

Let's go write that unit test.

# Bug With Target Cell

*Pages 118 to 121 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/118.html -->
<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/119.html -->

Fire the laser, let the target light up, then turn the mirror that feeds it. The beam goes somewhere else, and the target stays lit.

Page 118 states the rule the game will need one day — *my own preference would be to inhibit the modification of cells on the grid while the laser is active* — and then puts it aside: the target being lit by nothing is wrong whatever the rule turns out to be.

## Where the wrong answer lives

The first question of page 118 is whether the fault is in the model or in the drawing. The original answers it with the tools of a Squeak image: cover the morph with a Workspace and uncover it, so that it repaints. The target is still lit, so it is not a stale picture. Then command-click for the halos, take the wrench menu, *explore morph*, and walk the explorer down through `grid` to `cells`. There it is, in a list of every cell: `5@1: a TargetCell location = 5@1 ON`.

The port reads the same list from a tab, because Section 3.9 put the board and the beam in the inspector already, and the cells are the third view of the same object:

# Push A Cell

*Pages 122 to 124 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/122.html -->
<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/123.html -->
<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/124.html -->

Turning a mirror is one of the two moves of the game. This section writes the other one: pushing a mirror sideways into the empty square beside it.

Page 122 gives the rules before any code:

- only mirror cells move;
- the target never moves;
- one cell moves at a time, so two mirrors standing side by side do not travel together;
- and nothing is really pushed. A mirror and the blank cell beside it trade places.

That last line is the whole of the logic. *If the adjacent cell where we want to push is a blank cell, we trade places. Otherwise nothing happens.* Whether the neighbour is a mirror, the target, or the edge of the board with no cell at all, the answer is the same: nothing happens.

Neighbours are what the rule talks about, so the work belongs to `Grid`, which is the only object that knows what sits next to what.

```
Section 3.13 - Push A Cell: document the push protocol and test the cases page 123 leaves open

Pages 122 to 124 give the second move of the game: a mirror trades places
with the blank cell beside it, the target never moves, and two mirrors side
by side do not travel together. The captured 2007 source already contains
that logic in the shape page 124 refactors it into, together with the seven
push tests of page 123, so this section writes no new behaviour.

What it writes is the reasoning. The seven Grid methods that carry the push —
`pushCell:fromLocation:`, `swapCell:with:`, `pushCellAction:fromLocation:` and
the four direction methods — now say what rule they hold and why, including
the two things the captured source has that page 124 does not yet: the beam is
taken off the board and put back when a push happens under a running laser,
as for a rotation, and a push that really moved a cell is recorded for undo.

Four tests answer questions page 123 does not ask. A push off the edge of the
board reaches the only branch of `pushCell:fromLocation:` that no test of that
page reaches. A push against a mirror, and against the target as a neighbour
rather than as the cell being pushed, is refused. A pushed mirror is the same
object, with its lean, in its new place, and both cells know their new
locations — the page-123 tests ask only about classes, so a push that rebuilt
the cells would satisfy them and silently drop the lean. And a refused push
records no move.

147 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

``​`

## One arrow at a time

The cell element holds the picture of the hint it holds, and replacing it is what keeps the board clean — the fourth consideration of page 093, which the original has to solve by redrawing the cell:

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameCellElement >> updateHintElement
	"Show the picture of the hint I hold, and no other. The original drew its arrow straight onto
	the board form, which is why page 093 warns that old arrows have to be cleaned off; here the
	arrow is a child of mine, so the previous one goes when it is removed."

	hintElement ifNotNil: [ :each | self removeChild: each ].
	hintElement := hintRegion ifNotNil: [ :region |
		               region hintElementOfExtent: CellRenderer hintArrowExtent ].
	hintElement ifNotNil: [ :each |
		each position: CellRenderer hintArrowOffset.
		self addChild: each ]
``​`

The two methods of Section 3.3 that set and clear the hint now each end in it. Both start by comparing, so a pointer moving within one region does not rebuild anything: a mouse move arrives for every pixel crossed, and only a move into another region is a change.

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameCellElement >> showPositionHintAt: aPoint

**Page 125** (wiring): already in the captured source and exercised since 3.10 — `CellClickRegionInside class >> mouseUpWithinCellAtPoint:cell:withinGrid:` picks the push region for the point, each of the four push regions calls the matching `pushCell<Direction>FromLocation:`. Nothing to write.

**Page 126** (the halt-and-single-step hunt): the original finds a `MirrorCellRenderer` that still thinks it draws the cell the mirror left, and answers with a chain of return values up to a new `LaserGame >> redrawCell:`. The port has the returns already (`clickAt:` uses them to tell an action from a refused one), and the Morph half — `mouseUp:forMorph:cell:`, `mouseUpWithinBoardOffset:`, `redrawCell:` — was deleted in 3.10/3.11. But the same class of bug was still there one layer up:

> hover a mirror's push region, click it: the mirror leaves, a blank cell takes its place, and **the arrow stayed drawn over it**. `redraw` chose the renderer again but kept the hint region.

Reproduced first (`testTheArrowGoesWhenAPushEmptiesTheCellUnderThePointer` failed: "Assertion failed"), then fixed.

**Code in image (uncommitted)**

- `showPositionHintAt:` records the point before its unchanged-region early return; `clearPositionHint` forgets it.
- `redraw` re-asks the renderer for the hint at that point after choosing the renderer, instead of restoring the old region.

Commit message:

```
Section 3.14 - Push Cells With The Mouse: read the hint again after a redraw, so no arrow outlives the cell it belonged to

Page 125 sends the mouse-up of the inside region down to one of the four push
regions, and each of them to the matching push method on the grid. That wiring
came with the captured source and has been under test since Section 3.10.

Page 126 is the interesting half. It puts a halt in the push, single-steps
through the swap, and finds a mirror renderer that still believes it draws the
cell at the location the mirror has just left. The original answers with a
chain of return values and a new redrawCell: on LaserGame. The port has the
return values already, and uses them for a different question — whether the
click did anything at all — while the Morph half of that fix was deleted in
Sections 3.10 and 3.11, because a cell element rebuilds itself from the model.

The port had the same bug one layer up, in the hint rather than the cell. With
the pointer resting on a mirror, a push moved the mirror away and left its
arrow drawn over the blank cell that took its place: `redraw` chose the
renderer again, but kept the hint region it already had, and nothing asked the
question again because the pointer had not moved.

`LaserGameCellElement` now keeps the point its hint was read at, in a
`hintPosition` slot written by `showPositionHintAt:` and cleared by
`clearPositionHint`, and `redraw` reads the hint again at that point, from
whatever cell stands there after the action. Two tests hold both halves of the
rule: the arrow goes when a push empties the cell under the pointer, and it
stays when a turn leaves a mirror there.

149 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

mirror at 4@5 west, and the target stays lit although the beam no longer

draws the cell that now stands in it — the target included, lit exactly when
its cell is on.

150 tests, all green.

# Interacting With Cells

*Pages 074 to 077 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/074.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/075.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/076.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/077.html -->

The board is on the screen and the laser fires, so the game can now be played with the mouse. Only mirror cells react: a mirror can be rotated, and it can be pushed to the next square along. That is two different actions on one cell, and the mouse has one button, so the cell has to decide from *where* it was clicked which of the two was meant.

The original divides a cell into three areas, one inside the next:

- an **inside** region, a square around the centre. A click here pushes the cell.
- an **outside** region, the ring around it. A click here rotates the cell.
- an **ignore** region, the margin along the four edges. A click here does nothing: someone clicking that close to an edge is probably aiming at the cell next door, and guessing would be worse than dropping the click.

This chapter builds the classification a

# Interacting With Cells

*Pages 074 to 077 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/074.html
     http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/075.html

The board is on the screen and the laser fires, so the game can now be played with the mouse. Only mirror cells react: a mirror can be rotated, and it can be pushed to the next square along. That is two different actions on one cell, and the mouse has one button, so the cell has to decide from *where* it was clicked which of the two was meant.

The original divides a cell into three areas, one inside the next:

- an **inside** region, a square around the centre. A click here pushes the cell.
- an **outside** region, the ring around it. A click here rotates the cell.
- an **ignore** region, the margin along the four edges. A click here does nothing: someone clicking that close to an edge is probably aiming at the cell next door, and guessing would be worse than dropping the click.

Page 114 explains why the cell travels down with the message: *the MirrorCellRenderer knows about the cell object. The click-region classes do not.* A region is a piece of geometry with an opinion about what a click there means, and it is given everything it needs to act.

One method is new here. A region is also the right place to ask whether a click can do anything at all, and the ignore margin has to answer that question without a special case around it:

CellClickRegion class >> canActOnCellAtPoint: aPoint cell: aCell withinGrid: aGrid
	"Answer whether a click at aPoint can do anything to aCell. Nothing can be done in me: the
	ignore margin is a region where a click is a click on nothing, and the inside and outside
	regions each answer for the region the point really falls in. Page 114 of the original says
	the same of the mouse up handler it writes here: this guy will do nothing."

	^ false

## One arrow at a time

The cell element holds the picture of the hint it holds, and replacing it is what keeps the board clean — the fourth consideration of page 093, which the original has to solve by redrawing the cell:

	hintElement ifNotNil: [ :each |
		each position: CellRenderer hintArrowOffset.
		self addChild: each ]
``​`

# Source Management With Monticello

*Pages 128 to 129A of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/128.html

Pages 128 and 129 leave the game alone and put the code away: they open the Monticello browser, declare a package named `Laser-Game` over the three system categories `Laser-Game-Model`, `Laser-Game-Graphics` and `Laser-Game-Tests`, add a repository — a plain directory on disk — and save version `Laser-Game-sbw.1` into it. Page 128 also stops on the `*Extensions` entry of the snapshot browser, to show that the method added to `Object` travelled with the package because of the protocol it was filed under.

This port does not repeat that chapter. Pharo has replaced both tools: code lives in a Tonel repository under Git, and Iceberg is the browser that commits it. Explaining Iceberg here would duplicate a book that already exists and is kept up to date:

<https://books.pharo.org/booklet-ManageCode/pdf/2024-05-16-ManageCode.pdf>

What the two pages say about *why* still holds, and the port follows it: the code is one package, `Laser-Game`, with the same three concerns kept apart — the model classes, the Bloc graphics and the tests are each in their own tag — and every numbered section of this book is a commit of its own, so any state of the game can be reproduced and gone back to.

Page 129A closes Section 3 with an inventory of every class and method the reader should have. It is an inventory of the 2007 code, not of this port: most of the graphics classes on it are gone, `LaserGameForms` and the `Form` drawing with it, and the classes that replaced them — `LaserGameShapes`, `LaserGameBoardElement`, `LaserGameCellElement` and the rest — are not on it. # Push Cells With The Mouse

*Pages 125 to 126 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/125.html -->
<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/126.html -->

The model can push a mirror, the board has been drawing push arrows since Section 3.6, and nothing joins the two. Page 125 joins them, and page 126 goes looking for what the joining broke.

## The click reaches the push

The hook has been in place since page 114: the inside region of a cell asks which push region the point falls in, and sends it a mouse-up.

``​`smalltalk
CellClickRegionInside class >> mouseUpWithinCellAtPoint: aPoint cell: aCell withinGrid: aGrid
	| pushRegion |
	pushRegion := self pushRegionForPoint: aPoint.
	^pushRegion mouseUpForCell: aCell withinGrid: aGrid
``​`
``​`smalltalk
CellClickRegionInside class >> pushRegionForPoint: aPoint
	^self subclasses detect: [:cls | cls containsPoint: aPoint]
``​`

The four push regions answer it by pushing, each in its own direction:

``​`smalltalk
CellClickRegionPushNorth class >> mouseUpForCell: aCell withinGrid: aGrid
	^aGrid pushCellNorthFromLocation: aCell gridLocation
``​`
``​`smalltalk
CellClickRegionPushEast class >> mouseUpForCell: aCell withinGrid: aGrid
	^aGrid pushCellEastFromLocation: aCell gridL
… [826 more characters]

```
Section 4.1 - Communicate With Arrow Colors: hint arrows coloured by permission

Pages 130 to 133 of the 2007 tutorial. The arrow a mirror cell shows now says
whether the move it offers is allowed: green when it can be made, red when it
cannot.

The permission chain the pages build was already in the captured source and was
explained in Section 3.10: Grid >> canPushCell:fromLocation: with its four
direction methods, canPushCell:withinGrid: on the four push regions, and
canActOnCellAtPoint:cell:withinGrid: on the inside region, the outside region
and CellClickRegion itself. LaserGameColors allowActionArrowColor and
denyActionArrowColor were captured too. What this section adds is the use of
the answer, which page 132 makes inside the Form-drawing method deleted in
Section 3.6.

Which colour a point deserves is a question about the cell, so the renderer
answers it, split like hintRegionAt::

- CellRenderer >> hintColorAt: answers the neutral grey of LaserGameShapes,
  since a cell that reacts to nothing shows no hint;
- MirrorCellRenderer >> hintColorAt: asks the click region of the point whether
  the action is permitted and answers the allow or deny colour.

LaserGameCellElement >> updateHintElement paints the arrow with
background: (self renderer hintColorAt: hintPosition), inside the block that
already guards against a region with no picture, and reads the pointer position
Section 3.14 taught it to keep.

Deleted: MirrorCellRenderer >> hintArrowColorFor:offset:, the last unsent
remnant of the Form-era arrow colouring.

Two tests, both written first and failing with "Got Color gray instead of
Color green.": a push arrow is coloured by whether that push is allowed, on the
mirror at 4@1 which can go south but not east into the target; both rotate
arrows are the allowed colour even on a mirror boxed in on every side.

Page 133 versions the package in Monticello. That step is Iceberg and git here,
and the Pharo booklet on managing code covers it, so it is not ported.

152 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

	"Answer a cross hair of anExtent: two bars crossing at the centre. Page 083 drew the same

Commit message (code only):

```
Section 4.2 - Better Cursor Management: mark the pointer with a cross hair

Pages 134 to 136 replace the cursor picture with a cross hair while the
pointer is over a hint, and put the default back when it is not. Bloc can
change the cursor, but the object it hands the host window is a Cursor, a
subclass of Form, and no class in this package may depend on one. The page
is ported by its intent instead: the mark is drawn inside the cell, centred
on the point a click would be judged by, and shown exactly when a hint arrow
is shown.

The drawing itself was ported at 3.4, so page 134's own code goes:
LaserGameForms class >> drawCrossHair and crossHair, and the two lines that
cached the form. initializeCachedForms and initialize stay until the beam
masks go at 4.7.

CellRenderer class >> crossHairExtent answers the cell extent, which keeps
page 134's ten pixel arms in a thirty pixel cell as a third of the cell.
LaserGameCellElement gains a crossHairElement slot with its accessor and
updateCrossHairElement, which builds the mark once with the hint and only
moves it afterwards, since the pointer sends an event for every pixel it
crosses. updateHintElement drops the old mark before calling it, so the new
one is added after the arrow and drawn on top of it. showPositionHintAt:
calls it on the path that returns early, because the arrow is the same for a
whole region but the mark is not. redraw forgets it with the arrow. Page
135's reset needs no code: clearPositionHint already runs on leave.

Three tests cover the mark, its movement within a region and the cells that
show none; two older tests now count two children per hint. 155 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

LaserGameShapesTestCase >> testShapesAreBuiltAtWhateverSizeIsAsked
	"Vertices scale, so no shape has a size of its own. The original drew every arrow into a 330
	pixel form once, cached the bitmap and scaled it down on use, which is why its small arrows
	were ragged."

	{ 12 @ 12. 50 @ 50. 200 @ 200 } do: [ :extent |
		{ LaserGameShapes northArrowElementOfExtent: extent.

			self assert: (self requestedExtentOf: element) equals: extent ] ]
``​`

An element measures itself only when it is laid out, so a freshly built element answers zero for its extent. The size it was asked for is in its resizers, and one helper reads it:

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameShapesTestCase >> requestedExtentOf: anElement
	"Answer the extent anElement was built with, read from its resizers. An element measures
	itself only in a layout pass, so its extent is zero until it is laid out."

	^ anElement constraints horizontal resizer size
	  @ anElement constraints vertical resizer size
``​`

## The constants live with the cell size

Page 075 starts on the class side of `CellRenderer`, which already holds the size of a cell, and adds the numbers the regions need. The captured source has them, in a `constants` protocol as the page asks:

CellRenderer class >> outsideRegionExtent
	^self cellExtent - (2 * self ignoreRegionOffset)
``​`

Only `cellExtent` and `ignoreRegionOffset` are numbers; the other two are derived from them, which is why the port has not had to touch any of this while changing how a cell is drawn. With the captured cell size of 50 by 50 the inside square is 30 by 30, the outside square is 42 by 42, and the ignore margin is 4 pixels all round.

> **Note on the sizes.** The 2007 text works with a 30 by 30 cell and a 14 by 14 inside region, and page 077 is a debugging session about exactly those two numbers. The source this port inherits is the finished game, where the author had already enlarged the cells — page 137 of the tutorial — and rewritten `insideRegionExtent` as `cellExtent - 20`. 	"Answer the size of the square in the middle of a cell where a click asks for a push. Page

	width while the cell grows."

	^self cellExtent - 20''')

add('CellRenderer class', 'constants', '''outsideRegionExtent
	"Answer the size of the square where a click asks for a rotation: the cell less the ignore
	margin on each side. The margin is what is written down, not the region."

add('CellRenderer class', 'constants', '''ignoreRegionOffset
	"Answer the width, in pixels, of the margin along the edges of a cell where a click does
	nothing. Page 075 of the original picks four pixels, and four is right at any cell size: the

### Claude — 2026-09-28 17:57:26Z

Checked all of them. Same error 55 times:

```
NotFound: [:cls | cls regionRectangle containsPoint: aPoint] not found in SortedCollection
CellClickRegion class>>clickRegionForPoint:
MirrorCellRenderer>>hintRegionAt:
LaserGameCellElement>>showPositionHintAt:
LaserGameCellElement>>mouseMove:
```

Failing points: `(43.0@50.0)`, `(79.0@53.0)`, `(75.0@23.0)` … every one has x or y ≥ 50, up to 79.

**My fault, and a real bug.** The 'Larger cells' window I opened for the 4.3 visual check built the board at 80 pixels to the cell and then restored `cellExtent` to 50 inside `ensure:`. Cell elements are laid out once, at build time; click regions are recomputed from `CellRenderer cellExtent` on **every** mouse move. So the elements were 80 wide while the regions were 50 — the pointer spent most of its time on a point belonging to no region.

The hole underneath is not mine: `clickRegionForPoint:` was a `detect:` with no `ifNone:`. Safe only while some region contains the point. The ignore region covers the whole cell, so any point *in* a cell finds one; a point outside finds nothing and raises — from inside a mouse handler. A cell element is free to be bigger than the cell the regions come from, so this was reachable without my experiment.

Fixed:

```smalltalk
CellClickRegion class >> clickRegionForPoint: aPoint
	^self sortedSubclasses
		detect: [ :cls | cls regionRectangle containsPoint: aPoint ]
		ifNone: [ CellClickRegionIgnore ]
```

A point outside the cell is a point a click can do nothing with — which is what the ignore region already means. New test `CellClickRegionTestCase >> testAPointOutsideTheCellIsIgnored` covers the four ways out of a cell. Nothing else needs it: the four push regions answer four combinations of two booleans and the two rotate regions split on one, so those `detect:` calls always find exactly one subclass.

**157 tests pass, 0 failed, 0 errored.** Critics clean on both methods.

Cleanup: closed 53 debugger windows (the other 2 sessions had none), 0 debug sessions left after GC, 0 debugger windows displayed. Closed the inconsistent 'Larger cells' space.

Doc: the 4.3 chapter's visual-check recipe no longer restores the size behind an open window — raise, look, close, lower — with the reason spelled out, plus a new section recording the walkback and the fix. `doc/section3/section3.md` block for `clickRegionForPoint:` converted to untagged with a forward note. Verifier: 543 blocks, 404 identical, 0 mismatched, 139 skipped. `PROJECT_MAP.md` updated (157 tests, new counts, 4.3 row).

Revised 4.3 commit message — same as before, with this added before the closing line:

```
Looking at the board at eighty pixels also turned up a hole that has nothing
to do with the cell size as such. CellClickRegion class >> clickRegionForPoint:
was a detect: with no ifNone:, which is safe only while some region contains
the point. The ignore region covers the whole cell, so every point of a cell
finds one, and a point outside the cell finds none and raises NotFound out of
mouseMove:. A cell element may be larger than the cell its regions are computed
from, so the case is reachable. It now answers CellClickRegionIgnore, which is
what a point a click can do nothing with already means, and a test covers the
four ways out of a cell.

The nine constants and lines the two pages are about also get the method
comments they had been missing. 157 tests green.

"
I am the game board: the element that shows every cell of one grid.

I hold a grid and one child element per cell of it, built by the CellRenderer of each cell. A BlGridLayout places those children, one column per grid column, so a cell never computes where it sits: that was the job of the offsets the original tutorial needed when all cells drew into one shared Form.

The original tutorial computed the extent of that shared Form from the cell size, the border width and the grid dimensions. I keep the arithmetic as `LaserGameBoardElement class >> extentForGrid:`, because a window still has to be given a size, but nothing depends on it internally: I take the size of my cells through fitContent constraints, and cell borders are painted inside the cells, so they cost no space.

I also hold what the mouse is doing to my cells. Each cell element handles its own mouse events and tells me: `hoverCellElement:` and `unhoverCellElement:` keep `hoveredCellElement` current, and `clickCellElement:` records `clickedCell`. So `hoveredCell` answers the cell under the pointer, which the original had to compute from the hand position, the board offset and the cell size, and printed to the Transcript on page 078.

`LaserGameBoardElement openExample` opens the demo grid in a space.

"
I am the repository of the shapes the game draws on top of its cells: the four push arrows and the cross hair.

I hold each shape as a vertex array in the coordinates the original drew it in, around 260 pixels wide, and I answer elements: `pointsOf:scaledToExtent:` stretches an array onto the rectangle a caller asks for, and `arrowElementFromPoints:ofExtent:` wraps the result in a `BlElement` with a `BlPolygonGeometry`. A shape therefore has no size of its own, and the same array serves a hint of twelve pixels and a drawing of two hundred.

I replace `LaserGameForms` of pages 081 to 083, which cached one `Form` per shape. It drew an outline line by line into a form of 330 pixels, flood filled the inside, reversed black and white so that only the filled pixels would be painted, and scaled the bitmap down at the point of use. A polygon geometry is filled by the renderer and drawn at any size, so the workspace experiments of pages 081 and 082, the flood fill, the reversal and the cache all have no counterpart here. What survives from them is the numbers: my four vertex arrays are the ones those pages typed in.

# Making Larger Cells

*Pages 137 and 138 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/137.html

> For our next enhancement I want to change the size of our cells. Making them bigger will make the game cells easier to see, as well as any hint arrows within the mirror cells. It should also "illuminate" (pardon the pun) any issues we may have with unintended constants in our code.

The pun is the whole chapter. Raising the cell size is one line of work; finding everything that quietly assumed the old size is the rest of it, and the original spends both pages on it.

This port arrives at the chapter from the other end. The source it inherited is the finished 2007 game, in which the author had already enlarged the cells twice, so `CellRenderer class >> cellExtent` has answered fifty by fifty since Section 3.1, and every size derived from it was written as a derivation when it was first quoted. There is nothing here left to fix.

That makes this chapter a proof rather than a change: the cell size is raised and lowered again, and the geometry is asked whether it followed. The chapter does add something, though, because a promise nobody checks is not a promise. The experiment the original runs by eye is written down as a test, and the constants it is about get the comments that say what they are.

```
Section 4.4 - Add A Counter and Window Colors: a laser path counter and a colour ramp

Pages 139 to 142. The panel moves to the left of the board, the window is
filled with a gradient instead of a flat colour, and an LED counter at the top
of the panel shows how long the beam is while the laser fires.

Three of page 139's changes were already in place, since the port inherits the
finished 2007 source: the margin, the extent that accounts for it, and the
refactoring that separates the buttons from the panel. So was page 140's white
cell border. Page 140's boardRelativePositionFor: has no counterpart, because
Bloc hands each cell element an event already in its own coordinates.

LaserGameColors gains the ramp of page 140 as windowColorRamp and
windowColorRampDirection, the counter colours of page 141, and paints the
control panel transparent so that the ramp runs behind it.
LaserGameElement class >> windowBackgroundPaint turns the ramp into a
BlLinearGradientPaint; the flat window colour the original paints under its
ramp is left unused, since an element takes one paint.

LaserGameLedElement is new. LedMorph is a Squeak class that Pharo does not have
and a Morph besides, so the display is drawn here: seven rectangles per digit,
recoloured rather than rebuilt when the number changes. Every rectangle is
derived from digitExtent and segmentThickness, so the display can be drawn at
any size. The digit is 10 by 16 rather than page 141's 10 by 15, because three
bars and two arms of two pixels need an even height to divide. Numbers are
right aligned with blank leading digits, and highlighted: gives page 142 its
bright state.

LaserGameCounterElement is new: page 141's wrapPanel:label:, a transparent
rounded frame holding the display with its caption under it. Under, because the
original adds the label after the panel although its comment says above. The
complexAltInset bevel becomes a flat border, which is what a Bloc border can be.

The control panel holds the counter in an instance variable, so page 142's
findLaserPathCounter, which walks every morph of the game looking for a name,
has no counterpart. updateCounters is page 142's rule unchanged.

Both moments that change the beam now reach the counter. LaserGameElement >>
refresh sets it along with the fire button label. A click reaches the board,
which knows nothing about the game, so the board announces the move instead:
moveMade draws the cells and evaluates the block registered by whenMoveMadeDo:,
and LaserGameCellElement >> clickAt: sends moveMade in place of redrawCells. A
board opened on its own registers no block and plays as before.

Fifteen tests, 172 in all, green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

===== PAGE 143 =====
Squeak Development Example for Squeak 3.9 (2007)
		
		
			@import "css/tutorial2007.css";
		
	
	
		
			Section 4
			
		Add Move Counter And Randomizer
		
			We're going to keep adding enhancements to our LaserGame.
			Here's how it looks today.
		
		
		
			We will be adding 2 new features.  The first will be
			a Moves counter.  The moves counter will show the total
			number of cell clicks on the game board.
			The idea is that the player will want to minimize this
			count as they solve the puzzle.
		
		
			The second feature will be to add a random game generator.
			This will allow us to include a "New Game" button which
			will generate a new randomized mix of Mirror Cells on
			our board game grid.
		
		
			Let's get started.  The first thing to do is add a way to keep track
			of the moves count.  We will accomplish this by adding a new
			instance variable "moves" to the LaserGame class definition.
		
		
		
			Create the accessors that includes #moves and #moves:.  The #initialize
			method should be modified to set "moves" to zero.
		
		
			initialize
			    super initialize.

## Telling the counter what happened

Page 142 has to find the display before it can set it:

``​`
findLaserPathCounter
    ^self allMorphs detect: [:m | m knownName = 'laserPath'] ifNone: []
``​`

``​`
updateCounters
    | led |
    led := self findLaserPathCounter.
    led notNil ifTrue: [
        self laserActive
            ifTrue: [led 
                highlighted: true;
                value: self grid laserBeamPath size]
            ifFalse: [led
                highlighted: false;
                value: 0]
            ]
``​`

`findLaserPathCounter` walks every morph of the game looking for the one named `'laserPath'`, and `updateCounters` has to guard against not finding it. The panel holds its counter, so both the walk and the guard go:

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameControlPanelElement >> laserPathCounter
^I"Answer the counter showing how long the laser beam is. I hold it, so nothing has to search
^Ifor it: page 142 finds it by walking every morph of the game looking for the name
^I'laserPath'."

^I^ laserPathCounter

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameControlPanelElement >> updateCounters
^I"Show how long the beam is while the laser fires, and nothing while it does not. This is page
^I142's #updateCounters, which has to find the LED among the morphs of the game first; I hold
^Iit."

This is the method as this chapter writes it; Section 4.4 adds the counter of page 141 above the buttons and keeps the row in an instance variable of its own.

`cellSpacing:` is the gap between the buttons, the margin is the gap between the row and the two edges of the panel it is aligned to, and `alignLeft` with `alignBottom` is the corner. ## What the buttons do

The game gains the two actions, and the question the buttons ask it:

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameElement >> laserIsActive
	"Answer whether the laser is firing. The grid knows; I only ask."

	^ self grid laserIsActive
``​`

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameElement >> toggleLaser
	"Fire the laser, or stop it if it is already firing, and show the result. This is what the fire
	button does, and it is the original's #fireLaser on the morph."

	self laserIsActive
		ifTrue: [ self grid stopLaser ]
		ifFalse: [ self grid fireLaser ].
	self refresh
``​`

``​`smalltalk
LaserGameElement >> quit
	"Close the game. The original sends #delete to its morph."
```

Commit message (code only):

```
Section 4.5 - Add Move Counter And Randomizer: count the moves, deal a new board, ask before quitting

The game counts every move that changes the grid and shows it in a second
counter under the beam counter, a New button deals a fresh random board, and
Quit now asks before it closes.

Most of page 145 was already in the package: GridFactory came with the whole
randomizer, in page 147's generalized form. Two of its methods had never run
under Pharo and asked their generator for #nextInt:, which is Squeak's name;
both now send #nextInteger:. The class is classified and commented.

LaserGameElement gains moves, moves:, incrementMoves and moveMade, and
registers moveMade as the board's move action, so a click that changed the
grid counts one and then updates the counters. A click that changes nothing
is not counted, unlike the original, which counts every mouse up. newGame is
page 146's, without activeCellLocation: nil and initializeDirty, neither of
which the port keeps; it clears the cells before it randomizes, since
randomizeGrid: clears nothing.

The panel gains a three-digit Moves counter in the counter column and three
more lines in updateCounters. The third button forces page 144's button
layout arithmetic, which becomes newRowOfButtons: and a column of rows: the
New row above the Quit and Fire row. buttonRow and newGameRow read the
column's children, so the panel stays at eight instance variables.

Page 144's (self confirm: ...) cannot be had here, since nothing draws in
Morphic and a Bloc handler cannot wait inside the space that would draw the
dialog. LaserGameConfirmElement covers the game with a shade and a box of two
buttons and hands its answer to a block; quit asks through ask:onConfirm: and
close does what quit did. Three new colors on LaserGameColors.

Page 146's fillBackground, redrawCell and renderContents trio has no
counterpart: a cell element asks the grid what stands at its location when it
is redrawn, so refresh repaints a dealt board.

Twenty-one tests, with a new test case each for the randomizer and the
question. 193 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

'I am the whole game on the screen: a control panel on the left, a board on the right, and a margin around both.I replace the 2007 `LaserGame` morph of pages 065 to 067, which held a `SketchMorph` over a board form and a white rectangle for the panel. I hold a `LaserGameBoardElement` and a `LaserGameControlPanelElement` instead, and I take my size from them, the panel width and the margin, the way the original''s `calculatedExtent` did. Page 139 puts the panel on the left, and page 140 fills me with the colour ramp of `LaserGameColors windowColorRamp`.``​`LaserGameElement openExample``​`From page 143 I also count the moves the player makes, and from page 146 I can start a new game on a randomized grid. Page 144 asks before quitting, which the original does with `#confirm:`; I lay a `LaserGameConfirmElement` over myself instead, since a Bloc element cannot wait for an answer.Instance variables:- `grid`: the grid played on. Setting it rebuilds what I hold.- `board`: the `LaserGameBoardElement` showing that grid.- `controlPanel`: the panel beside it, holding the buttons and the counters.- `moves`: how many moves have been made on the board.- `confirmation`: the question laid over me, nil while none is asked.I know nothing about the rules. The grid answers those, and the model-side `LaserGame` of the later sections will own the moves, the counters and the undo stack.'
