### Claude — 2026-09-28 20:08:07Z

Section 4.6 done, in the image.

**What page 147 asked for that was already there**: the whole randomizer half — `randomizedGridOfExtent:`, `emptyRandomLocationsFor:` marking the target corner used, `randomizeGrid:targetAt:`, the one-line `randomizeGrid:`, and `defaultGrid` (8@10). Section 4.5 already read those in their page-147 form. Three new tests pin them.

**What was new**: page 147's `initializeForGrid:` split is the port's `on:`/`grid:` since 2.11, so the work is the openers — `LaserGameElement class >> onRandomOfExtent:`, `openRandomOfExtent:`, `openStandardExample` (page 148's workspace, on `GridFactory defaultGrid`). `openExample` keeps the demo board.

**Nothing assumed 5×5**: board is a grid layout of one element per cell, panel takes panel width and board height, `extentForGrid:` follows both. Three tests hold it (size follows the grid, New keeps the size, three-digit counters still hold what 80 cells make — paths run in the tens, max 37 over 200 deals). Class comments of `GridFactory` and `LaserGameElement` updated.

Tests 200 passed, 0 failed, 0 errored. Critics clean on `GridFactory`, `LaserGameElement` and both test cases except the pre-existing package-name rule. Live check on `openStandardExample`: space 530@520, panel `(10,10)-(120,510)`, board `(120,10)-(520,510)`, 80 cells, 32 mirrors, target at 8@1, Fire still 10 px off the board. Window left open.

Doc: 4.6 chapter appended to `doc/section4/section4.md`; all 501 method blocks verify identical to image. `PROJECT_MAP.md` and memory anchor updated (reader position end of `148.html`; 4.7 = pages 149–155, Drawing The Laser Beam, next).

Commit message:

```
Section 4.6 - A Bigger Game Board: play on a board of any size

The game can be opened on a randomized board of any extent, and the standard
board of page 148 is eight columns by ten rows.

Most of page 147 was already in the package. GridFactory came with
randomizedGridOfExtent:, with emptyRandomLocationsFor: marking the target
corner used before a mirror is dealt, with randomizeGrid:targetAt: and with
the one-line randomizeGrid: that reads the corner from the board. Three tests
now say so: a board of any extent is dealt ready to play, the corner is
marked used whatever the size of the board, and defaultGrid is the eight by
ten board of page 148.

The rest of page 147 splits LaserGame >> initialize into initializeForGrid:
so that a game can be handed a board. The port has had that split since
Section 2.11, because a Bloc element is initialized before anything can hand
it a grid: LaserGameElement class >> on: is initializeForGrid:, and grid:
rebuilds. So the new code is the makers and the opener:
onRandomOfExtent:, openRandomOfExtent: and openStandardExample, which is page
148's workspace. openExample keeps the demo board the earlier chapters are
written around.

Nothing in the port assumed a five by five board. The board element is a grid
layout of one element per cell, the panel takes the width of a panel and the
height of the board, and extentForGrid: follows both. Three tests hold that:
the game takes the size of whatever board it is given, New keeps that size,
and the three-digit counters of Section 4.4 still hold what eighty cells
produce, since the paths of such a board run in the tens.

Class comments of GridFactory and LaserGameElement updated.

Six tests. 200 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

'	"Answer how much the game has to be scaled by to fill a window of anExtent without changing', cr,
'	its shape: the tighter of the two directions, so the whole board stays in view and the cells', cr,
'	stay square."', cr, cr,
'	| natural |', cr,
'	natural := self naturalExtent.', cr,
'	^ ((anExtent x / natural x) min: (anExtent y / natural y)) asFloat') classified: 'geometry'.

'	"Answer where the scaled game sits in a window of anExtent: in the middle of it, with the', cr,
'	leftover of the looser direction split between the two sides."', cr, cr,
'	^ (anExtent - (self naturalExtent * (self scaleToFitIn: anExtent))) / 2') classified: 'geometry'.

This is the method as this chapter writes it; page 140 paints the panel transparent so that the window ramp runs behind it, and Section 4.4 follows it.

Page 061 asked for every color of the game to be written down in one place, and the rule holds: neither of these two is a `Color` literal anywhere else.

> **Which side is the panel on?** Page 066 says "I'd like to place the game board on the left side of the morph and have a vertical control panel on the right", and that is the order we use: the board is the first child, the panel the second. The finished 2007 code does the opposite — its `setupMorphs` gives the control panel the fractions `0@0 corner: 0@1` at the left edge and offsets the board by `gameMargin + panelWidth` — so somewhere after this page the author changed their mind. We follow the sentence on the page, and turning the game around later means swapping two `addChild:` sends.

There is a third pane in the original's `setupMorphs`, a four pixel strip under the left edge of the board called the laser-home morph. It marks where the beam enters. It belongs with the beam, so it arrives in Section 4 with the rest of the drawing of the laser.

```
Port addition - A window the player can resize: scale the game to its space

The 2007 original is a Morph of a fixed size, and the port opened its space
at the extent the grid asks for and left it there, so dragging the corner of
the window left the game the size it was.

LaserGameElement now answers its drawn size as #naturalExtent and scales from
it: #scaleToFitIn: takes the tighter of the two directions so the cells stay
square, #positionToCenterIn: splits the leftover of the looser one between the
two sides, and #fitIn: sets the transformation and the position from both. A
window of no size is ignored, since a space announces one while it opens.

LaserGameElement class >> openOn: keeps the element it adds and subscribes the
space root to BlElementExtentChangedEvent, fitting the game to the new extent
each time it changes. The space is still opened at the natural extent, and
#fitIn: is sent once before #show, so a game that is never resized looks as it
did before.

Nothing else changed. The cells are geometries rather than bitmaps, so they
are drawn at any scale without a redraw, and Bloc hit-tests through the same
transformation it draws through, so the click code needs no change.

Four tests, all headless: they call #fitIn: on a detached element and read
back #transformation matrix and #constraints position.

204 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

'digits: anInteger	"Answer a display of anInteger digits, showing zero."	| led |	led := self new.	led digitCount: anInteger.	^ led

segmentsForDigit: anInteger	"Answer the names of the segments the digit anInteger lights."	^ #( #( #a #b #c #d #e #f ) #( #b #c ) #( #a #b #g #e #d )	     #( #a #b #g #c #d ) #( #f #g #b #c ) #( #a #f #g #c #d )	     #( #a #f #g #e #c #d ) #( #a #b #c ) #( #a #b #c #d #e #f #g )	     #( #a #b #c #d #f #g ) ) at: anInteger + 1

updateDigits	"Color every segment of every digit for the number I show. The number is right aligned, the	digits in front of it stay blank, and a number too long for me keeps its last digits."	| text |	text := value printString.	text size > digitCount ifTrue: [ text := text last: digitCount ].	digitElements withIndexDo: [ :digit :index |		| position segments |		position := index - (digitCount - text size).		segments := position > 0			            ifTrue: [			            self class segmentsForDigit: (text at: position) digitValue ]			            ifFalse: [ #(  ) ].		digit children withIndexDo: [ :segment :segmentIndex |			segment background:				((segments includes: (self class segmentNames at: segmentIndex))					 ifTrue: [ self onColor ]					 ifFalse: [ self offColor ]) ] ]

value: anInteger	"Show anInteger."	value := anInteger.	self updateDigits

segmentNames #(#a #b #c #d #e #f #g)
digit 1 lit #()
digit 2 lit #()
digit 3 lit #(#a #b #c #d #e #f)
segmentBoundsOf: aSymbol	"Answer the rectangle segment aSymbol occupies in a digit, in the digit''s own coordinates. The	three bars run across the top, the middle and the bottom, and the four arms fill the two gaps	the bars leave, so every size follows the digit size and the segment thickness."	| width height thickness arm |	width := self digitExtent x.	height := self digitExtent y.	thickness := self segmentThickness.	arm := height - (3 * thickness) // 2.	aSymbol == #a ifTrue: [ ^ thickness @ 0 extent: width - (2 * thickness) @ thickness ].	aSymbol == #b ifTrue: [ ^ width - thickness @ thickness extent: thickness @ arm ].	aSymbol == #c ifTrue: [		^ width - thickness @ (thickness + arm + thickness) extent: thickness @ arm ].	aSymbol == #d ifTrue: [		^ thickness @ (height - thickness) extent: width - (2 * thickness) @ thickness ].	aSymbol == #e ifTrue: [ ^ 0 @ (thickness + arm + thickness) extent: thickness @ arm ].	aSymbol == #f ifTrue: [ ^ 0 @ thickness extent: thickness @ arm ].	aSymbol == #g ifTrue: [		^ thickness @ (thickness + arm) extent: width - (2 * thickness) @ thickness ].	^ self error: ''No segment is named '' , aSymbol printString'

rebuildDigits	"Replace my digits with digitCount fresh ones and take the size they need."	self removeChildren.	digitElements := (1 to: digitCount) collect: [ :each | self newDigitElement ].	digitElements do: [ :each | self addChild: each ].	self extent: (self class extentForDigits: digitCount).	self updateDigits

newDigitElement	"Answer one digit: an element of the digit size holding one rectangle per segment, in the	order the segment names are in. The rectangles stay; showing another number recolours them."	| digit |	digit := BlElement new.	digit extent: self class digitExtent.	digit background: BlTransparentBackground new.	self class segmentNames do: [ :name |		| area segment |		area := self class segmentBoundsOf: name.		segment := BlElement new.		segment extent: area extent.		segment position: area origin.		digit addChild: segment ].	^ digit

digitExtent	"Answer the size, in pixels, of one digit. 	"Replace my digits with digitCount fresh ones and take the size they need."

LaserGameLedElement >> updateDigits
	"Color every segment of every digit for the number I show. The number is right aligned, the
	digits in front of it stay blank, and a number too long for me keeps its last digits."

	| text |
	text := value printString.
	text size > digitCount ifTrue: [ text := text last: digitCount ].
	digitElements withIndexDo: [ :digit :index |
		| position segments |
		position := index - (digitCount - text size).
		segments := position > 0
			            ifTrue: [
			            self class segmentsForDigit: (text at: position) digitValue ]
			            ifFalse: [ #(  ) ].
		digit children withIndexDo: [ :segment :segmentIndex |
			segment background:
				((segments includes: (self class segmentNames at: segmentIndex))
					 ifTrue: [ self onColor ]
					 ifFalse: [ self offColor ]) ] ]

### Claude — 2026-09-28 20:34:01Z

Yes — both show numbers. They were unreadable, two defects.

**What was wrong**

1. **Colors.** Original `LedMorph` sits on a dark slab and paints unlit segments *in the slab color*, so they vanish. Port took page 141's two colors but left the display transparent → every unlit segment showed against the page 140 ramp. All seven segments visible on each digit = "88…". Sampled the page-148 screenshot: slab is `(0.33, 0.33, 0.52)` — same color the port used for "off".
2. **Clipping.** LED is 34 px wide for 3 digits, but digits stood at 2, 14, 26 → third ended at 36, two past the edge, clipped. Cause: `BlLinearLayout cellSpacing:` spaces cells from its own edges too — same fault as the Fire button in 4.5.

**Fix (image, `Laser-Game`)**
- `LaserGameColors class >> counterBodyColor` new (the slab); `counterDigitOffColor` answers it; `LaserGameLedElement >> initialize` paints the display in it.
- `counterDigitHighlightColor` new, near-white — page 148 shows the firing counter almost white, not two lavenders a few percent apart. `onColor` uses it.
- `rebuildDigits`: gap is a left margin on every digit but the first; row has no cell spacing. Digits now 0–10, 12–22, 24–34.
- 3 tests (2 new, 1 updated). **206 passed, 0 failed, 0 errored.** Critics 0 on touched classes (one pre-existing `ReTestClassNotInPackageWithTestEndingNameRule`).

Verified on the open window: Laser Path shows `9` white while firing, Moves `0` lavender, both on a dark slab.

Two deliberate port differences kept: no leading zeros (original pads to `012`), caption under the digits (original above). Say if you want either changed.

**Docs** — new chapter *Counters The Player Can Read* at end of `doc/section4/section4.md`; three now-stale 4.4 blocks untagged with forward notes. Checker: 515 method blocks identical, 0 mismatched. `PROJECT_MAP.md` section 9 renamed to additions **and corrections** with a second row; memory updated.

Commit message, separate from the resize one:

```
Port correction - Counters the player can read: hide unlit segments and stop clipping the last digit

Both counters read 88E rather than a number. The values were right and
updateCounters set them on every move and every shot; the colours were wrong.

The original's LedMorph draws itself on a dark slab and paints the segments it
does not light in the colour of that slab, so they disappear into it. Sampling
the screenshot of page 148 gives that slab as (0.33, 0.33, 0.52), which is the
colour this port was already painting an unlit segment in - but the display was
transparent, so those segments showed against the window ramp of page 140
instead, and every digit lit all seven of them.

LaserGameColors class >> counterBodyColor is new and is the slab,
counterDigitOffColor answers it, and LaserGameLedElement >> initialize paints
the display in it. The same screenshot has the highlighted counter nearly white,
where the port had two shades of lavender a few per cent apart, so
counterDigitHighlightColor is new and #onColor answers it.

Reading the digit positions turned up a second fault: a three digit display is
thirty four pixels wide and its digits stood at 2, 14 and 26, so the last one
ended two pixels outside and was clipped. BlLinearLayout spaces its cells from
its own edges as well as between them, which is the fault the Fire button had in
Section 4.5. The gap is now a left margin on every digit but the first, and the
row spaces nothing of its own.

Three tests: unlit segments take the colour of the body, the digits fit inside
the display, and the highlight test of Section 4.4 with the two colours it now
expects.

206 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

I am one step of the laser beam: a `Cell` and the side the beam enters it from. `Grid >> calculatePath` starts one of me at the laser and follows `nextElementIn:` until a cell swallows the beam or the beam leaves the board, keeping the chain as the grid's `laserBeamPath`.

`nextElementIn: aGrid` asks my cell which side the beam leaves by, steps one cell that way, and answers the element for the cell it lands on, or `nil` when there is none. `activateCell` and `clearCell` turn the light of my cell on and off for the side the beam enters from.

LaserPathElement class >> cell: aCell entrySide: aSymbol [
	| model |

	model

	self cell laserEntersFrom: self entrySide

	self cell clearCell

Cell >> laserEntersFrom: aSymbol [
	| exit |
	self activeSegments at: aSymbol put: true.

	self activeSegments at: exit put: true.
]

{ #category : 'printing' }
Cell >> printDetailsOn: aStream [
	"Print what distinguishes me from another cell of my kind at the same place. There is nothing
	but my location, so a mirror adds the way it leans. `Point >> printOn:` puts brackets round
	itself, which would read badly inside my own, so the two coordinates are printed by hand."

	aStream
		print: self gridLocation x;
		nextPut: $@;
		print: self gridLocation y
]

{ #category : 'printing' }
Cell >> printOn: aStream [
	"Say where I am and whether the laser lights me, on one line. Page 108 of the original says the
	same on three, which reads well in a Squeak debugger pane and badly everywhere Pharo prints an
	object: a list, an inspector header, a code pane. What the page wanted from those extra lines
	is in my inspector tab instead."

	super printOn: aStream.
	aStream nextPut: $(.
	self printDetailsOn: aStream.
	aStream
		nextPutAll: ', ';
		nextPutAll: (self isOn ifTrue: [ 'on' ] ifFalse: [ 'off' ]);
		nextPut: $)
]

	"Answer a cross hair of anExtent: two bars crossing at the centre. Page 083 drew the same
	figure as two lines in a form of one cell, and Section 4.2 puts it under the pointer while
	the pointer is over a hint of a mirror."

	| span thickness |
	span := (anExtent x min: anExtent y) // 3.
	thickness := (span // 5) max: 1.
	^ BlElement new
		  extent: anExtent;
		  background: Color transparent;
		  addChild: (self crossHairBarOfExtent: span @ thickness within: anExtent);
		  addChild: (self crossHairBarOfExtent: thickness @ span within: anExtent);
		  yourself
]

4. Errors and fixes:
   - **`space extent: 900@700` left `space root extent` at 530@520** — not a bug; the root follows only after pulses. `3 timesRepeat: [ space pulse ]` then showed root 900@700, scale 1.3461, position 93.27@0.
   - **`write_resize.py` appended nothing** (file still 3238 lines) — I had omitted the trailing `open(...,'a').write(out.getvalue())`; appended it and re-ran (3410 lines).
   - **Doc mismatch after the resize work** — `doc/section2/section2.md:1420 LaserGameElement class >> openOn:`; fixed by untagging the block and adding a forward note (never by editing the image).
   - **User-reported "88-" on both counters** — two causes: unlit segments painted `counterDigitColor muchDarker` on a transparent display over the bright ramp (the original hides them by making the slab that same color), and the third digit clipped because `cellSpacing` pushed digits to 2/14/26 in a 34-wide display. Fixed with `counterBodyColor` + margins, verified live.
   - **`asForm` on `panel counterColumn` looked clipped** (label read "Laser Patl") — capture artifact of rendering a sub-element of a scaled game, not a layout fault; rendering `space root asForm` showed the true window.
   - **`from PIL import Image` → ModuleNotFoundError** — used Pharo's `JPEGReadWriter formFromFileNamed:`, `copy:`, `magnifyBy:`, `PNGReadWriter putForm:onFileNamed:` instead.
   - **`SystemNavigation >> #senders:` DNU** — used `#extentForDigits: implementors , #extentForDigits: senders`.
   - **`mcp__pharo__method_source` with `className: 'LaserGameElement class'` → "class not found"** — read metaclass source via `(LaserGameElement class >> #openOn:) sourceCode`.
   - **Empty `v2_darkled.png`** — `col` was captured before `panel rebuild` replaced the elements; re-fetched `panel counterColumn` after the rebuild.
   - **British/US spelling drift** — new comments used "colour" while `LaserGameColors` uses "color"; normalized the touched methods to "color".

	masked
		displayOn: self targetForm
		at: (cellPosn + offset)
		clippingBox: self targetForm boundingBox
		rule: Form oldPaint
		fillColor: aColor

Drawing The Laser Beam
The game is fun without the laser beam being visible. You can find

## The original's repository of forms

Page 083 gives the drawings a home: `LaserGameForms`, a subclass of `Object` with no instance variables and one class variable, `CachedForms`. The workspace code becomes a class method, the four arrays become four class methods, and a fifth method fills the cache:

``​`
LaserGameForms class >> arrowFormFromPointsArray: pts
	"LaserGameForms initializeCachedForms"
	| form fillForm index startPoint nextIndex endPoint line offset |
	offset := 2@2.
	form := Form extent: 330@330 depth: 1.
	form fillColor: Color white.
	fillForm := Form extent: 1@1 depth: 1.
	fillForm fillColor: Color black.
	index := 1.
	[index <= pts size] whileTrue: [
		startPoint := pts at: index.
		nextIndex := index = pts size
			ifTrue: [1]
			ifFalse: [index + 1].
		endPoint := pts at: nextIndex.
		startPoint := startPoint + offset.
		endPoint := endPoint + offset.
		line := Line from: startPoint to: endPoint withForm: fillForm.
		line displayOn: form.
		index := index + 1].
	form floodFill: Color black at: 1@1.
	form reverse.
	^form copy: (form tightRectangleAroundColor: Color black)
``​`

Commit message:

```
Section 4.7 - Drawing The Laser Beam: beam as geometry, beam forms deleted

Pages 149 to 155 paint the beam by hand in the paint tool, capture it with
Form fromDisplay:, write it out with storeOn: as drawLaserBeamForm, pull a
splatter mask and a centre mask out of it by colour substitution and
makeBWForm:, mirror the form so that two cells meet without a seam, and cache
the three bitmaps. All the port keeps of that is the two colours page 155
settles on, which came in with the captured package.

LaserGameShapes draws the beam instead: horizontalLaserBeamElementOfExtent:
and verticalLaserBeamElementOfExtent: answer a pale laserBeamSplatterColor
band across the cell with a thinner laserBeamCenterColor bar along its middle,
both centred by laserBeamBarOfExtent:within:color:, in the style of the cross
hair's bar. laserBeamSplatterThicknessFor: is a third of the cell and
laserBeamCenterThicknessFor: a sixth, each at least one pixel, so the beam
scales with the cell as the original's bitmap does. Rectangles are symmetric,
so page 153's mirrored form has no counterpart, and beams in neighbouring
cells join without a seam.

Deleted from LaserGameForms: drawLaserBeamForm, drawCenterLaserBeamMask,
drawSplatterLaserBeamMask, the accessors laserBeam, centerBeamMask and
splatterBeamMask, and extractLaserBeamMaskForms, with the three beam lines of
initializeCachedForms. The unreachable CellRenderer mask-painting chain stays
until the cells learn to draw the beam themselves.

Three tests. 209 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

"
I am the element that shows one cell of the grid, and I am the thing a player clicks on.

I keep the CellRenderer that built me, so I can answer the cell I show, where that cell sits in the grid, and — through `clickRegionAt:` — which click region a point of mine falls in. The point is in my own coordinates, which is what Bloc hands to an event handler, so nothing has to subtract my position from a board-wide coordinate first. The original tutorial had no such element: every cell drew into one shared Form, and a click had to be converted into a grid location by dividing by the cell size (`CellRenderer >> offsetWithinGridForm` and the `cellForEvent:` family on the LaserGame morph).

I listen to the mouse myself: entering, leaving, moving and clicking all reach me because Bloc delivers an event to the element it happened in. I tell my board what happened (`hoverCellElement:`, `unhoverCellElement:`, `clickCellElement:`), and my board holds the state the game reads. The original registered five events on one board morph, added itself as a listener of the hand morph to see moves with the button up, and searched the submorphs under the pointer for the morph named 'board'; none of that has a counterpart here.

While the pointer is in me I also keep a hint: `showPositionHintAt:` asks my renderer what applies at that point and `clearPositionHint` forgets it when the pointer leaves. Only a mirror answers a region, since a click acts on mirrors only.

"
I am the game board: the element that shows every cell of one grid.

I hold a grid and one child element per cell of it, built by the CellRenderer of each cell. A BlGridLayout places those children, one column per grid column, so a cell never computes where it sits: that was the job of the offsets the original tutorial needed when all cells drew into one shared Form.

The original tutorial computed the extent of that shared Form from the cell size, the border width and the grid dimensions. I keep the arithmetic as `LaserGameBoardElement class >> extentForGrid:`, because a window still has to be given a size, but nothing depends on it internally: I take the size of my cells through fitContent constraints, and cell borders are painted inside the cells, so they cost no space.

I also hold what the mouse is doing to my cells. Each cell element handles its own mouse events and tells me: `hoverCellElement:` and `unhoverCellElement:` keep `hoveredCellElement` current, `clickCellElement:` records `clickedCell`, and `moveMade` says that a click changed the grid. So `hoveredCell` answers the cell under the pointer, which the original had to compute from the hand position, the board offset and the cell size, and printed to the Transcript on page 078.

	^ CellRenderer rendererFor: aTargetCell grid: grid

TargetCellRenderer >> maskOffHorizontalOn: aMask [
	| newMask halfExtent halfRect offset |
	halfExtent := (aMask width // 2)@(aMask height).
	newMask := Form extent: aMask extent depth: aMask depth.
	newMask fillColor: Color white.
	(self cell activeSegments at: #west)
		ifTrue: [offset := 0]
		ifFalse: [offset := halfExtent x].
	halfRect := (aMask boundingBox origin + (offset@0)) extent: halfExtent.
	aMask
		displayOn: newMask
		at: offset@0
		clippingBox: halfRect
		rule: Form paint
		fillColor: Color black.
	^newMask
]

{ #category : 'drawing' }
TargetCellRenderer >> maskOffVerticalOn: aMask [
	| newMask halfExtent halfRect offset |
	newMask := Form extent: aMask extent depth: aMask depth.

	halfExtent := (aMask width)@(aMask height // 2).
	(self cell activeSegments at: #south)

	aMask
		displayOn: newMask
		at: 0@0
		clippingBox: halfRect
		rule: Form paint
		fillColor: Color black.
	^newMask
]

| src |
src := 'horizontalLaserBeamElementOfExtent: anExtent enteringFrom: aSymbol
	"Answer an element of anExtent drawing the beam where it enters a cell from the side aSymbol
	names, west or east, and stops in the middle of it, which is what a cell that swallows the
	light shows. Pages 160 and 162 of the original draw the whole beam and then black out the half
	the light never reaches, with a mask built for the purpose; half a bar needs no mask. The bars
	are as thick as the ones of a whole beam, since the cell they cross is the same size."

	| length left splatter centre |
	length := anExtent x // 2.
	left := aSymbol = #west
		        ifTrue: [ 0 ]
		        ifFalse: [ anExtent x - length ].
	splatter := self laserBeamSplatterThicknessFor: anExtent.
	centre := self laserBeamCenterThicknessFor: anExtent.
	^ BlElement new
		  extent: anExtent;
		  background: Color transparent;
		  addChild: (self
				   laserBeamBarOfExtent: length @ splatter
				   at: left @ ((anExtent y - splatter) / 2)
				   color: LaserGameColors laserBeamSplatterColor);
		  addChild: (self
				   laserBeamBarOfExtent: length @ centre
				   at: left @ ((anExtent y - centre) / 2)
				   color: LaserGameColors laserBeamCenterColor);
		  yourself'.

Section 4.9 - Laser On Target Cell: half a beam, drawn under the target

The target swallows the light, so the beam crosses only half of its cell,
and the target has to stay visible through it.

LaserGameShapes answers half beams: horizontalLaserBeamElementOfExtent:
enteringFrom: and verticalLaserBeamElementOfExtent:enteringFrom: draw bars
half as long, as thick as a whole beam's, flush against the side the light

refactoring is the renderLaserOn: / renderBeamOn: split already made in 4.8.

	"Answer the thickness, in pixels, of the mirror. The original drew its diagonal with a two

	^ 2

	^ MirrorCell

{ #category : 'drawing' }
MirrorCellRenderer >> addMirrorFrom: aPoint to: anotherPoint on: anElement [
	"Add the mirror to anElement as a child carrying a line geometry. The child covers the whole
	cell, so both points are cell local, and the stroke is centered on the line so that the
	mirror is as thick on one side of it as on the other."

	| mirror |
	mirror := BlElement new.
	mirror extent: self class cellExtent.
	mirror geometry: (BlLineGeometry from: aPoint to: anotherPoint).
	mirror outskirts: BlOutskirts centered.
	mirror border: (BlBorder
			 paint: LaserGameColors mirrorColor
			 width: self class mirrorWidth).
	anElement addChild: mirror
]

| defs |
defs := OrderedCollection new.

	"Answer the bar of a beam that runs across a cell of anExtent, as thick as aThickness and
	painted in aColor. It runs the whole way when both the west and the east side of the cell are
	lit, and half the way, from the lit side to the middle, when only one of them is."

	| length left |
	length := ((aCollection includes: #west) and: [
		           aCollection includes: #east ])
		          ifTrue: [ anExtent x ]
		          ifFalse: [ anExtent x // 2 ].
	left := (aCollection includes: #west)
		        ifTrue: [ 0 ]
		        ifFalse: [ anExtent x - length ].
	^ self
		  laserBeamBarOfExtent: length @ aThickness
		  at: left @ ((anExtent y - aThickness) / 2)
		  color: aColor'.

Pages 159 to 165 draw the beam on the cell it ends in. A target swallows the light, so the beam crosses only half of the cell, and the target itself has to stay visible through it: two differences from the blank cell of the last chapter, and both of them are about the half of the picture that is not drawn.

	are a cell the beam goes straight through, two sides at a right angle are the turn at a mirror,

### Claude — 2026-09-28 21:24:13Z

4.10 done. 224 tests green, critics clean (only accepted pre-existing ones), all protocols classified, doc blocks verified 537/537 identical.

**What the port does**

One fact replaces eight pages: lit sides of cell say whole picture. New `Cell >> litSides`. New pair of bar builders on `LaserGameShapes class` — whole bar when both sides of axis lit, half bar from lit side otherwise — under new `laserBeamElementOfExtent:fromSides:`, which draws both pale bands first, both bright cores over them. `CellRenderer >> renderBeamOn:` stops being empty hook and becomes the single method drawing blank, target, mirror and any of them crossed twice. Mirror gets no drawing code of its own.

**Deleted:** `MirrorCellRenderer` `renderLaser`, four `maskFor*` quadrant masks, three `removeLaserFromInactive*`, two `maskOff*` stubs; `BlankCellRenderer >> renderBeamOn:` and `TargetCellRenderer >> renderBeamOn:`; `CellRenderer >> renderLaser`, its eight `renderLaserHorizontal*`/`renderLaserVertical*` methods and `render` (dead since board became elements); four superseded shape builders plus senderless `laserBeamBarOfExtent:within:color:`. Quadrant masks and the 1-pixel/3-pixel fudges of pages 168–169 have no counterpart.

**Visual check:** demo grid fired — beam turns square at 4@5 and 4@1, stops in target, no notch at either elbow.

**Doc:** new chapter *Laser On Mirror Cell* in `doc/section4/section4.md`; 13 blocks from 4.7/4.8/4.9 untagged with forward notes. `PROJECT_MAP.md` and memory updated — Section 4 complete, next is 5.1 A Missed Bug (page 174).

Commit message ready:

```
Section 4.10 - Laser On Mirror Cell: one beam drawing for every kind of cell

Pages 166 to 173 draw the beam on the cell that turns it. The original
draws both whole beams, then blacks out the two quadrants the light never
reaches with four flood-filled quadrant masks, repairs the borders those
masks painted over, repaints one bright core so that both cores land over
both bands, and writes a five-pixel and a three-pixel correction into the
offset arithmetic to centre the result.

One fact runs under all of it: the sides of a cell that carry light say
the whole of what is drawn. Cell >> litSides answers them.
LaserGameShapes gains horizontalLaserBeamBarOfExtent:sides:thickness:color:
and its vertical twin, each a bar running the whole way across when both
sides of its axis are lit and half the way from the lit side otherwise,
and laserBeamElementOfExtent:fromSides: draws the two pale bands first and
the two bright cores over them, which is page 167's order without its
repetition.

CellRenderer >> renderBeamOn: stops being an empty hook and becomes the
one method that draws the beam of every kind of cell: a blank cell the
beam crosses, the target it ends in, the mirror it turns at, and any of
them crossed twice, which is what page 170 finds on the board and page 173
fixes for the blank cell. The mirror needs no drawing code of its own, and
the mirror line lies over the light because the beam is added before the
contents.

Deleted: MirrorCellRenderer >> renderLaser, its four maskFor... quadrant
masks, the three removeLaserFromInactive... methods and the two maskOff...
stubs; BlankCellRenderer >> renderBeamOn: and TargetCellRenderer >>
renderBeamOn:; CellRenderer >> renderLaser with the eight
renderLaserHorizontal... and renderLaserVertical... methods page 165 had
moved up into it, and render, which was their only caller and which
nothing has called since the board became elements; the four superseded
beam builders on LaserGameShapes and the now senderless
laserBeamBarOfExtent:within:color:. The quadrant masks and the two pixel
corrections have no counterpart: nothing is painted that must be taken
away again, and a bar centred by (anExtent - aThickness) / 2 does not
drift.

Six new tests, six older beam tests rewritten to the one builder.
224 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

The window can be any size; this one is the	size the drawing is scaled from."	^ self class extentForGrid: self grid' 'scaleToFitIn: anExtent	"Answer how much the game has to be scaled by to fill a window of anExtent without changing	its shape: the tighter of the two directions, so the whole board stays in view and the cells	stay square."	| natural |	natural := self naturalExtent.	^ ((anExtent x / natural x) min: (anExtent y / natural y)) asFloat' 'positionToCenterIn: anExtent	"Answer where the scaled game sits in a window of anExtent: in the middle of it, with the	leftover of the looser direction split between the two sides."	^ (anExtent - (self naturalExtent * (self scaleToFitIn: anExtent))) / 2')

# Communicate With Arrow Colors

*Pages 130 to 133 of the 2007 tutorial.*

<!-- http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/130.html

The game works. Section 4 is a list of things that could be better, and page 130 starts with the one the player notices first:

> For the existing code we are painting grey arrows. What if we made the color of the arrows dependent on whether the choice was valid or not?

A hint arrow says which way a click would move the cell, and says nothing about whether it could. The mirror at 4@1 in the demo grid offers four push arrows, and only two of those pushes can happen: north is off the board and east is the target, which never moves. The arrow that promises the impossible is worse than no arrow, because the player has to click to find out.

# Drawing The Laser Beam

The game plays without the beam being drawn. The counter says how many cells the beam runs through, the target lights up when the beam reaches it, and the player works the rest out. Pages 149 to 155 draw the beam itself, and they are the longest detour in the tutorial: seven pages, of which the last half page is the only one the port keeps.

## Seven pages in a paint tool

Page 149 opens a `RectangleMorph`, makes it large, sets its colour to white from an inspector, and drags the paint tool out of the objects tool onto it. The author then paints the beam by hand: a wide band of light yellow with the fattest brush, no effort made to keep the edges smooth, two nearly white lines outside it that overlap the yellow so there are no gaps, and on page 150 some dabbing with smaller brushes and brighter colours until it looks right. The sketch is kept, dropped on the white panel, and made thinner, with the deep yellow part centred as well as the hand can centre it.

5.1 done. 224 tests green, critics clean, protocols classified, doc blocks 543/543 identical.

**Finding.** Three of the original's four failures cannot happen here — port's tables ask `CellClickRegionInside/Outside regionRectangle` instead of writing pixels down, since 3.5. Page 177's real bug (both `containsPoint:` comparing against whole cell height, missing `// 2`) was never written: both were correct at 3.8, and `testAPointOnTheDividingLineTurnsTheMirrorClockwise` fails on the original's version. Page 179's `testCellOffsetCalculations` has no counterpart — `offsetWithinGridForm` belongs to the shared board form the port does not have.

**Checked the claim instead of making it.** Recompiled `CellRenderer class >> cellExtent` to 30@30 and 64@64, ran full suite at each. Same bug found in port's own tests:

- `LaserGameElementTestCase` — `testAGameScalesToFillTheWindowItIsGiven`, `testAGameShrinksWithASmallerWindow`, `testAGameIgnoresAWindowOfNoSize`, `testAGameKeepsItsShapeInAWindowOfAnotherShape` wrote `380 @ 270` and multiples of it. Now read `game naturalExtent`.
- `LaserGameCellElementTestCase >> testTheCrossHairFollowsThePointerWithinOneRegion` stepped 4 pixels, left the push region at 26. Now steps a quarter of the inside region.

Suite green at 26, 30, 40, 64, 100. Below 26 it cannot be green: `insideRegionExtent` is `cellExtent - 20`, so a 24-pixel cell has a 4-pixel push region whose corners and centre collapse. Limit of page 138's design, recorded as the floor. No production code changed.

**Doc:** `doc/section5/section5.md` created, chapter *A Missed Bug*; 5 superseded blocks in section4.md untagged with forward notes. `PROJECT_MAP.md` + memory updated — reader at end of 179, next 5.2 Adding More Game Stats. Note 5.1 pre-empts part of 5.7 (pages 190–196, less brittle test design).

'I am the control panel of the game: the column beside the board that holds its buttons and its counters.I replace the panel the 2007 `LaserGame` morph built in `makeControlPanelMorph` and filled through `addButtonsToPanel:` and `addCountersToPanel:`. I hold Toplo buttons instead of `PluggableButtonMorph`s, and I hold what I am asked about in an instance variable, so nothing has to search the children by name the way `findFireButton`, `findLaserPathCounter` and `findMovesCounter` do.Three buttons: Quit, which asks the game to close, and Fire, whose label says what a click will do — `''Fire''` while the laser is off, `''Stop''` while it fires, both from page 068 — and New, from page 144, which deals a new randomized board. Quit and Fire share the bottom row and New has the row above it, which is how page 144 numbers them. Two counters, from pages 141 and 143: the length of the beam, bright while the laser fires, and the number of moves made, never bright. The buttons sit at my bottom left corner and the counters at my top left corner, which is where the original''s layout frames put them. Page 140 paints me transparent, so the window ramp behind me shows through. The divider, Undo and Reset come with their own pages.Instance variables:- `game`: the `LaserGameElement` I control. Setting it builds everything I show.- `quitButton`, `fireButton`, `newGameButton`: the three buttons.- `buttonColumn`: the column of button rows. `buttonRow` and `newGameRow` read its two rows.

{ #category : 'tests' }
LaserGameElementTestCase >> testAGameTakesTheSizeOfWhateverBoardItIsGiven [
	"Page 147 hands the game a grid instead of building one, so the size of the board is the size
	of the grid. The game is one cell per location, the panel keeps its width and takes the height
	of the board beside it, and the window is the two of them and the margins. The sizes are read
	from the layout constraints, since nothing is laid out until a space shows it."

	| game wanted |
	game := LaserGameElement onRandomOfExtent: 8 @ 10.
	wanted := LaserGameElement extentForGrid: game grid.
	self assert: game board children size equals: 80.
	self

#('canPushCell: aGridDirection fromLocation: aPoint	| cell vector swapLoc swapCell |	cell := self at: aPoint.	cell class = MirrorCell ifFalse: [^false].	vector := aGridDirection vector.	swapLoc := aPoint + vector.	swapCell := self at: swapLoc.	swapCell isNil ifTrue: [^false].	swapCell class = BlankCell ifFalse: [^false].	^true' 'pushCell: aGridDirection fromLocation: aPoint	"Push the cell at aPoint one step in aGridDirection and answer the cell that ended up where	it started. Page 122: only a mirror cell moves, the target never does, and the move happens	only when the neighbour in that direction is a blank cell, which includes there being a	neighbour at all. Nothing is really pushed — the mirror and the blank trade places. The beam	is taken off the board first and put back afterwards if the laser is on, as in	rotateCellClockwiseAt:, so the cells lit before the push go dark and the new path lights up.	Page 127 is where the original adds those two lines, after a push under a running beam left	the target lit by nothing."	| cell vector swapLoc swapCell |	cell := self at: aPoint.	cell class = MirrorCell ifFalse: [ ^ cell ].	vector := aGridDirection vector.	swapLoc := aPoint + vector.	swapCell := self at: swapLoc.	swapCell isNil ifTrue: [ ^ cell ].	swapCell class = BlankCell ifFalse: [ ^ cell ].	self clearCellsInPath.	self swapCell: cell with: swapCell.	self laserIsActive ifTrue: [ self activateCellsInPath ].	^ swapCell')

     	| actionAssociation symbol location reverseAction arguments |

     	reverseAction := ReverseLaserGameAction reverseActionSymbolFor: symbol.
     	arguments := Array with: location.
     	self perform: reverseAction withArguments: arguments.
     	self movesStack removeLast.
     	^true
     reset   "[self undo] whileTrue: []"
     stackAction: aSymbol forCell: aCell   "self movesStack add: aSymbol->(aCell gridLocation)"

Quit and Fire share the bottom row and New has the row above it, which is how page 144 numbers them. Four counters, from pages 141, 143 and 181: the length of the beam, the number of moves made, the number of mirrors standing on the board, and the number of those the beam lights. The buttons sit at my bottom left corner and the counters at my top left corner, which is where the original''s layout frames put them. 	"A push that the rules refuse is not a move, so nothing goes on the stack the undo of

	| grid |

	grid pushCellNorthFromLocation: 1 @ 1.
	grid pushCellWestFromLocation: 1 @ 2.
	grid pushCellEastFromLocation: 2 @ 3.
	grid pushCellSouthFromLocation: 5 @ 1.
	self assert: grid movesStack isEmpty.
	grid pushCellNorthFromLocation: 3 @ 3.
	self assert: grid movesStack size equals: 1

Commit message:

```
Section 5.3 - Undo: Undo button, game undo, and a round-trip grid test

The model half of pages 183 to 187 came with the 2007 source in Section 1
and has been green since: the seven Reverse*LaserGameAction classes, their
reverseActionClassFor:/reverseActionSymbolFor: and the six actionSymbol/
reverseActionSymbol pairs, and Grid's movesStack, stackAction:forCell: and
undo. Page 185's refactoring of the four pushes into pushCellAction:
fromLocation: and the stacking line of the two rotations were ported in
Sections 3.12 and 3.14.

GridTestCase >> testUndoActions and testUndoStackAfterPush are rewritten
from should:/shouldnt: to assert:equals:/deny: and given comments.

testUndoingEveryMoveGivesTheGridBackAsItWas is new and is not in the
tutorial: it plays five pushes and turns mixed together, asserts each one
was recorded, undoes them all and compares every cell with what it was.
It holds the assumption behind undo's second removeLast, which is right
only as long as every reverse action stacks exactly one entry.

LaserGameControlPanelElement gains the undoButton instance variable,
newUndoButton, its accessor, an assignment in rebuild and a second element
in newNewGameRow: page 186 places the button by layout frame at row two,
column two, and the port already builds that row. The original's
state: nil has no counterpart, the fire button alone changing its label.

LaserGameElement >> undo is page 186's, with refresh for
updateGameBoardAndControls and an early return instead of completed
ifTrue:. An undo counts as a move, since page 183 removes no count from
the player's total.

Three GUI tests: Undo beside New in the upper row, an undo that takes a
push back and counts a second move, and an undo on an untouched board that
counts nothing and redraws nothing. testNewGameButtonHasTheRowAboveTheOthers
gives up asserting that the row holds New alone.

233 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Page 128 also stops on the `*Extensions` entry of the snapshot browser, to show that the method added to `Object` travelled with the package because of the protocol it was filed under.

This port does not repeat that chapter. Pharo has replaced both tools: code lives in a Tonel repository under Git, and Iceberg is the browser that commits it. Explaining Iceberg here would duplicate a book that already exists and is kept up to date:

### Claude — 2026-09-29 01:24:04Z

5.4 done in image. 233 tests green (`run_tests` now takes `Laser-Game-Tests`).

What changed:
- 22 test classes moved from the `Tests` tag of `Laser-Game` into a new package `Laser-Game-Tests`; the tag disappeared with its last class. `Laser-Game` keeps 49 classes, tags `Model` and `Graphics`. On disk the Tonel files move to `src/Laser-Game-Tests/`.
- `BaselineOfLaserGame >> baseline:` rewritten: both packages, `Laser-Game-Tests requires: 'Laser-Game'`, groups `core` / `tests` / `default`.
- Same method gains the **Toplo baseline, missing since 4.1** — panel buttons are `ToButton`s and only Bloc was declared, so a fresh image loading this baseline would compile the panel against a class it does not have. Only the dev image's pre-loaded Toplo hid it.
- Spec resolved offline for checking: `BaselineOfLaserGame project version spec packageSpecsInLoadOrder` → `('Bloc' 'Toplo' 'Laser-Game' 'Laser-Game-Tests' 'default' 'tests' 'core')`. Not load-tested in a fresh image (no load attempted).

No code changed, nothing renamed or deleted.

Side effect: `ReTestClassNotInPackageWithTestEndingNameRule` — the accepted pre-existing critique on all 22 test classes — is gone. Full critic sweep of `Laser-Game-Tests`: clean. `Laser-Game` sweep shows only inherited 2007 leftovers (`LaserGame`, `LaserGameForms`, `MorphPath`, `Arc`, `Circle`, `Line`, `GridDirection*`, the `Reverse*` classes: no comment / not referenced).

Doc: chapter *Modify Package Definition* appended to `doc/section5/section5.md`; checker 0 mismatches, 583 method blocks identical. `PROJECT_MAP.md` and memory updated (reader position now `188.html`, 5.5 Reset).

Commit message:

```
Section 5.4 - Modify Package Definition: tests in their own package

Page 187A splits the unit tests off so that the game can be distributed
without them. Squeak has one level of grouping, so the page renames a
system category and is done. Pharo has two: a tag groups classes inside a
package, but cannot be loaded on its own, left out of a load, or named in
a baseline, and the Tests tag this port has carried since Section 1 is a
tag.

The 22 test classes move to a new package, Laser-Game-Tests, and their
Tonel files with them; the Tests tag disappears with its last class.
Laser-Game keeps its 49 classes under the Model and Graphics tags. The
name follows Pharo's convention rather than the page's LaserGame-Tests.

BaselineOfLaserGame declares both packages, with the tests requiring the
game, and three groups: core loads the game alone, which is what the page
is for, tests loads the tests, default loads both.

The same baseline now declares Toplo, which it should have declared since
Section 4.1: the control panel's buttons are ToButtons and only Bloc was
named, so a fresh image loading this baseline would have compiled the
panel against a class it did not have. The development image had Toplo
loaded before the port began, which is why nothing complained.

No code changed and nothing was renamed. One consequence worth noting:
ReTestClassNotInPackageWithTestEndingNameRule, reported as an accepted
pre-existing critique on all 22 test classes since the first one was
written, is gone.

233 tests, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

	"Answer the height, in pixels, of everything I hold: my counters, stacked with a gap between
	them and a gap above and below, and the rows of buttons under them, spaced the same way. A
	counter takes the size of its caption, so one is built and measured; nothing is laid out and
	nothing is opened. The original never needs this number, since it places its counters at fixed
	offsets from the top of a panel that is always taller than they are."

	| counter |

	^ ((self counterCount * counter measuredExtent y)
	   + ((self counterCount + 3) * self counterGap)
	   + (self buttonRowCount * self buttonHeight)
	   + ((self buttonRowCount + 1) * self buttonGap)) ceiling'.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - Pharo 13 driven live through `pharo` MCP tools: `evaluate_pharo` (`code`), `run_tests` (`package`), `compile_method` (`class_name` + `source`), `delete_method` (`class_name` + `selector`), `run_critics` (`class_name`), `method_source` (**param is `className`**, not `class_name`).
   - `compile_method` cannot target a metaclass; class-side methods go through `evaluate_pharo`: `Cls class compile: src classified: '...'`, with LF→CR conversion (`copyReplaceAll: (String with: Character lf) with: (String with: Character cr)`) to avoid `ReMethodSourceContainsLinefeedsRule`.
   - `compile_method` classifies new methods `as yet unclassified` and resets protocol on recompile; fix with `(cls >> #sel) protocol: 'name'`.
   - `ReExcessiveVariablesRule` limit is exactly 10 (`basicCheck:` uses `>=`), which drove not holding `resetButton`.
   - Measuring without a layout pass: `anElement measure: BlExtentMeasurementSpec unspecified` then `measuredExtent` (`forceLayout` forbidden in package code).
   - Pharo packages vs tags: a tag can't be loaded or named in a baseline; `aClass package: (Smalltalk packageOrganizer ensurePackage: 'Laser-Game-Tests')` promotes classes to a real package; `PackageOrganizer` API: `ensurePackage:`, `ensurePackage:withTags:`, `ensureTag:inPackage:`; `Class` API: `package`, `package:`, `package:tag:`, `packageTag`, `packageTag:`, `category`.
   - Metacello offline spec check: `BaselineOfLaserGame project version spec packageSpecsInLoadOrder` (no `groups`/`packageSpecsInLoadOrder:` selectors exist on `MetacelloVersionSpec`).
   - Screenshots: `PNGReadWriter putForm: (element asForm magnifyBy: n) onFileNamed: '<image path>'`, then Read the PNG, then delete it; `forceLayout` is fine inside an evaluation.
   - Path mapping: shell `/home/me/workspace` == image `/home/renaud/devzone/sources/PharoLaserGameTutorial`. The image's `FileSystem disk workingDirectory` is the *image* directory, not the repo — always write dumps with an absolute repo path.
   - Doc pipeline (cwd = repo): `python3 $S/collect_blocks.py` → `python3 $S/verify.py` (writes `verify.st`) → image evaluates `Smalltalk compiler evaluate: '/home/renaud/devzone/sources/PharoLaserGameTutorial/verify.st' asFileReference contents` → `python3 $S/compare.py`; then `rm -f verify.st tmp_verify.txt`.
   - Chapter generators (`write53.py`, `write54.py`) parse a dump of `@@@ Cls >> #selector` headers + `sourceCode`; dumps must be converted CR→LF (`tr '\r' '\n'`) before Python parses them. Helpers `m(name)` (```smalltalk method block), `old(text)` (untagged 2007 block), `snip(text)`. `doc/*.md` uses LF endings.

### Commit convention

One commit per numbered subsection, in order. Subject line: `Section <n.m> — <tutorial heading>: <what
changed>`. The body names the original pages covered. A commit carries two things together:

1. the code, compiled in the image and written out by Iceberg;
2. green tests (`run_tests` on `Laser-Game-Tests`) and a clean critics run on what changed.

A commit carries **code only**. No book text, no chapter file, no `pillar.conf` change. Never bundle
two subsections in one commit.

### Book files — Markdown under `doc/`

The book text is Markdown, one file per tutorial section: `doc/section1/section1.md` …
`doc/section6/section6.md`, with images in the sibling `figures/` directory. `doc/` is untracked so
far.

Text may be written as soon as the code it describes exists, and it is written by adapting the Pillar
chapters: same explanations, Markdown syntax instead of Pillar markup (`!`/`!!` become `#`/`##`,
`[[[ … ]]]` becomes a fenced ``​`` ``​`smalltalk ``​`` block, `''…''` becomes `*…*`, `""…""` becomes
`**…**`, `@@note` becomes a `>` blockquote, the page URLs become an HTML comment).
```

Section 5.5 - Reset (and a bug fix): Reset button, taller panel, counters at open

Page 188 of the 2007 tutorial.

Grid >> reset and GridTestCase >> testResetGrid came with the 2007 source
captured in Section 1 and have been green since; only the test's comment
is new. The page's stub-then-test-then-body has no counterpart here.

The GUI is page 188's makeResetButton and its third layout frame:
newResetButton, newResetRow, and a third addChild: at the head of
newButtonColumn, which reads from the top, so the original's row three is
child one. Reset is the first button the panel does not hold in an
instance variable: a tenth would trip ReExcessiveVariablesRule, so
resetRow reads the row from the column and resetButton the button from
the row, the way buttonRow and newGameRow already did.

A third row of buttons makes the panel taller than before, so
contentHeight is stated over the new buttonRowCount and answers 320 where
it answered 290; heightForGrid: takes the larger of board and panel, so
the demo game is 380@340 and the eight-by-ten board is unchanged at
530@520.

LaserGameElement >> reset is page 188's without activeCellLocation: nil
and initializeDirty, the two lines newGame dropped in Section 4.5 for the
same reasons: Bloc delivers the click, and every cell draws itself.

The page also fixes a bug of the original's, where a game just opened
shows zero mirrors because the counters are written only when a move is
handled. The port cannot have it: the panel's rebuild ends with
updateCounters. testAGameShowsItsCountsBeforeAnythingHappens says so, for
a fresh game and for one dealt by newGame, and passed the first time it
ran.

testNewGameButtonHasTheRowAboveTheOthers broke for the second section
running and now reads the rows by index - the button row last, the New
row directly before it - so a row added above cannot break it again.
testResetButtonHasTheTopRowToItself asserts the new row and the order of
all three.

236 tests pass.

I replace the 2007 `LaserGame` morph of pages 065 to 067, which held a `SketchMorph` over a board form and a white rectangle for the panel. I hold a `LaserGameBoardElement` and a `LaserGameControlPanelElement` instead, and I take my size from them, the panel width and the margin, the way the original''s `calculatedExtent` did. Page 139 puts the panel on the left, and page 140 fills me with the colour ramp of `LaserGameColors windowColorRamp`.

``​`
LaserGameElement openExample
LaserGameElement openStandardExample
LaserGameElement openRandomOfExtent: 12@12
``​`

From page 143 I also count the moves the player makes, and from page 146 I can start a new game on a randomized grid. Page 144 asks before quitting, which the original does with `#confirm:`; I lay a `LaserGameConfirmElement` over myself instead, since a Bloc element cannot wait for an answer.

I play on the grid I am given, of any size: page 147 splits the original''s `#initialize` into `#initializeForGrid:` for that, and `#on:` is the same split. The board is one element per location, the panel keeps its width and takes the height of the board, and my own size follows both, so nothing but the grid decides how big the game is.

Instance variables:
- `grid`: the grid played on. Setting it rebuilds what I hold.
- `board`: the `LaserGameBoardElement` showing that grid.
- `controlPanel`: the panel beside it, hold

'testBlankCellElement	"A blank cell is a square of the board background with a border and nothing inside.	The element is checked before any layout pass, so the size is read from the layout	constraints rather than from the extent, which stays zero until the element is laid out."	| grid element |	grid := Grid new.	element := (CellRenderer rendererFor: (grid at: 1 @ 1) grid: grid)		           newElement.	self		assert: element constraints horizontal resizer size		equals: CellRenderer cellExtent x.	self		assert: element constraints vertical resizer size		equals: CellRenderer cellExtent y.	self assert: element geometry class equals: BlRectangleGeometry.	self		assert: element background paint color		equals: LaserGameColors gameBoardBackgroundColor.	self assert: element border width equals: CellRenderer borderWidth.	self		assert: element border paint color		equals: LaserGameColors cellBorderColor.	"A blank cell draws nothing inside its border."	self assertEmpty: element children'

### Claude — 2026-09-29 01:47:04Z

Section 5.6 done. 238 tests pass, critics clean on `LaserGameElement` and `LaserGameElementTestCase`.

**Code:**
- `LaserGameElement`: instVar `laserHome` (sixth), `newLaserHome`, `newBoardColumn`, `laserHome` accessor; `initialize` drops bottom padding; `rebuild` builds the board column and gives the panel a bottom margin. Class-side `laserHomeExtent` = `CellRenderer cellExtent x @ gameMargin`.
- Original pins its `SketchMorph` to the window corner with a layout frame; port has no absolute frames and a linear layout places every child, so the band is made instead of pinned: board + mark in a vertical column, bottom margin moved from the game's padding to the panel and the column.
- Sizes unchanged — `extentForGrid:` untouched, demo 380@340, 8@10 530@520, mark laid out at `(120.0@510.0) corner: (170.0@520.0)`, exactly the original's offsets. Screenshot confirms the bar under the bottom-left cell.
- Tests: `testGameShowsWhereTheLaserComesFrom`, `testTheLaserHomeSitsInTheMarginAndCostsNoSize` new; `testGameHoldsABoardAndAControlPanel`, `testAnsweringNoLeavesTheGameAsItWas`, `testGameTakesTheExtentItCalculates` adjusted for the deeper tree.

**Doc:** chapter "Showing Laser Home Visually" appended to `doc/section5/section5.md` (274 lines). Verifier 607 identical, 0 mismatched; four superseded section4 blocks untagged with forward notes.

**Bookkeeping:** `PROJECT_MAP.md` reader position → end of `189.html`, `190.html` begins 5.7; tests 238; 5.6 row, doc counts, git row. Memory updated.

Commit message:

```
Section 5.6 - Showing Laser Home Visually: mark where the beam enters the board

Page 189 of the 2007 tutorial.

The beam has been drawn since Section 4.7 and appears at the bottom of the
first column out of nowhere. Page 189 marks the square it comes from: a bar
one cell wide and one margin tall, in the colour the beam splatters the
board with, under the bottom left cell. Grid >> startingCell has said where
that is since Section 1, and calculatePath gives the first element #south
as the side the beam enters by.

The original fills a Form, wraps it in a SketchMorph and pins it to the
bottom left corner of the window with a layout frame, one pixel in from the
left and two from the right to clear the outline it draws around its board.

The port has no absolute frames, and a linear layout places every child it
is given, so the band is made rather than pinned. newBoardColumn puts the
board and the mark in a vertical column; initialize drops the bottom
padding and rebuild gives the control panel a bottom margin instead, so the
column ends where the game ends and the mark fills the band between the
last row of cells and the bottom edge.

Every size is unchanged. extentForGrid: is untouched, the demo game is
380@340 and the eight-by-ten board 530@520, and the mark of the big board
is laid out at (120.0@510.0) corner: (170.0@520.0), which is the rectangle
the original's offsets describe.

LaserGameElement gains laserHome, its accessor, newLaserHome,
newBoardColumn and the class-side laserHomeExtent. Two new tests say what
the mark is and that it costs no size, the second measuring the board
column and repeating the game's own addition rather than laying anything
out. Three older tests read the board's column as the second child or
assert padding on the three sides that still have it. No model code
changed.

238 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

regionRectangle
	"CellClickRegionInside regionRectangle"
	| outer delta |
	outer := 0@0 extent: CellRenderer cellExtent.
	delta := CellRenderer cellExtent - CellRenderer insideRegionExtent.
	^outer insetBy: (delta // 2)

@@@ CellClickRegionOutside class >> #regionRectangle
regionRectangle
	"CellClickRegionOutside regionRectangle"
	| outer delta |
	outer := 0@0 extent: CellRenderer cellExtent.
	delta := CellRenderer cellExtent - CellRenderer outsideRegionExtent.
	^outer insetBy: (delta // 2)

@@@ CellClickRegionIgnore class >> #regionRectangle
regionRectangle
	^0@0 extent: CellRenderer cellExtent

@@@ CellClickRegion class >> #clickRegionForPoint:
clickRegionForPoint: aPoint
	"Answer the region of a cell aPoint falls in. My subclasses are tried innermost first, and the
	ignore region covers the whole cell, so any point within a cell finds one. A point outside the
	cell finds none, and is ignored: a click there can do nothing, which is what the ignore region
	already means. A mouse event carries such a point whenever the element under the pointer is
	larger than the cell the regions are computed from, and answering it here keeps the case out of
	every mouse handler."

	^self sortedSubclasses
		detect: [ :cls | cls regionRectangle containsPoint: aPoint ]
		ifNone: [ CellClickRegionIgnore ]

Goal: finish the original Squeak tutorial (pages `tut2007/html/049.html` onward) on Pharo 13, keeping the chapter-by-chapter explanation structure.

## Hard constraints, stated 2026-09-26 and 2026-09-27

1. **All code is written in the image.** No detached working copy. Never hand-edit `.class.st` Tonel files, never call `TonelWriter` or `fileOut`. Changes go through the MCP tools. If the image and the clone diverge, repair the image's Iceberg repository instead of patching files.

**tool — Bash**

```bash
cat > /home/me/.claude/projects/-home-me/memory/reference_pharo_class_creation_api.md <<'EOF'
---
name: reference-pharo-class-creation-api
description: Pharo 13 dropped subclass:instanceVariableNames:classVariableNames:package:; the fluid `<<` builder must be told to install
metadata:
  type: reference
---

In Pharo 13, `TestCase subclass: #Foo instanceVariableNames: '' classVariableNames: '' package: 'P'` fails with `Message not understood: TestCase class >> #subclass:instanceVariableNames:classVariableNames:package:` — that API is gone.

The fluid form `Superclass << #Foo` answers a `ShiftClassBuilder`, not a class. Sending `slots:`/`package:` only configures it; nothing exists in the image until `install` (or `fluidInstall`) is sent, and an expression that reads the result as a class fails with a confusing error instead. So:

```smalltalk
| b |
b := LaserGameTestCase << #CellRendererTestCase.
b slots: {}; package: 'Laser-Game-Tests'.
b install
```

Installing over an existing class keeps its methods, protocols and comment, which makes this the way to **reparent** a class: take `aClass definitionString`, swap the superclass, evaluate, `install`.

For a plain new class the `pharo` MCP `class_create` tool is simpler than either form.

Related: [[feedback-pharo-standards]], [[reference-pharo-critics-api]].
EOF
python3 - <<'PY'
p='/home/me/.claude/projects/-home-me/memory/MEMORY.md'
t=open(p,newline='').read()
line="- [Pharo class creation API](reference_pharo_class_creation_api.md) — `subclass:instanceVariableNames:...` gone in Pharo 13; `Super << #Name` gives a builder that needs `install`; install over an existing class to reparent it.\n"
a="- [Pharo critics API](reference_pharo_critics_api.md)"
i=t.index(a)
t=t[:i]+line+t[i:]
open(p,'w',newline='').write(t)
print('ok')
PY
```

**1. Why Iceberg says "modified" with empty diff**

`Laser-Game` is flagged dirty, content identical to HEAD. Cause: my new sweep tests call `withCellExtent:do:`, which recompiles `CellRenderer class >> cellExtent` and compiles the original source back in an `ensure:`. Recompiling identical source marks package dirty. Nothing to commit there. Clear with `wc markAllPackagesAsClean` (or `refreshDirtyPackages`).

**2. Real problem: test package tracked nowhere**

```
wc packages -> #('BaselineOfLaserGame' 'Laser-Game')

```

Section 5.4 moved 22 test classes out of `Laser-Game` into a new package `Laser-Game-Tests`. Commit `d6ac757` deleted their `.class.st` files from `src/Laser-Game/` and **never added `src/Laser-Game-Tests/`** — the new package was never added to the Iceberg working copy. So every test class, 23 of them now, lives only in the image. Sections 5.4, 5.5, 5.6 test edits and all of 5.7 are outside git. Image loss = 269 tests gone.

Fix, in image:

```smalltalk

```

Then Iceberg shows 23 new class files plus `package.st` under `src/Laser-Game-Tests/`, and the commit writes them.

Consequence to decide: that one commit carries the test work of 5.4 through 5.7 together, since the earlier ones never reached disk. Options — (a) run the add now and let the 5.7 commit carry all of it, message saying so; (b) run the add, commit the file addition alone as a repair commit, then commit 5.7 on top. Say which; I do not commit either way.

@@@ LaserGameShapes class >> #arrowElementFromPoints:ofExtent:
arrowElementFromPoints: anArrayOfPoints ofExtent: anExtent
	"Answer an element of anExtent whose geometry is the outline anArrayOfPoints describes. The
	outline is a polygon, so it is drawn at whatever size it is given and needs no flood fill:
	the original drew the outline line by line, filled the inside with black and reversed the
	form, which is what pages 081 and 082 spend their workspace code on."

	^ BlElement new
		  geometry: (BlPolygonGeometry vertices:
					   (self pointsOf: anArrayOfPoints scaledToExtent: anExtent));
		  extent: anExtent;
		  background: self arrowColor;
		  yourself

@@@ LaserGameShapes class >> #clockwiseArrowElementOfExtent:
clockwiseArrowElementOfExtent: anExtent
	"Answer an element drawing the clockwise rotate arrow at anExtent."

	^ self
		  arrowElementFromPoints: self clockwiseArrowPoints
		  ofExtent: anExtent

@@@ LaserGameShapes class >> #clockwiseArrowPoints
clockwiseArrowPoints
	"Answer the outline of the arrow that turns a mirror clockwise, which page 099 makes by
	flipping the other one horizontally."

	^ self counterClockwiseArrowPoints collect: [ :each |
		  each x negated @ each y ]

@@@ LaserGameShapes class >> #counterClockwiseArrowElementOfExtent:
counterClockwiseArrowElementOfExtent: anExtent
	"Answer an element drawing the anticlockwise rotate arrow at anExtent."

	^ self
		  arrowElementFromPoints: self counterClockwiseArrowPoints
		  ofExtent: anExtent

Extension { #name : 'Form' }

{ #category : '*Laser-Game' }
Form >> anyOfColor: aColor inColumn: int [
	| color |
	1 to: self height do: [:row |
		color := self colorAt: int@row.
		color = aColor ifTrue: [^true]].
	^false
]

{ #category : '*Laser-Game' }
Form >> anyOfColor: aColor inRow: int [
	| color |
	1 to: self width do: [:column |
		color := self colorAt: column@int.
		color = aColor ifTrue: [^true]].
	^false
]

{ #category : '*Laser-Game' }
Form >> firstColumnOfColorFromLeft: aColor [
	| x |
	x := 1.
	[self anyOfColor: aColor inColumn: x] whileFalse: [
		x := x + 1.
		x >= self width ifTrue: [^nil]].
	^x
]

{ #category : '*Laser-Game' }
Form >> firstColumnOfColorFromRight: aColor [
	| x |
	x := self width.
	[self anyOfColor: aColor inColumn: x] whileFalse: [
		x := x - 1.
		x <= 1 ifTrue: [^nil]].
	^x
]

{ #category : '*Laser-Game' }
Form >> firstRowOfColorFromBottom: aColor [
	| y |
	y := height.
	[self anyOfColor: aColor inRow: y] whileFalse: [
		y := y - 1.
		y <= 1 ifTrue: [^nil]].
	^y
]

{ #category : '*Laser-Game' }
Form >> firstRowOfColorFromTop: aColor [
	| y |
	y := 1.
	[self anyOfColor: aColor inRow: y] whileFalse: [
		y := y + 1.
		y >= self height ifTrue: [^nil]].
	^y
]

   - **Pharo 13 class creation:** `subclass:instanceVariableNames:classVariableNames:package:` is gone (DNU). `Superclass << #Name` answers a `ShiftClassBuilder`; `slots:`/`package:` only configure it — `install` is required. Installing over an existing class keeps methods, protocols and comment, so `definitionString` + swapped superclass + `install` is the way to **reparent**.
   - `compile_method` cannot target a metaclass; class-side methods go through `evaluate_pharo` with `Cls class compile: src classified: '...'` and LF→CR conversion.
   - New methods land in `as yet unclassified`; fix with `(cls >> #sel) protocol: 'name'`. `(m protocol) name` — `Protocol` is not indexable, so `protocol name`.
   - **Pharo builds an abstract `TestCase`'s suite out of its subclasses**, so reparenting to an abstract test case makes those subclasses run twice: 241 test methods reported as 269 runs.
   - Iceberg API that works: `wc packages`, `wc modifiedPackages`, `wc diffToReferenceCommit`, `wc addPackageNamed:`, `wc markAllPackagesAsClean`, `wc refreshDirtyPackages`. `diffToFileSystem` and `calculateDiffToRepository` are DNU on `IceWorkingCopy`.
   - Recompiling identical source (as `withCellExtent:do:` does in its `ensure:`) marks a package dirty with an empty diff.
   - Path mapping: shell `/home/me/workspace` == image `/home/renaud/devzone/sources/PharoLaserGameTutorial`.
   - Doc pipeline (cwd = repo): `python3 $S/collect_blocks.py` → `python3 $S/verify.py` → in-image `Smalltalk compiler evaluate: '<repo>/verify.st' asFileReference contents` → `python3 $S/compare.py`; then `rm -f verify.st tmp_verify.txt`.
   - Chapter generators parse `@@@ Cls >> #selector` dumps (CR→LF via `tr '\r' '\n'`); helpers `m(name)` (tagged smalltalk block), `old(text)` (untagged 2007 code), `snip(text)`. Docs use LF and straight ASCII apostrophes.
   - Untag scripts take `(path, line, note)` triples, search upward for '```smalltalk', apply edits in reverse line order.
   - Page text extraction: `python3 -c "import re,html; t=open('NNN.html',encoding='latin-1').read(); ... print(html.unescape(t).strip())"`.
   - Sizes read headlessly via `anElement constraints horizontal/vertical resizer size` (extent is 0 before layout); `measure: BlExtentMeasurementSpec unspecified` + `measuredExtent` where a measurement is needed; `forceLayout` forbidden in package code.

@@@ LaserGameShapes class >> #pointsOf:scaledToExtent:
pointsOf: anArrayOfPoints scaledToExtent: anExtent
	"Answer anArrayOfPoints moved to the origin and stretched to fill anExtent exactly. The
	vertex arrays are written at the size the original drew them at, around 260 pixels, and every
	user asks for the size it needs. The original could not do this: it drew one 330 pixel bitmap
	per arrow, cached it, and scaled the pixels afterwards."

	| bounds scale |
	bounds := Rectangle encompassing: anArrayOfPoints.
	scale := anExtent x / bounds width @ (anExtent y / bounds height).
	^ anArrayOfPoints collect: [ :each |
		  ((each - bounds origin) * scale) asFloatPoint ]
@@@ CellRenderer class >> #hintArrowExtent
hintArrowExtent
	"Answer the size a hint arrow is drawn at: a couple of pixels smaller than a cell, which is
	the size page 094 scales its arrow form to."

	^ self cellExtent - 2
@@@ CellRenderer class >> #hintArrowOffset
hintArrowOffset
	"Answer where a hint arrow sits within its cell: centred, as page 094 computes it from the
	two extents."

	^ (self cellExtent - self hintArrowExtent) // 2
@@@ CellRenderer class >> #cellExtent

**Tests** (3 new, 244 methods, 273 runs, all green; critics clean on every class touched)

- `CellRendererTestCase >> testTheHintArrowIsCentredInItsCellAtEveryCellSize`
- `LaserGameCellElementTestCase >> testTheHintArrowSitsCentredInTheCellAtEveryCellSize` — hovers real mirror cell at 30/40/80 px, measures margins.
- `withCellExtent:do:` moved to `LaserGameTestCase class`; instance method passes it on, so a test case outside that hierarchy sweeps sizes without reparenting (avoids more 5.7 double counting).

**Text** (uncommitted, as always): 304-line chapter *Better Hint Arrows Alignment* in `doc/section5/section5.md`; two superseded blocks untagged with forward notes (`section4.md` `initializeCachedForms`, `section5.md` instance-side `withCellExtent:do:`); block checker 625 identical, 0 mismatched. `PROJECT_MAP.md` and memory updated; reader position now end of `199.html`, `200.html` begins 5.9 Minor Cosmetic Tweaks.

Commit message:

```
Section 5.8 - Better Hint Arrows Alignment: delete LaserGameForms and the Form extension, prove the arrows are centred

The original's hint arrows sit off-centre because each arrow was drawn
into a white Form big enough to hold it and cached as it fell. Page 197
adds seven Form extension methods that scan the bitmap for the ink, page
198 trims the cached form with them and recentres what is left, page 199
looks at the result.

This port has no margin to trim: an arrow is a polygon whose points are
scaled onto the rectangle asked for, so its ink is that rectangle, and
CellRenderer class >> hintArrowExtent and hintArrowOffset have centred it
in its cell since Section 3.6.

The seven Form methods and LaserGameForms were still in the image from
the Section 1 capture, unreachable since the beam masks went at 4.7:
tightRectangleAroundColor: was sent by arrowFormFromPointsArray: alone,
and LaserGameForms was named by its own initialize alone. Both are
deleted here rather than ported, as the port's second rule requires.
Laser-Game is 47 classes now and Form carries no extension of ours.

Three tests state what the original checks by eye:

  LaserGameShapesTestCase >> testEveryArrowFillsTheRectangleItIsGiven
  CellRendererTestCase >> testTheHintArrowIsCentredInItsCellAtEveryCellSize
  LaserGameCellElementTestCase >> testTheHintArrowSitsCentredInTheCellAtEveryCellSize

The last of these hovers a real mirror cell at 30, 40 and 80 pixel cells
and measures the space left around the arrow it shows. It needs the cell
size sweep of 5.7 without being a LaserGameTestCase, so withCellExtent:do:
moved to the class side and the instance method passes it on.

244 test methods, all green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

	"Answer the height, in pixels, of everything I hold: my counters, stacked with a gap between
	them and a gap above and below, and under them the divider bar and the rows of buttons,
	spaced the same way. A counter takes the size of its caption, so one is built and measured;

	places its counters at fixed offsets from the top of a panel that is always taller than they

in the original's grey; Alexandrie draws it under the element, so the
board keeps the size its cells give it. The bar is newPanelDivider, five
pixels tall and a gap in from each edge, filled with the original's
gradient. It is the first child of the column of button rows rather than
a morph hung off the bottom edge of the panel at an offset of -105, so a
further row of buttons could never run into it. The panel counts the new
cell in contentHeight: 320 becomes 335, and a game on the demo board 380

# Introduction

An activity I enjoy is writing simple games in Pharo. I also enjoy sharing this powerful development environment with interested developers. This is one of the reasons I write these tutorials.

For this development example I'd like to try something different and take the student through the process of writing a game in Pharo. Proceed linearly through the example. The development process described here will be very specific to the way I work. Consequently, you will see how I encourage organization of files and other processes as part of Pharo development. In a very real way, Smalltalk development is a personal expression.

Let's assume the student has downloaded Pharo and has some understanding of the Smalltalk programming language.

The user may also click on a mirror cell and cause it to slide 1 grid-cell in a vertical or horizontal direction. Note that a mirror cell cannot move through the grid walls nor through another mirror cell nor the target cell. In this way the user can adjust the mirror cells to get a desired result.

Since, initially, this is a solitaire game, it becomes more interesting to have the user manipulate the mirrors to stil have the laser complete its path by hitting the target but also by finding the longest path possible.

For example, the user could move the mirror cell shown, one cell to its left and cause the laser to take an alternate path.

! Discovery of Objects

% http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/009.html

When we look over the game drawings and think about what objects our game may need, a few come immediately to mind. There must be some kind of Grid and several Cells. There are different kinds of Cells too.

Cells and a Grid are obvious objects of the game and we'll probably discover other objects as we explore a little. It's perfectly fine to explore and then throw code away if we later learn we're not heading in the right direction.

Exploring with objects is easy to do with Pharo. We very much enjoy spending time thinking about designs but we've also learned you need to ''dive in'' sometimes to better understand the objects needed in your design.

As we once heard someone say, ''You can read about swimming all you want. But, you'll never learn about swimming until you actually dive in the water.''

Of course we believe the water here is safe. The worst we could do is write some code and throw it away. And that's nothing to worry about. A per method version history in maintained for you to quickly review and restore previous code.  Development in Pharo encourages experimentation and quick idea exploration.

Let's have a look at the objects.

!! Grid

The Grid holds our Cells. It also contains the source of our laser beam. Let's go with the idea that the user will ask the Grid to fire our laser beam.

! Test Driven Development

% http://squeak.preeminent.org/tut2007/html/011.html

We will use the SUnit unit testing framework to implement the game model (have a look at the Pharo by Example SUnit Chapter for a deeper discussion). More than likely we'll not concern ourselves with writing unit tests for the actual behavior of the GUI because it is tedious. But there's plenty we can accomplish by unit test driving our development of the game model.

We are not too attached to how we code the very first few lines of code. An approach we've seen used by many people is to begin with the Unit Tests, even to the point of not having any objects to test before the first test is written. Another approach is to implement some basic model and then drive from that point forward using Unit Tests.

Now what is important to understand is that Unit tests accomplish several things:

- They help us to develop our objects because creating tests to exercise an object's api makes us consider how our objects will be used.
- They provide a consistency check as we continue to add and evolve code. This helps us to quickly identify when and where we break existing code, which is a tremendous help to stay on track.

Good unit tests capture your requirements and help you as you implement design. Often, when you write a unit test you are forced to think about your design as if it were finished.
